sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Part One of this study ended with the Son who gives life: the man who hears Him and believes has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life. Now John shows you what that life feeds on and what it sees by. He starts with a boy’s lunch on a hillside.

The dust is good at arithmetic. It counts what is in your hands, counts what is in front of you, and gives you the answer before God has said a word. Not enough money for the note on the land. Not enough patience for the boy who won’t listen. Not enough left in you for the wife who needs more than you have been giving. And once the dust has done the math, it tells you the rest: God works with what a man brings, so a small man gets a small God.

That lie sounds like humility. It is unbelief in work clothes, and it has fooled a lot of good men. It keeps you from praying about the thing that matters most, because the thing that matters most is bigger than your supply, and you have quietly decided your supply is the ceiling. So you hold the little you have, you hold it tight, and you call it being realistic. You stop asking. You stop giving. You stop expecting God to do anything you could not have done yourself.

A man who lives that way long enough ends up face-down in his own sums, saying what the psalmist said with his mouth in the dirt: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The reviving word in John 6 is not a promise that your supply will grow. It is a Man taking five loaves into His own hands and giving thanks over them.

sections.heading: A Hillside at Passover
pulls: The dust counts what is in your hands and calls the total your ceiling. John 6 puts five barley loaves in the hands of Christ, and the only number that matters after that is twelve baskets left over.
paras: John tells you the season before he tells you the sign. Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand. The last Passover John named, Jesus threw the money-changers out of the temple. The last one in this Gospel is the one where the Lamb of God is killed. Between them stands this hillside, where the Lord feeds a multitude with bread broken in His own hands.

Read all of John 6 in one sitting before you start the week. The feeding, the storm, the long argument in the synagogue at Capernaum, the crowd walking away — it is one chapter with one subject: who this Man is, and what a soul lives on. John wrote these signs down that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name. The loaves point past themselves to the hands they were in. Keep your eyes on those hands all week.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: A TEST HE ALREADY KNEW
paras: A great multitude followed him, because they saw his signs which he did on those who were sick. Mark the reason. They came for what He did. John will spend the rest of this chapter showing how far a man can follow Jesus for His works without believing in Him. But first the Lord sits down on the mountain with His disciples, lifts His eyes, and sees the crowd coming.

Then He asks Philip, Where are we to buy bread, that these may eat? John lets you in on what Philip did not know: He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do. Jesus was never short a plan. The question was not for His information. It was for Philip — to bring up into the light what Philip leaned on when the need outran the money.

Philip answers like an honest man with a pencil behind his ear. Two hundred denarii worth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may receive a little. He is not wrong. He has counted heads and counted cost, and the numbers do not close. That is the trouble. His answer is all arithmetic and no Christ. He is standing next to the One through whom all things were made, and he is figuring wages.

You have done the same. The bill comes, the scan comes back, your son calls from the county jail, and you go straight to the numbers. The numbers are real. But a test from this Lord is never a trap. He already knows what He will do. He asks so you will find out what you were leaning on, and so that when the bread comes you will know exactly where it came from.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: WHAT ARE THESE AMONG SO MANY
paras: Andrew does a little better. At least he brings something. There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many? Half that sentence is faith and half is doubt, and both halves are honest. He found the food. He could not see what good it would do.

Look at what is on the table. A boy. Barley loaves. Two fish. Nothing in that list is impressive, and John does not dress it up. The Lord does not wait for a better offering or send for a bigger one. He takes what is there. The miracle does not begin when the supply grows. It begins when the supply is handed to Him. Once before, God fed a hundred men from twenty barley loaves through Elisha, and they ate, and had some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). Here the loaves are fewer, the crowd is far bigger, and the One holding the bread is greater than any prophet.

Then comes the order: Have the people sit down. John adds a detail you would not expect. Now there was much grass in that place. A man who knows the Psalms hears it — He makes me lie down in green pastures. Before there is a crumb to eat, the men sat down, in number about five thousand.

Sitting is a strange thing to ask of hungry men. It means you stop scrambling. It means you are no longer the one in charge of getting fed. That is where every man starts with Christ: down on the grass, empty-handed, waiting on what He will give. Before He fills a man, He settles him.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: HE GAVE THANKS AND GAVE
pulls: He gave thanks for five loaves before anything had happened. The Son lifted the little to the Father, and it fed thousands with twelve baskets to spare. What you put in His hands is never measured by what it was.
paras: Here is the key verse of the week. Jesus took the loaves; and having given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were sitting down; likewise also of the fish as much as they desired. Watch His hands. He takes. He gives thanks. He gives out. The thanks comes before anything has multiplied. The Son lifts five loaves to the Father, and from that moment they are enough.

As much as they desired. Not a taste, not a ration. John does not tell you how the bread grew. He tells you the people ate until they were full. He does not ration bread to men He half trusts. He feeds them until they push the plate away. The God who rained bread on Israel in the wilderness is standing on a Galilean hillside in a body, breaking it with His own hands.

Then comes the part men skip. Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost. The scraps fill twelve baskets. There is more after the meal than there was before it, and Jesus will not let a crumb go to waste. Hold on to that. Before this chapter ends He will speak of losing nothing again, about something far more precious than bread.

The crowd sees the sign and gets it half right: This is truly the prophet who comes into the world. Then they get it wrong. They are about to come and take him by force to make him king. They want a King who keeps the bread coming. He withdrew again to the mountain by himself. He did not come to be a free lunch with a crown on it. He came to give Himself, and the crowd was not ready to hear that yet.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: IT IS I IN THE DARK
paras: Evening comes. The disciples go down to the water and push off for Capernaum. John gives three short facts every man knows from the inside. It was now dark, and Jesus had not come to them. The sea was tossed by a great wind blowing. And they rowed, about twenty-five or thirty stadia, a long way out with nothing to show for it.

Notice who is in that boat. The same men who carried baskets of bread off the hill that afternoon are now soaked, alone, after dark. A full stomach at noon does not keep the wind down after dark. You can be exactly where the Lord’s men belong and still be pulling against a headwind at midnight. Men who have just seen a miracle still get afraid.

Then they saw Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing near to the boat; and they were afraid. The water that was beating them was a floor under His feet. Job said of God that He alone stretches out the heavens, and treads on the waves of the sea. John does not explain it. He sets it beside the loaves and lets you see it: the hands that broke the bread made the sea.

It is I. Don’t be afraid. He does not scold them for their fear. He gives them Himself. In John’s Greek those first words are egō eimi, the same two He will use when He says I am the bread of life. Then the ending comes in a breath. They were willing therefore to receive him into the boat. Immediately the boat was at the land where they were going. All night at the oars, and the shore came the moment Christ was aboard.

stations.verse: There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?
stations.question: John says Jesus himself knew what he would do before Andrew ever found the boy with his loaves; what changes in how I bring my little to Christ if He is never scrambling over my shortage?
body: Paidarion is the small form of pais: a little boy, a lad. In later everyday Greek it could lose some of that smallness and mean simply a young fellow. Either way, he is nobody of standing. This is the only verse in the New Testament where the word is found.

John gives the boy no name, no speech, and no reward. He is in the story for one reason: he had something, and it ended up in the hands of Jesus. Andrew’s question, what are these among so many?, was about the food. It could as easily have been asked about the boy. Christ was troubled by neither.

The dust wants you to wait until you are bigger before you bring anything — older, cleaner, better stocked. Paidarion says the Lord fed five thousand men from the lunch of a lad no one bothered to name. He is short of nothing. What He takes, He blesses, and what He blesses feeds more than you can count.
stations.live: Name one thing you have held back because it looked too small — an hour, a skill, a few dollars, a word to your son. Give it away this week without measuring it first: ‘It is small. He is not.’

stations.verse: There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?
stations.question: Andrew named the five barley loaves and two fish and in the same breath doubted they could feed so many; what need have I stopped praying about because I have already decided what I hold cannot touch it?
body: Krithinos means made of barley. It is formed from krithē, and in the Greek Old Testament it stands for the Hebrew word for barley. In the New Testament it shows up in just two verses, both in this chapter: the boy’s loaves in verse 9 and the leftovers in verse 13.

John names the grain twice, as if he wants you to remember what kind of bread it was. Plain bread, the kind a field gives without ceremony. The same barley that went into Christ’s hands came back out filling twelve baskets. Nothing about the grain changed. The hands made the difference. It went in as barley and came back as barley, enough to feed a hillside.

The dust tells you the plain stuff of your life is beneath God’s notice — the night shift, the fuel bill, the long marriage with no shine on it. Krithinos answers that the Son of God gave thanks over barley. Plain things are not shut out of grace.
stations.live: Pick one ordinary duty you have treated as unspiritual — the shift, the bills, the dishes. Before you start it each day this week, give thanks over it the way Christ gave thanks over barley.

stations.verse: When they were filled, he said to his disciples, “Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost.
stations.question: Jesus fed the crowd until they were filled, then said, Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost; what part of my life have I decided He would let fall in the grass?
body: Klasma comes from the verb klaō and means a broken piece, a fragment. Every one of its nine New Testament verses has to do with Jesus feeding the crowds. It is a word for leftovers, and the Gospels keep careful count of them.

Jesus could have let the scraps lie in the grass. Instead He said, Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost. Later He made the disciples say the number out loud: how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up? The fragments were evidence. They told the truth about how much He had given, and He wanted it remembered.

The dust says broken is the same as finished — the friendship that cracked, the years you wasted, the man you were at thirty. Klasma says Christ gathers broken pieces on purpose. In His hands they are not trash. They are proof of how much was given.
stations.live: Write down one broken piece of your past you have written off. Bring it to Christ by name in prayer each day this week and ask Him to gather it: ‘Let nothing be lost.’

stations.verse: So they gathered them up, and filled twelve baskets with broken pieces from the five barley loaves, which were left over by those who had eaten.
stations.question: From five barley loaves the disciples carried away twelve baskets of leftovers, more than they started with; where am I treating Christ’s giving as barely enough when He has given more than I have used?
stations.gloss: a basket; a carrying basket for food
body: Kophinos is a basket, most likely woven of wicker, the kind carried for food. It appears in six New Testament verses, and every one of them looks at the same afternoon: the baskets filled after Christ fed the five thousand.

Twelve of them came back full, after everyone had eaten. Christ did not make just enough. He made more than enough, and He had His disciples carry it off the hill in their own arms. Later, when they fretted over forgetting bread, He asked them, Don’t you yet perceive, neither remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you took up?

The dust has a short memory for provision and a long memory for lack. It will remind you of every time you came up short and forget every time you were carried. Kophinos is a word for remembering. The baskets were full, and the Lord told His men not to forget them.
stations.live: Write down five times God supplied more than you needed. Keep the list in your lunch pail this week, add to it as you remember more, and read it the next time the numbers do not close.

stations.verse: When therefore they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing near to the boat; and they were afraid.
stations.question: The disciples had rowed hard into the night when they saw Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing near to the boat; what storm am I still fighting alone because I have not looked for Him coming across it?
body: Elaunō means to drive. The New Testament uses it of wind driving ships and clouds, of sailors rowing a boat, and once of a demon driving a man into the desert. Five New Testament verses use it. Here it names the hard work of men pulling against the weather.

The disciples drove that boat twenty-five or thirty stadia through the dark while the wind drove back at them. Mark says Jesus saw them distressed in rowing, for the wind was contrary to them. Then He came to them on the same water they were fighting. They rowed. He walked. What was against them was under Him.

The dust tells you everything rides on your arms: pull harder or go under. Elaunō shows you men doing all they could and getting nowhere until He came. The shore was not reached by better rowing. It was reached when they took Him into the boat, and it came all at once.
stations.live: Name the place you have been rowing alone. Each morning this week, before you pick up the oars again, stop, look for Him, and pray: ‘It is You. I will not be afraid.’

practices.title: BRING THE SMALL THING
practices.body: Andrew brought five loaves and two fish and apologized for them in the same breath. Bring yours without the apology. Pick one thing you have held back as too small to matter — an hour on Saturday, a tool you could lend, a word you owe your wife — and name it to Christ in prayer. Then give it. Do not measure what comes of it. Measuring was never your job. The boy never saw the count of the baskets, and he did not need to.

practices.title: GIVE THANKS BEFORE THE BREAD GROWS
practices.body: Jesus gave thanks over five loaves, not over five thousand fed. At every meal this week, before you eat, stop and give thanks out loud for what is in front of you, even if it is a gas station sandwich eaten in the cab. Thank the Father for it as it is, not as you wish it were. Then thank Him for His Son, who fed a multitude from almost nothing. Let your thanks run ahead of the supply.

practices.title: SIT DOWN ON THE GRASS
practices.body: The first thing Christ told the hungry crowd was to sit. Choose one morning this week to sit before you scramble — fifteen minutes before the phone, before the news, before the list. Read John 6:1–21 out loud. Ask for nothing until you have read it all. Let your morning take the order of the hillside: He feeds, and you receive. When the fifteen minutes are up, give thanks for one thing in the passage before you stand.

practices.title: GATHER THE FRAGMENTS
practices.body: Christ would not let the broken pieces be lost. Write down one broken thing you have given up on — a friendship gone cold, a brother you no longer call, a calling you walked away from. Pray over it by name every day this week. If there is a phone call to make or a letter to write, make it by Saturday, even if the words come out rough. Leave what comes of it with Him. He gathers what you cannot.

practices.title: TAKE HIM INTO THE BOAT
practices.body: The disciples rowed half the night and got nowhere until they took Christ into the boat. Name the storm you have been fighting with your own arms — the debt, the temper, the bottle, the dread. Tell one brother in Christ about it this week and ask him to pray with you. Do not wait until the storm is over to say it. Each time the wind picks up, say His words back to yourself: ‘It is I. Don’t be afraid.’

title: Five Loaves and Two Fish
subtitle: from dust to a hand that feeds thousands
keyVerse: Jesus took the loaves; and having given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were sitting down; likewise also of the fish as much as they desired.

passage.text: After these things, Jesus went away to the other side of the sea of Galilee, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias.
A great multitude followed him, because they saw his signs which he did on those who were sick.
Jesus went up into the mountain, and he sat there with his disciples.
Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.
Jesus therefore lifting up his eyes, and seeing that a great multitude was coming to him, said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, that these may eat?”
He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do.
Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may receive a little.”
One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,
“There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?”
Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in that place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand.
Jesus took the loaves; and having given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were sitting down; likewise also of the fish as much as they desired.
When they were filled, he said to his disciples, “Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost.”
So they gathered them up, and filled twelve baskets with broken pieces from the five barley loaves, which were left over by those who had eaten.
When therefore the people saw the sign which Jesus did, they said, “This is truly the prophet who comes into the world.”
Jesus therefore, perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea.
They entered into the boat, and were going over the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not come to them.
The sea was tossed by a great wind blowing.
When therefore they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing near to the boat; and they were afraid.
But he said to them, “It is I. Don’t be afraid.”
They were willing therefore to receive him into the boat. Immediately the boat was at the land where they were going.

stationsIntro: Five small words from this chapter: a boy, barley, scraps, a basket, an oar pulled against the wind. Read each verse slowly, answer the question straight, and let the small words show you a large Christ.
lifeIntro: The Son of God took a boy’s lunch, gave thanks for it, and fed five thousand men until they were full. That same night He walked across the wind to men who were losing to it. Each practice below starts from what He did on that hillside and on that water, and asks you only to receive it and answer it this week.
lifePulls: Christ never asked the boy for more than he had. He took five barley loaves, gave thanks, and fed a hillside. He asks for what is in your hands, not for what you wish were there.
prayer: Father, You fed Your people bread in the wilderness, and Your Son fed five thousand on a hillside. I come with little in my hands, and I have been ashamed of how little it is. Take what I have — my time, my strength, my plain work — and do with it what only You can do. Teach me to give thanks before I see the supply grow, and to trust You when it does not. Gather up the broken pieces of my life, and let nothing be lost. When I am rowing in the dark and the wind is against me, let me hear Christ say, It is I. Make me willing to take Him into the boat. Thank You that He walked across the water to men who could not reach Him. Keep me from wanting a King who only fills my stomach, and make me hungry for Him. In Jesus’ name, amen.

bottomLine: A boy had five barley loaves and two fish. Philip counted the cost and came up short. Andrew found the food and doubted it. Jesus took it, gave thanks, and fed five thousand men until they were full, with twelve baskets left over. That night He walked across the wind to men losing at the oars. The dust says your supply is your ceiling. Put what you have in His hands, and take Him into the boat.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and look at His hands. Look at the hands that took five barley loaves from a lad no one bothered to name. Look at the hands that held them up while the Son gave thanks to His Father. Look at the hands that broke and gave and kept on giving until five thousand men were full and there was more bread on the grass than there had been at the start. Those hands have not shrunk since that afternoon.

The dust has been doing your arithmetic for you. It counted your money and your strength and your patience, and then it told you what was possible. But the Lord who tested Philip already knew what He would do. He was never waiting on your total. He asks what you have so that you will see who He is, and He gives thanks over it before you can see any change. The miracle was never in the size of the boy’s basket. It was in the One who took it, and He is the same One who sits at the right hand of the Father now.

And when night comes — it will — and the wind is against you, and you have rowed farther than you have strength for, He is not on the mountain looking the other way. He is walking on the very water that is beating you. He sees you straining. He comes near. He does not wait for you to reach the shore on your own and then meet you there. He walks out to where you are. And His first word is not a rebuke. It is Himself and His peace: It is I. Don’t be afraid.

So hold this on Tuesday, when the bill is bigger than the check. Christ took the little, gave thanks, and fed a multitude. Christ had His men gather the broken pieces that nothing be lost. Christ came across the dark water to men who could not reach Him, and when they took Him into the boat, they were at the shore. He is the same Lord this morning. Put what you have in His hands. He will give thanks over it. He will not run short, and He will not lose you.
closingVerse: Jesus took the loaves; and having given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were sitting down; likewise also of the fish as much as they desired.
carry: Jesus took five loaves, gave thanks, and fed them as much as they desired; what are you holding back from His hands this week because you counted it first and found it too small?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust teaches a man to live on wages. You learned it early. Work and you eat. Quit and you go hungry. Nothing is free, and anybody who says otherwise is selling something. That rule has kept a lot of families fed, and it is true as far as it goes. It just does not reach as far as your soul.

The dust carries that rule straight into your dealings with God. Now He is the foreman and grace is a paycheck. Pray more, give more, clean up your mouth, and maybe He keeps you on. And the hunger never quits, because no man can work enough to fill a soul made for God. You eat and are hungry again by evening. You catch up and are behind again by Monday. So you keep a quiet tally — the Sunday you skipped, the money you held back, the temper you lost in front of the kids — and you never once feel paid up.

There is a second lie tucked inside the first. It says that even when you come to Jesus, you come for what He can do for you — the better job, the healed back, the quiet house. Christ is the means and the bread is the point. That is exactly why the crowd crossed the lake in John 6. They were not wrong to want bread. They were wrong to want only bread, and to want Jesus for the sake of it.

When a man finally sees how hungry all that work has left him, he has come down to where the psalmist lay: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The word that revives in this passage is short enough to carry in your shirt pocket. I am the bread of life. Not a wage. A Person, given.

sections.heading: The Morning After the Miracle
pulls: The dust says grace is a paycheck and God is the foreman. Christ says the work God asks is to believe in the One He sent — and the bread you could never earn is standing in front of you.
paras: John 6:22–40 picks up the day after the hillside. The crowd wakes to find Jesus gone. They know He did not leave in the boat with His disciples. So they take boats from Tiberias, cross to Capernaum, and come seeking Jesus. On the surface it looks like hunger for God. Jesus will show them it is hunger for bread. He does it without flattering them and without sending them away.

What follows is less a sermon than an argument, the crowd asking and Jesus answering. They ask about timing, then about work, then about signs, then about Moses. Each time He turns the talk from what they want to who He is. In chapter 4 He offered a woman living water. Here He offers a crowd bread from heaven. Same Lord, same offer: what you need, He is. Read verses 22–40 straight through before you begin, and listen for how many times the word give comes up, and who is doing the giving.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: WHY YOU CAME LOOKING
paras: They find Him on the far shore and open with small talk: Rabbi, when did you come here? Jesus does not answer that question. He answers the one underneath it, the one they never asked out loud. Most certainly I tell you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves, and were filled.

That is a hard word, and a mercy. They had crossed a lake for Him. They had gone to real trouble. But the sign had pointed at Christ and they had looked at the bread. They saw a Man who could feed them, and they wanted to be fed again. He was a meal ticket, and they had come to punch it.

Then the turn. Don’t work for the food which perishes, but for the food which remains to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. Think about the food that perishes. You set a table, clear it, and set it again tomorrow. You fill the pantry and it empties. You earn, spend, and earn again. None of that is sin. But if that is all you labor for, you will die hungry with a full freezer.

Look closely at the sentence. He says work for the food that remains, and in the same breath says the Son of Man will give it. It is labor for a gift, which means the only labor is to come and receive. For God the Father has sealed him. The Father has set His mark on the Son. The bread is approved, stamped, and offered. You do not have to inspect it before you eat. The Father already has.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE ONE WORK GOD ASKS
paras: The crowd hears the word work and leans in. Here at last is something they understand. What must we do, that we may work the works of God? Hand them a list. Tell them the hours. A man would rather be handed a long list than be told the list is already finished.

Jesus answers in one line. This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent. They asked about works, plural. He answers with work, singular. And the one work is no work in their sense at all. It is to believe — to quit leaning on yourself and put your whole weight on the One the Father sent.

Here is the gospel in a sentence, said in the language of the wage-earner. God does not hire you. He gives you His Son and calls you to trust Him. Paul says it this way: to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness. Faith is not one more task on the list. It is the empty hand that takes the bread.

Christ calls believing the work of God. It is the work God asks of you, and before the chapter is done Jesus will show you it is also the work God does in you (6:37, 44). You did not find your way to the table. You were brought. So you can come with empty hands and not be ashamed of them. A man who thinks his faith is his own wages will soon start counting it. A man who knows it was given will just keep eating.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: NOT MOSES, BUT MY FATHER
pulls: The manna fed bodies for a day and spoiled if a man tried to keep it. The bread the Father gives came down from heaven in a body, and whoever comes to Him will never go hungry.
paras: What then do you do for a sign, that we may see and believe you? The men asking this ate miracle bread the day before. Still they want more. And they name their price: Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness. In the wilderness the manna came every morning for forty years. Five thousand men on one afternoon looks thin beside that. Beat Moses, they say, and then they will believe.

Jesus corrects them twice in one breath. It wasn’t Moses who gave you the bread out of heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread out of heaven. First, the giver was never Moses. It was God. Second, the manna was not the true bread. It was a sign, like the loaves, pointing ahead to something it could not be. It fed bodies for a day, and when men tried to keep it overnight it bred worms and became foul.

For the bread of God is that which comes down out of heaven, and gives life to the world. The true bread does what manna never could. It does not keep a body going one more day. It gives life, and it gives it to the world, not to one nation in one desert. The Father is still the giver. But the gift no longer lies on the ground at dawn. It is Someone who came down, and you do not gather Him. You receive Him.

They answer, Lord, always give us this bread. It sounds like faith. It is still a request for a supply — bread on a standing order. They have not yet seen that the bread is a Man. A lot of men pray that way for years — give me this, keep it coming — and never once ask for the Giver.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: NONE OF HIS WILL BE LOST
paras: Then He says it plainly. I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty. Not I have bread, but I am bread. Coming and believing are one act said two ways, and the promise on the far side of it is whole. No hunger left over. No thirst saved for later. The man who has Christ has bread for every day he has left.

Then the hard truth: you have seen me, and yet you don’t believe. Seeing is not enough. A man can watch bread multiply and walk away hungry. So Jesus tells them where believing comes from. All those whom the Father gives me will come to me. The Father gives. The given come. Nothing in that sentence is left to chance.

And in the same verse, the open door: He who comes to me I will in no way throw out. The Father’s giving shuts out no one who comes. It is the reason anyone comes at all. And the invitation is real: whoever comes. If you come, you were given — and you will not be thrown out, not for the old sin, not for the slow faith, not for the bad year.

Then the Father’s will, said twice. The Son is to lose nothing of all the Father has given Him, but should raise him up at the last day. And everyone who sees the Son, and believes in him, should have eternal life. Life now, held in the hand today. A raised body then. The Christ who would not let a crumb be lost on the hillside will not lose one of His own. He keeps them through the long middle of life, and He keeps them through death itself.

stations.verse: Don’t work for the food which perishes, but for the food which remains to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For God the Father has sealed him.
stations.question: The crowd crossed the lake because they ate of the loaves, and were filled, and Jesus pointed them to food which the Son of Man will give; what do I keep coming to Jesus for that is smaller than Jesus Himself?
body: Brōsis means eating, and then food — the thing eaten. John uses it for the food Jesus gives and for the food He Himself lived on. Matthew uses the same word for the rust that eats away a stored treasure.

That second use deserves a slow look. The word for what you eat is also the word for what eats your things. Jesus warns of treasure laid up on the earth, where moth and rust consume. Everything stored here gets eaten in the end. In John 6:27 He offers a different brōsis, the food which remains to eternal life — food that does not spoil and is not eaten away.

The dust says a full barn and a paid-off note are as good as it gets. Brōsis says the barn is being eaten while you sleep. The food that lasts is a gift from the Son of Man, and the Father has set His seal on Him.
stations.live: Write down the three things that take most of your working hours. Next to each, write what will be left of it in a hundred years. Then thank Christ by name for the food that remains, and ask Him to keep you hungry for it.

stations.verse: Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.
stations.question: Asked what works God wants, Jesus answered, This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent; what am I still adding to that answer, as if believing in Christ were not enough?
stations.gloss: work; a deed; a task given
body: Ergon is the plain word for work: a task, a deed, a thing done or made. It is one of the busiest words in the New Testament, turning up in 157 verses. John uses it often for the works of God and of Christ.

The crowd asked for works, a list they could keep. Jesus gave them one: that you believe in him whom he has sent. Then look whose work gets done. Christ said His food was to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work. At the end He told the Father, I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do. The work that saves was His, and He finished it.

The dust wants a job description — more prayer, more giving, cleaner habits — so you can grade yourself. Ergon in John 6:29 hands you no list. It points you to the Son who did the work and calls you to rest your weight on Him.
stations.live: Each time this week you catch yourself trying to earn God’s favor — after a good day or a bad one — stop and say it plainly: ‘The work is to believe in Him. He finished the rest.’

stations.verse: Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness. As it is written, ‘He gave them bread out of heaven to eat.’
stations.question: Men who had eaten Jesus’ bread the day before held up the manna as the bar He must clear before they would believe; what am I demanding of God before I will rest on the Son He has already given?
stations.gloss: manna; the bread God gave from heaven
body: Manna is a Hebrew and Aramaic name carried into Greek unchanged; it takes no Greek endings. It names the bread God gave Israel in the wilderness. The New Testament has it in four verses: twice in John 6, once of the golden pot kept in the ark, and once of the hidden manna Christ promises to the one who overcomes.

When the bread first lay on the ground, Israel did not know what it was. Moses told them, It is the bread which Yahweh has given you to eat. Every morning it was there, and every morning it was gift. Yet the men in John 6 used the manna as a bargaining chip: Moses did that, so what will you do? They had turned a gift into a yardstick for testing God.
The dust remembers past mercy only to demand more of it. Manna in Christ’s mouth points past the wilderness. The Father who gave bread on the ground has now given the true bread out of heaven.
stations.live: Name one past provision you have used as a measuring stick for God. This week, thank Him for it as a gift, and then thank Him for the Son, the true bread out of heaven.

stations.verse: Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.
stations.question: The crowd asked, Lord, always give us this bread, and Jesus answered, I am the bread of life; where am I asking Him for a steady supply while keeping my distance from Him?
body: Artos is bread, a loaf, and by extension food of any kind. In the Greek Old Testament it chiefly stands for the Hebrew word for bread. It appears in 89 New Testament verses, and twenty of those are in John — all but three of them in this one chapter.

Jesus taught His men to pray, Give us today our daily bread. Bread is the plain stuff of staying alive. So when He says I am the bread of life, He is not reaching for a fancy word. He takes the most common thing on the table and says: that is what I am to your soul. Not the dessert. Not an extra. The thing you die without.

The dust offers a hundred substitutes — the second drink, the screen at midnight, the next purchase, the praise of other men. Each one fills you for an hour. Artos in John 6:35 says the Son Himself is bread, and whoever comes to me will not be hungry.
stations.live: Name the substitute you reach for when your soul is hungry. This week, when you reach for it, stop and pray first: ‘You are the bread of life. I am coming to You.’

stations.verse: This is the will of my Father who sent me, that of all he has given to me I should lose nothing, but should raise him up at the last day.
stations.question: Jesus says the Father’s will is that of all he has given to me I should lose nothing; what fear of falling away would loosen its hold if I believed my keeping rests on that will rather than on my grip?
body: Anistēmi is a compound of ana and histēmi. With an object it means to raise up, and it is used of raising the dead. Without one it means to rise — from bed, from a seat, from the grave. It is found in 107 New Testament verses.

Four times in John 6 Jesus promises to raise up His own, in verses 39, 40, 44 and 54. It is the promise He keeps coming back to, and He has the right to make it. John says the disciples did not yet understand that he must rise from the dead, and Peter would later preach, This Jesus God raised up. The One who promises to raise was raised first.

The dust gets the last word on every man, or seems to. It takes the body back and closes over it. Anistēmi says the dust does not get the last word. The Son will lose nothing the Father gave Him, but should raise him up at the last day.
stations.live: Read John 6:39–40 aloud at the end of each day this week. When you lie down, say it: ‘He will raise me up at the last day.’ Let your sleep each night rehearse the morning He has promised.

practices.title: NAME YOUR MEAL TICKET
practices.body: The crowd crossed the lake for more bread, not for Christ. Be honest about what you have been coming to Him for. Write down your last ten prayers as best you remember them. Mark the ones that asked for a supply and the ones that asked for Him. There is no shame in asking for bread; Christ taught you to. But look at the balance. Then pray once this week asking for nothing but Christ Himself: to know Him, to trust Him, to be fed by Him.

practices.title: WORK THE ONE WORK
practices.body: Christ said the work of God is to believe in the One the Father sent. When you catch yourself keeping score with God this week — the good day you think earned something, the bad day you think cost you something — stop and read Romans 4:5 out loud. Faith is not one more chore to finish. It is resting your weight on the Son who finished His. Say it on the good day as plainly as on the bad one, because both days tempt you to keep books.

practices.title: SET THE TABLE FOR THE TRUE BREAD
practices.body: Bread was the most common thing on the table, and Christ said He is that to your soul. Read John 6:22–40 at a meal this week with whoever eats with you — your wife, your children, the men on your crew at lunch. Read it slowly. Ask one question: what does Jesus say He is? Let the answer sit on the table with the food. If no one says much, that is fine. The Word does its own work.

practices.title: STARVE ONE SUBSTITUTE
practices.body: Name the thing you reach for when your soul is hungry — the drink, the screen, the overtime, the praise. For seven days, set it down. Each time the hunger comes, pray John 6:35 in its place. The point is not to prove your grit. The point is to find that the bread of life is enough when the substitute is gone. If you fail on Wednesday, come back to Him Wednesday night. He does not throw out the man who comes.

practices.title: REHEARSE THE LAST DAY
practices.body: Christ promised four times in this chapter to raise up those who come to Him. Pick one grave you will visit or think about this week — a father, a friend, a child. Stand there, or sit with the memory, and read John 6:40 out loud. If that one believed, say it plainly: ‘He will be raised up at the last day.’ Then say it about yourself, with your name in it. Let the promise be as plain in your mouth as it was in His.

title: The Bread of Life
subtitle: from dust to bread that never runs out
keyVerse: Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.

passage.text: On the next day, the multitude that stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was no other boat there, except the one in which his disciples had embarked, and that Jesus hadn’t entered with his disciples into the boat, but his disciples had gone away alone.
However boats from Tiberias came near to the place where they ate the bread after the Lord had given thanks.
When the multitude therefore saw that Jesus wasn’t there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats, and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.
When they found him on the other side of the sea, they asked him, “Rabbi, when did you come here?”
Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves, and were filled.
Don’t work for the food which perishes, but for the food which remains to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For God the Father has sealed him.”
They said therefore to him, “What must we do, that we may work the works of God?”
Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.”
They said therefore to him, “What then do you do for a sign, that we may see and believe you? What work do you do?
Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness. As it is written, ‘He gave them bread out of heaven to eat.’ ”
Jesus therefore said to them, “Most certainly, I tell you, it wasn’t Moses who gave you the bread out of heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread out of heaven.
For the bread of God is that which comes down out of heaven, and gives life to the world.”
They said therefore to him, “Lord, always give us this bread.”
Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.
But I told you that you have seen me, and yet you don’t believe.
All those whom the Father gives me will come to me. He who comes to me I will in no way throw out.
For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.
This is the will of my Father who sent me, that of all he has given to me I should lose nothing, but should raise him up at the last day.
This is the will of the one who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son, and believes in him, should have eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day.”

stationsIntro: Five words from the morning after the miracle: food, work, manna, bread, and the word for being raised. Read each verse aloud, answer the question without dressing it up, and let each word send you back to the One who gives Himself.
lifeIntro: The Father has given His Son as bread out of heaven, and the Son has promised to lose none of those the Father gave Him. Everything below rests on that gift. None of these practices buys you a seat at the table; the seat was given. They are ways of coming hungry to the One who feeds, and of coming back when you wander.
lifePulls: You cannot earn bread that is given, and you cannot keep bread that spoils. Christ is the bread of life, sealed by the Father, and whoever comes to Him will not be hungry.
prayer: Father, You gave bread from heaven to Israel, and You have given Your Son as the true bread for me. I confess I have come to Jesus for what He can give more than for Him. I have worked for food that spoils and called it a life. Thank You that the work You ask is to believe in the One You sent, and that He has finished the work You gave Him to do. Thank You that all You give to Him will come, and that He will in no way throw out anyone who comes. Make me hungry for Christ, and keep me coming to Him. When I fail, bring me back, and do not let me believe the lie that He will throw me out. Raise me up at the last day, and let that hope steady me now. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You gave bread from heaven to Israel, and You have given Your Son as
the true bread for me.
I confess I have come to Jesus for what He can give more than for Him.
I have worked for food that spoils and called it a life.
Thank You that the work You ask is to believe in the One You sent, and that He
has finished the work You gave Him to do.
Thank You that all You give to Him will come, and that He will in no way throw
out anyone who comes.
Make me hungry for Christ, and keep me coming to Him.
When I fail, bring me back, and do not let me believe the lie that He will throw
me out.
Raise me up at the last day, and let that hope steady me now.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: The crowd crossed the lake for another meal, and Jesus told them so. Don’t work for food that spoils. The one work God asks is to believe in the One He sent. Moses never gave the bread; the Father did, and now He gives the true bread out of heaven. Jesus is that bread. Whoever comes to Him will not be hungry, will not be thrown out, and will be raised up at the last day.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and see the bread that came down. It came down when you could not climb up. It came down into a body that grew tired by a well and hungry on the road. It came down not to be admired from across the room but to be received, trusted, taken in. It came down for men who had crossed a lake for the wrong reason. It came down for a crowd that wanted bread and missed the Giver. It came down for you, with your tally and your hunger and your mixed motives.

The dust kept you on wages. It taught you to work for the bread and then told you the bread would never be enough. It was right about the second part. No paycheck ever filled a soul. But the Father has stopped your striving with a gift. The work He asks is to believe in the One He sent. That is not one more shift on the schedule. It is coming home hungry and being fed. You do not have to earn the plate. You only have to come to the One who is the bread, and the Father has already pulled out the chair.

And when you come, you are kept. Hear the Son: He who comes to me I will in no way throw out. Not after the first failure. Not after the hundredth. The Father gave you to the Son, and the Son came down from heaven to do the Father’s will — and the Father’s will is that He lose nothing. Not one of the given. Not you on your worst day. The keeping rests on the will of the Father and the faithfulness of the Son, not on your grip.

So hold this when you stand at a graveside, or when you lie down tired enough to feel your own mortality: Christ has promised, in plain words, to raise up His own at the last day. The ground that takes your body will give it back. The Son who walked out of His own tomb will call you out of yours. Until then you have eternal life now, today, in the bread that never runs out. Come and eat.
closingVerse: Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.
carry: Jesus said, Whoever comes to me will not be hungry; what hunger are you trying to quiet this week with something other than coming to Him?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust keeps a back door open. It never asks you to quit Christ out loud. It only reminds you there are other places to go. When His word presses on the money, there is the money. When it presses on the grudge, the grudge is still warm. When it presses on the second drink, the bottle is in the cabinet where you left it. So you keep Jesus the way you keep a spare tire under the bed of the truck — glad it is there, never planning to need it, sure you can drive a long way on the four you have.

And when His words turn hard, the dust has the answer ready. Walk. You came for the bread, not for this. Nobody can make you stay. That last line sounds like freedom, and it is one of the oldest lies in the field. A man who walks away from Christ does not walk out into open country. He walks back into the ground he was taken from. Every road out there ends in the same dirt.

The psalm does not ask for a better road. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) A man face down in the dirt asks for one thing, and it is a word. John 6 ends with another man saying the same thing in fewer words. The crowd has thinned. The hard saying hangs in the air. Simon Peter has no plan and no other address. He does not argue. He has only this: Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.

sections.heading: The Synagogue at Capernaum
pulls: Every road away from Christ ends in the same ground you came from. Peter had no better offer and no other address — only a Man whose words carry eternal life.
paras: The loaves were eaten the day before. The crowd crossed the lake after Jesus and found Him on the far side, and He told them plainly that they had come for bread. Then He offered them Himself: I am the bread of life. Last week you heard the offer. This week you hear what the offer does to a crowd. John tells you where it happened: He said these things in the synagogue, as he taught in Capernaum. Read verses 41 through 71 in one sitting and watch the room empty. It starts with murmuring. It moves to arguing, then to walking off, and it ends with twelve men and one question. Watch also who never changes. The crowd shifts with every sentence. Jesus stands where He stood at the start. He does not chase the ones who leave. He does not sand down a word to keep them. He tells the truth about the Father’s drawing, about His own flesh given for the world, and about the betrayer at His own table. Then He turns to the men who are left and asks them a question every man reading must answer for himself.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: UNLESS THE FATHER DRAWS
paras: The Jews therefore murmured concerning him. Murmuring is a low sound passed down a row of men with their arms crossed. Their fathers made the same sound over the same subject. In the wilderness, hungry for bread, the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured. Bread from heaven has always drawn complaint from men who would rather have bread from their own fields.

Their trouble is that they think they know too much. Isn’t this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? They can name the family. A man they can place cannot have come down out of heaven. That is how the dust reasons. If I can account for it, it cannot be God.

Jesus does not argue the family tree. He tells them why they cannot see. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up in the last day. Read it slowly. Coming to Christ is not something a man does on his own steam. Left alone, every man murmurs. The Father has to draw. And look at the end of the verse. The man the Father draws, the Son raises. Nobody is dropped between the drawing and the last day.

Then Jesus reaches back to the prophets: They will all be taught by God. The Father does not only pull. He teaches. Everyone who hears from the Father and has learned, comes to me. And no one who comes is turned back at the door — He said so a few verses earlier: He who comes to me I will in no way throw out. If you find in yourself any hunger for Christ you did not make, that is the Father at work.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: MY FLESH FOR THE WORLD
paras: Most certainly, I tell you, he who believes in me has eternal life. Has. Not will earn. Not may someday receive. Then Jesus sets two breads side by side. Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness and they died. Manna was real bread from God, a true mercy. It held off hunger for a day. But every man who ate it was buried. Bread that only buys you one more day is not life.

I am the living bread which came down out of heaven. Then the offer takes the shape of a cross: the bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh. Bread is broken before it feeds anyone. Christ will hand His own body over to death so that a world of dying men may live.

Then the words that set the room arguing: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you don’t have life in yourselves. The crowd heard butcher’s talk. Jesus had already told them what He meant. In verse 47 believing ends in eternal life. In verse 54 eating ends in eternal life and the last day. The two are one act. To eat His flesh and drink His blood is to take Christ crucified into yourself by faith — to rest your whole life on His body given and His blood poured out, the way a hungry man rests his strength on bread.

And the fruit of that eating is a home. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood lives in me, and I in him. Not a visit. A dwelling. He who feeds on me, he will also live because of me. The life is His. You live on it.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: SPIRIT AND LIFE
pulls: The flesh profits nothing. The words of Jesus do not describe life from a safe distance — they carry it. When His word lands on a dead man, the man gets up.
paras: This is a hard saying, they said. Who can listen to it? Look at who says it. Not the far-shore crowd, but many of his disciples. They did not call the saying unclear. They understood enough. It was hard the way a dry plank is hard against the palm. It would not give.

Jesus does not take a word back. Does this cause you to stumble? Then He raises the stakes: Then what if you would see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? The One speaking is no local man with a large claim. He came down, and He will go back up. His words do not shrink to fit the room.

Then the key to the whole discourse: It is the spirit who gives life. The flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life. The eating was never about teeth. The flesh — human reach, human appetite, human effort — gets a man nothing toward God. The Spirit gives life, and He gives it through words. The words of Jesus do not describe life from a safe distance. They carry it. When His word lands on a dead man, the man lives.

And Jesus says once more why some still will not come: no one can come to me, unless it is given to him by my Father. He says it to men about to leave. He says it so you will know that faith is a gift. If you believe, you were given to believe. That does not leave room for pride. It leaves room for thanks, and it steadies you, because the Father’s will is that of all he has given to me I should lose nothing.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: TO WHOM WOULD WE GO
paras: At this, many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. John does not soften it. Men who had eaten the loaves on the grass turned around and went home. Then Jesus turns to the twelve: You don’t also want to go away, do you? He does not plead. He does not lower the price. He asks.

Peter answers for the rest: Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life. Listen to what he leaves out. He does not say the saying was easy. He does not say he understood all of it. He says there is no one else. Every other voice can only speak about death, or about how to get through the days before it. One voice speaks words that carry eternal life. Then the confession: We have come to believe and know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God. That is the Father’s drawing of verse 44, showing up as a fisherman’s plain words. Then the shadow falls across the table. Didn’t I choose you, the twelve, and one of you is a devil? John names him: Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, for it was he who would betray him, being one of the twelve. John does not explain Judas, and you should not try. What he shows you is that Jesus is not caught off guard. Jesus knew from the beginning. He chose the twelve with His eyes open and kept walking toward the very death verse 51 promised.
So the chapter leaves you here. The crowd is gone. Yesterday’s bread is long digested. What is left is a Man whose words carry eternal life, and a question with one honest answer.

stations.verse: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up in the last day.
stations.question: Jesus told the murmuring crowd that no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him; what in my faith have I been treating as my own achievement instead of the Father’s gift?
stations.gloss: to draw; to haul; to lead or impel
body: Helkō means to draw. John uses it for a sword pulled out and a net hauled in full of fish. In Acts it is Paul dragged from the temple. In John 6:44 and 12:32 it turns to a deeper work: the Father, and then the lifted-up Son, drawing men to Christ. Of its eight New Testament verses, five are John’s.

That is no gentle hint. A net does not decide to come ashore. Peter drew the net to land, and the net did not tear. Your coming looks like that from heaven’s side. You walked to Christ on your own feet. Under your walking was the Father’s pull, and it did not fail.

The dust says you found God, so you can lose Him. It says your grip is what holds you. Helkō says the rope was in the Father’s hands from the start, and the Son promises the end of the line: I will raise him up in the last day.
stations.live: Write down how you came to Christ — the names, the place, the words that landed. Under it write one line: ‘The Father drew me, and the Son will raise me up.’

stations.verse: It is written in the prophets, ‘They will all be taught by God.’ Therefore everyone who hears from the Father and has learned, comes to me.
stations.question: Jesus says that everyone who hears from the Father and has learned, comes to me; where has my Bible reading stopped at knowing about God without bringing me to His Son?
body: Didaktos means taught. It appears in only two verses of the New Testament. Here Jesus uses it to quote the prophets — Isaiah 54:13, All your children will be taught by Yahweh. Paul uses it for words which the Holy Spirit teaches. Both times the weight sits on the Teacher, not the pupil.

Men are taught by God. Not by a hunch, and not by a mood on a good morning. The Father speaks, and the man who hears and learns comes to Christ. Jesus does not say the clever will come. He says everyone who hears from the Father and has learned, comes to me. A man who never finished school can be taught by God. A man with a wall of diplomas can sit in the synagogue and murmur.
The dust says faith is a matter of figuring God out, and you are not the type. Didaktos turns that over. The Teacher does the work. Your part is the open Bible and the bowed head.
stations.live: Each morning this week, before you read, pray one sentence: ‘Father, teach me Your Son.’ Then read John 6:41–51 slowly and stop wherever Jesus speaks of the Father.

stations.verse: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day.
stations.question: Jesus promised eternal life to the one who eats my flesh and drinks my blood, as He had to the one who believes; what besides His body given and His blood shed am I quietly resting on?
body: Trōgō once described an animal gnawing or munching. By New Testament times it was a plain everyday word for eating. It shows up in six verses, four of them in John 6:54–58. One is Matthew’s picture of men eating and drinking before the flood.

The last is John 13:18, at the supper, and it should stop you. Jesus applies the Scripture to His betrayer: He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me. Judas ate the bread and went out into the night. Eating at the table is not the same as feeding on Christ. The difference is faith — taking Him in as your life: he who feeds on me, he will also live because of me.
The dust wants you close to the bread without eating it — in the pew, near enough to smell it. Trōgō is not a word for looking. Christ gave His flesh to be received, and He has not run short.
stations.live: Before one meal each day this week, read John 6:57 aloud. Then say before you eat: ‘I live because of Him. Not because of this plate, and not because of me.’

stations.verse: For my flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.
stations.question: When Jesus says my flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed, He calls His death the true food of my soul; what have I been treating as more real than that?
body: Posis comes from the verb to drink. It can mean the act of drinking, as when Paul writes, God’s Kingdom is not eating and drinking. In John 6:55 it means the drink itself, paired with the word for food. It occurs in three verses of the New Testament, and only here in John.

My flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed. Indeed means the real thing. Everything else you pour down your throat is a picture at best. The blood of Christ is His life poured out at the cross so your guilt could be washed away. In Part One He offered a woman at a well water that ends thirst. Here He names what that water cost Him.

The dust says your thirst is yours to manage. One more drink. One more purchase. One more hour on the screen. Posis points to the only drink that is true all the way down, and Christ does not ration it.
stations.live: Name what you reach for when you are dry — the phone, the overtime, the bank balance. Each time you reach for it this week, stop and say: ‘His blood is drink indeed. This is not.’

stations.verse: Therefore many of his disciples, when they heard this, said, “This is a hard saying! Who can listen to it?
stations.question: Many of His own disciples called His words about His flesh a hard saying and walked away; which word of Jesus am I keeping at arm’s length because it cuts against what I want?
body: Sklēros comes from a verb meaning to dry. It describes what is hard to the touch, rough, the opposite of soft. Five New Testament verses carry it: of a master called a hard man, of fierce winds driving ships, of the hard things ungodly men speak against the Lord, and of the risen Christ telling Saul, It is hard for you to kick against the goads.

The disciples called the saying hard. They did not call it unclear. Look who else uses the word. The servant in Matthew 25 called his master hard, then buried what he had been given. Saul found it hard to kick against the goads — and the Christ he was kicking made him new.

The dust says that when a word of Jesus feels hard, the trouble is the word. Sklēros shows you where the hardness may sit instead — in a hand that will not open. The Lord who spoke to Saul on the road gives new hearts still.
stations.live: Write out the one saying of Jesus you push back on hardest. Pray it back to Him by name: ‘This is hard. You have the words of eternal life. Open my hand.’

practices.title: FEED BEFORE YOU WORK
practices.body: Christ gave His flesh to be received, and feeding on Him means believing in Him crucified. So before the phone, before the news, before the first job of the day, read John 6:47–58. Read it slowly, the way you would eat a meal you had worked for all morning. Then tell Him in one plain sentence what you are resting on today: His body given, His blood poured out, nothing of your own. Do it before you have earned anything, so you remember the meal was never wages.

practices.title: NAME YOUR OTHER ADDRESSES
practices.body: Peter had nowhere else to go. You likely have several, and the dust keeps them lit. Write down the places you run when His word presses on you — the drink, the screen, the overtime, the silence toward your wife. Next to each one, write plainly where that road has taken you before and where it ends. Then write John 6:68 at the bottom of the page and keep the sheet where you will see it at night.

practices.title: STAY WITH THE HARD SAYING
practices.body: Many disciples left over one hard word. Jesus did not soften it, and He did not need to, because His words are spirit and life. This week, take the saying of His you resist most and read it every day without arguing back. Ask the Spirit who gives life to open it. Do not walk off from a word because it is hard. Stay under it like a man waiting out rain under a porch roof, and let it feed you in its own time.

practices.title: PRAY FOR THE MAN WHO LEFT
practices.body: No one comes unless the Father draws him — which means your prayers for a man who has walked away are not wasted breath. Name one man who no longer walks with Christ: a brother, a son, a friend from the old crew. Pray for him by name each day this week. Ask the Father to draw him back the way He drew you. Then leave the drawing to the Father, and do not mistake your nagging for His pull.

practices.title: SAY PETER’S CONFESSION
practices.body: At the end of each day, before you sleep, say Peter’s words out loud in your own house: Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life. Then add the rest: you are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Say it on the good days and the bad ones. Say it when you do not feel it. A confession said in the dark has a way of holding in the morning, because it rests on who He is, not on how you feel.

title: To Whom Shall We Go?
subtitle: from dust to the words of eternal life
keyVerse: Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.

passage.text: The Jews therefore murmured concerning him, because he said, “I am the bread which came down out of heaven.”
They said, “Isn’t this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he say, ‘I have come down out of heaven?’ ”
Therefore Jesus answered them, “Don’t murmur among yourselves.
No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up in the last day.
It is written in the prophets, ‘They will all be taught by God.’ Therefore everyone who hears from the Father and has learned, comes to me.
Not that anyone has seen the Father, except he who is from God. He has seen the Father.
Most certainly, I tell you, he who believes in me has eternal life.
I am the bread of life.
Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness and they died.
This is the bread which comes down out of heaven, that anyone may eat of it and not die.
I am the living bread which came down out of heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. Yes, the bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”
The Jews therefore contended with one another, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”
Jesus therefore said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you don’t have life in yourselves.
He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day.
For my flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.
He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood lives in me, and I in him.
As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father; so he who feeds on me, he will also live because of me.
This is the bread which came down out of heaven—not as our fathers ate the manna, and died. He who eats this bread will live forever.”
He said these things in the synagogue, as he taught in Capernaum.
Therefore many of his disciples, when they heard this, said, “This is a hard saying! Who can listen to it?”
But Jesus knowing in himself that his disciples murmured at this, said to them, “Does this cause you to stumble?
Then what if you would see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?
It is the spirit who gives life. The flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life.
But there are some of you who don’t believe.” For Jesus knew from the beginning who they were who didn’t believe, and who it was who would betray him.
He said, “For this cause I have said to you that no one can come to me, unless it is given to him by my Father.”
At this, many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.
Jesus said therefore to the twelve, “You don’t also want to go away, do you?”
Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.
We have come to believe and know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
Jesus answered them, “Didn’t I choose you, the twelve, and one of you is a devil?”
Now he spoke of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, for it was he who would betray him, being one of the twelve.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE HARD SAYING
stationsIntro: Read each verse slowly, the way a man reads a letter he expects to keep. Let the hard words stay hard until they turn into bread, and let the Greek sharpen the verse rather than replace it.
lifeIntro: The Son gives His flesh for the life of the world. The Father draws men to Him, and the Spirit gives life through the words Jesus speaks. None of what follows earns a seat at the table; each practice is a way of eating at a table already set for you.
lifePulls: Faith is not your grip on the rope. It is the Father’s pull on the other end — and the Son has promised to raise up on the last day every man the Father draws.
prayer: Father, no one comes to Your Son unless You draw him, and You drew me. Thank You for giving me to Christ, and for His promise to lose nothing You have given Him. Lord Jesus, You are the living bread that came down out of heaven. You gave Your flesh for the life of the world, and I rest my whole weight on it. Forgive me for the other doors I keep open, and for the hard sayings I walk away from. Holy Spirit, You give life; let the words of Jesus land in me as spirit and life. When the crowd thins and the words feel hard, keep me where Peter stood. To whom would I go? You have the words of eternal life. Raise me up at the last day, as You have promised, and keep me feeding on You until then. In Jesus’ name, amen.
