bottomLine: The crowd came for bread and left over words. Jesus told them the truth: no one comes unless the Father draws him, His flesh is given for the life of the world, and His words are spirit and life. Many walked. Peter stayed, not because he had it figured out, but because there was nowhere else to go. There still isn’t. Feed on Christ crucified, close the back door, and stay.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the One still standing in the synagogue when the room has emptied. Look at the One who did not chase the crowd and did not soften His word to keep it. Look at the One who knew from the beginning who would leave and who would betray, and chose the twelve anyway. Look at the One the Father sent down out of heaven, not to visit the dust, but to give His own flesh for the life of a dying world.

The dust told you there was always somewhere else to go. You have tried a few of those roads. You know where they end, because you have tasted the dirt at the end of them. The bottle ends there. The money ends there. The grudge you fed for years ends there. Your own good sense ends there too, and so does the reputation you worked so long to build. Every one of those doors opens onto the ground you came from, and none of them has a word that can raise a man out of it.

But Christ does. He did not stand at a distance and hand you a better rule. He gave His body over to death at the place of a skull and poured out His blood so that a man who feeds on Him by faith would never die the death that matters. The Father who drew you is the Father who gave you to the Son, and the Son has said in plain words that He will lose nothing the Father gave Him. That is not a hope you have to hold up by yourself. It is His will, and He has never failed to do His Father’s will.

So when the hard saying comes this week, and the crowd in your own head starts to murmur, stay where Peter stood. You do not need to have it all worked out. You need only know who is speaking. Nothing behind those other doors has ever said a word over a grave. He has. He gave His flesh for the life of the world, and He walked out of the tomb still speaking. So when the old doors swing open on Tuesday, answer them with Peter: Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.
closingVerse: Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.
carry: When many walked away, Peter stayed because Jesus has the words of eternal life; when His word presses on you this week, where will you be tempted to run instead of staying with Him?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Doctrine, the dust says, is just men talking. Some preacher’s opinion. Some church’s rulebook. A stack of old arguments that have nothing to do with a man who has a crew to pay on Friday. Take what fits and leave the rest. Your own read on God is as good as anybody’s, and better than most, because you have lived it. You have buried your father. You have watched a business go under. Nobody in a pulpit gets to tell you what God is like.

Under that lie sits a second one. It says you can size up Jesus by looking at Him. A man from Galilee with no schooling anyone could name. His own brothers did not believe Him, and the crowd split down the middle about Him. Judge by what you see and you will land where the crowd landed — a good man, maybe, or a fraud, but nobody whose word gets the last say over your money, your marriage, or your mouth.

That road leaves a man standing on nothing but his own opinion, and opinion is dust. It blows with the weather. What a soul in the dirt needs is a word from outside itself, and the psalm asks for exactly that: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) Not my word, not the crowd’s, not the voice in my own head that sounds so sure at midnight. Yours. In John 7, Jesus stands up in the temple and tells the crowd whose word He has brought them: My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.

sections.heading: Up to the Feast of Booths
pulls: Opinion is dust. It blows with the weather and the crowd. Jesus did not bring His own opinion about God. He brought the Father’s word, and a man can build a life on that.
paras: Chapter 7 opens with a death threat. Jesus stays in Galilee because the Jews sought to kill him. The healing at the pool in chapter 5, done on a Sabbath, is the reason they want Him dead (5:16–18), and Jesus will bring that healing up Himself before this passage is out. Now the Feast of Booths is at hand, and everyone is going up to Jerusalem. The pressure on Jesus comes from three sides at once — His own family, the whispering crowd, and the leaders in the temple.

Read verses 1 through 24 straight through. You will hear many voices: brothers who needle Him, a crowd that whispers, leaders who marvel and then accuse. Through all of it one voice keeps saying the same thing in different ways. My time belongs to the Father. My teaching belongs to the Father. The glory I seek belongs to the Father. Watch a Man who never once speaks from Himself, who will not be rushed, flattered, or scared off, and ask why that is the best news a sinner could hear.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: MY TIME HAS NOT YET COME
paras: His brothers have advice for Him. Depart from here and go into Judea, that your disciples also may see your works which you do. Then they press: If you do these things, reveal yourself to the world. It is the counsel the world always gives a man with a gift. Get seen. Work the crowd. John adds one plain line that explains the rest: For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.

Sit with that. The men who grew up under the same roof did not believe. If you have a brother, a father, or a son who thinks your faith is a weakness, Jesus has stood where you stand. And He did not answer them with a show.

My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready. His life ran on the Father’s clock. Every step to Jerusalem, every word in the temple, every hour toward the cross was set by the One who sent Him. His brothers’ time was always ready because the world had no quarrel with them. The world can’t hate you, but it hates me, because I testify about it, that its works are evil. Jesus tells the truth about the world, and the world cannot stand to hear it.

And the Father’s time did come. Paul names it: at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. The Son who would not be hurried by His brothers went to the cross on the day appointed — not early, not late. And the brothers who scoffed were not left where they stood. After He rose, Acts finds them in the upper room, praying with his brothers among the disciples. The Lord who kept the Father’s time also kept His own family.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: A CROWD THAT WHISPERS
paras: Jesus goes up to the feast after all, not publicly, but as it were in secret. Nothing in Him is afraid. He is keeping the Father’s time, not the crowd’s, and He goes up to the city where men are waiting to kill Him. Meanwhile the leaders hunt for Him: Where is he?

And the crowd talks. There was much murmuring among the multitudes concerning him. Some said, He is a good man. Others answered that he leads the multitude astray. Both verdicts are formed from the edge of the crowd. Neither group has sat at His feet. One side pays Him a compliment that costs nothing. The other side calls Him a liar. Neither one bows. Neither one asks Him who He is.

Then the sentence that should sting a little: Yet no one spoke openly of him for fear of the Jews. Fear of men shut every mouth. They talked about Jesus in low voices, in corners, where it was safe. You know that silence. The break room goes quiet when someone mocks the faith, and you study your coffee. Your son asks what you believe, and you change the subject. A coworker’s marriage is cracking, and you say nothing about the One who can mend it.

But look at Jesus before you look at yourself. He was not ashamed to be named with sinners. He went up to the very city that wanted Him dead, and before long He would stand in the open court and teach. He spoke openly of you to the Father, and He still does — he lives forever to make intercession for them. The Man who was not ashamed of you is the Man who loosens your tongue.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: NOT MINE, BUT HIS WHO SENT ME
pulls: Jesus is the only man who ever sought nothing but the glory of the One who sent Him. No unrighteousness was found in Him — and He carried yours to the cross.
paras: When it was now the middle of the feast, Jesus went up into the temple and taught. The leaders are stunned. How does this man know letters, having never been educated? They measure a teacher by where he studied and who signed for him. Jesus has no paper they can check, no teacher whose name will settle the matter.

His answer goes past paper to the source. My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. The Son did not invent a message. He did not add to the Father’s word or trim it for the crowd. Later He will say it again: I spoke not from myself, but the Father who sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say. What Jesus teaches is what God thinks, spoken by God the Son in a Galilean voice.

Then the way in: If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God. Knowing does not start with a debate. It starts with a heart bent toward God’s will — and that bent is itself the Father’s gift, the drawing of 6:44. A man who wants God’s will hears the Father in the Son’s words the way a son knows his own father’s voice across a field.

Then the test of any teacher: He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and no unrighteousness is in him. Only one Man has ever fit that line all the way through. Every other teacher has some of his own glory mixed in, and so does every man. Jesus had none. That is the One who stood in your place, and His clean record is the one God counts as yours.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: JUDGE RIGHTEOUS JUDGMENT
paras: Then Jesus turns the court around. Didn’t Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keeps the law? Why do you seek to kill me? The men who want Him dead for breaking the Sabbath are breaking the law in their hearts as they stand there. The crowd laughs it off. You have a demon, they say. Who seeks to kill you?

Jesus names the real charge. I did one work and you all marvel because of it. One work — the man at the pool, sick thirty-eight years, told to rise and walk. Then He reasons from their practice. They circumcise a boy on the Sabbath so the law of Moses is not broken. Are you angry with me, because I made a man completely healthy on the Sabbath? If marking one part of a body is lawful on the Sabbath, how much more making a whole man well.

Don’t judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment. They looked at the surface. A man carrying his mat on the wrong day. A teacher with no school behind Him. They called it sin and missed the work of God standing in front of them. You do the same. You judge Jesus by how small He looks in your week. You judge your wife by her worst hour and yourself by your best.

Here is the hope under the warning. The One judged by appearance and condemned was the only righteous Man ever put on trial. He let the false verdict stand against Him, and on the cross He bore the true verdict your sin had earned. Now He judges, and He says of Himself, my judgment is righteous. Because of Him, the verdict God speaks over you is not by appearance. It is by His Son.

stations.verse: Jesus therefore said to them, “My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready.
stations.question: His unbelieving brothers pushed Jesus to go show Himself, and He answered, My time has not yet come; where am I pushing God to act on my timetable instead of trusting the Father who kept His Son’s hour?
stations.gloss: a fixed time; the fitting season
body: Kairos is a word for time, but not time as a length. Time as duration has its own word, chronos. Kairos is a fixed and definite season, the right moment for a thing. It runs through eighty verses of the New Testament, and John uses it in only two: 7:6 and 7:8.

My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready. His brothers could go any day. Every step Jesus took was set by the Father. And the season came. Paul names it: at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. The cross was not late. It came on the Father’s day, for men too weak to help themselves.

The dust says time is running out on you, that God moves too slow and you had better force it. Kairos says the season is in the Father’s hand. He kept the Son’s appointment to the hour. He will keep yours: we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up.
stations.live: Name one thing you are trying to force before its season — a deal, a son’s change of heart, an answer from God. Hand it back each morning this week: ‘Father, the season is Yours.’

stations.verse: The Jews therefore marveled, saying, “How does this man know letters, having never been educated?
stations.question: The leaders marveled that Jesus knew so much having never been educated, and measured Him by where He had studied; by what measure have I been deciding whether His words get a say over my life?
stations.gloss: to learn; to learn by practice
body: Manthanō means to learn — by asking and hearing, or by use and practice until a thing becomes habit. Twenty-four New Testament verses use it. In 7:15 the leaders use it to say Jesus never studied: having never been educated. Back in 6:45 Jesus used the same verb for the man who has learned from the Father and comes to Him.

The leaders think learning needs a teacher with a name. Jesus had the Father. And the word turns once more: though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered. He did not learn obedience because He had been disobedient. He learned it the way a man learns a trade — by doing it, all the way to the cross. That obedience is counted to you.
The dust says you are too far behind to learn. Jesus says, learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart. He is no hard foreman waiting for you to fail. He teaches empty-handed men.
stations.live: Write Matthew 11:29 on a card and carry it in your shirt pocket this week. When you feel behind, read it and say: ‘I am learning from a gentle Teacher.’

stations.verse: Jesus therefore answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.
stations.question: Jesus said, My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me; which of His teachings have I been treating as one man’s opinion I can set aside rather than the Father’s own word?
body: Didachē is teaching — both what is taught, the doctrine itself, and the act of teaching it. It runs through twenty-nine verses. The Gospels use it for the crowds’ astonishment at Jesus, for his word was with authority. In Acts the first believers continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching.

My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. Jesus did not build a doctrine of His own. He did not improve the Father’s word or cut it down to fit the crowd. What He taught was the Father’s own mind, spoken by the Son. That is why doctrine is not dry paper. It is God telling you what is true about Himself, about you, and about the Son He sent to save you.

The dust says doctrine only divides, and a man does better with a feeling about God. Feelings shift with the weather. Didachē hands you ground to stand on: He who remains in the teaching has both the Father and the Son.
stations.live: Learn one plain sentence of Jesus’ teaching by heart this week: he who believes in me has eternal life. Say it on the drive in, and teach it to one of your children before Sunday.

stations.verse: He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and no unrighteousness is in him.
stations.question: Jesus is the one Man who sought only the glory of him who sent him, with no unrighteousness in Him; where does my talk about God quietly bend back toward my own name?
body: Adikia is unrighteousness — injustice, iniquity, and the wrong acts that come out of a bent heart. It is found in twenty-four verses. Paul sets it against truth: love doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth. John 7:18 does the same, setting true beside no unrighteousness is in him.

Jesus says this of the man who seeks the glory of the One who sent him, and He alone fits it without a crack. You do not — the pride that reads like competence, the story told so you come off well. In Christ there is no adikia at all. That is why He could stand in your place.

The dust says your unrighteousness is the last word on you. John’s letter answers that God is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. And He has promised, I will be merciful to their unrighteousness.
stations.live: Name one place you have been working for your own glory — at the shop, at church, at home. Confess it to God by name. Then read 1 John 1:9 out loud and take Him at His word.

stations.verse: Don’t judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
stations.question: The crowd saw a Sabbath broken where Jesus had made a man completely healthy; whose life am I judging according to appearance while missing what God may be doing in it?
body: Opsis can mean the act of seeing, a face, or the outward look of a thing. It occurs in only three verses — twice in John’s Gospel and once in Revelation. Lazarus walks out of the tomb, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. The risen Christ appears, and His face was like the sun shining at its brightest. In 7:24 it is appearance — the surface men judge by.

The crowd judged by appearance. A Galilean. A man with no schooling. A healer who worked on the Sabbath. They looked at the surface and called it a demon. Men still do it — to Jesus, to their neighbors, and to themselves in the mirror.

The dust says what you see is all there is: a tired face, a record, a wasted year. But the face men dismissed in Galilee now shines like the sun. And God does not judge you by your surface. He sees you in His Son, and He judges righteous judgment.
stations.live: Pick one man you have written off by how he looks or talks. Ask him one honest question this week and listen to the answer. Then pray: ‘Lord, judge righteous judgment in me.’

practices.title: LET HIM KEEP THE CLOCK
practices.body: Jesus would not be hurried by His brothers, and the Father’s time came right on the day. Write down the one thing you are pushing hardest to make happen on your schedule. Each morning this week, before you push, pray Romans 5:6 back to God: Christ died at the right time. Then do the next honest piece of work in front of you and leave the season with the Father who set it. He was not late with His Son. He will not be late with you.

practices.title: SPEAK HIS NAME IN THE OPEN
practices.body: The crowd only whispered about Jesus, for fear of the Jews. Jesus was not ashamed of you, and He speaks for you before the Father now. This week, name Christ out loud to one person who does not expect it — a coworker, a neighbor at the feed store, your own son. No speech. One plain sentence about what He has done for you, and then let it stand. Do not argue it or dress it up. If your voice shakes, let it shake. The word is His, not yours to polish.

practices.title: SIT UNDER THE TEACHING
practices.body: The teaching of Jesus is the Father’s own word. So give it the first hour, not the last scrap of the day. Read John 7:14–24 aloud every morning this week. Underline each place Jesus speaks of the One who sent Him, and count them by Saturday. Notice how often the Son points away from Himself. Ask the Father to bend your will toward His, since Jesus promised that the man who desires His will is the man who will know His teaching. Ask, then read again.

practices.title: WORK FOR ANOTHER’S GLORY
practices.body: Christ sought only the glory of the One who sent Him, and there was no unrighteousness in Him. His record is the one God credits to you. Pick one task this week that nobody will see — a job done right at the back of the shop, a repair at home, a kindness with no name on it. Do it well, tell no one, and do not mention it at supper. When you are tempted to, thank God that the righteousness you stand in was never your own.

practices.title: JUDGE BY HIS VERDICT
practices.body: The crowd judged by appearance and called the work of God a demon. Before you give a verdict on your wife, your son, or a man on the crew this week, stop and ask what God may be doing that you cannot see on the surface. Then turn the same question on yourself, on the man in the mirror at five in the morning. In Christ, the Father’s verdict on you is righteous, not a reading of your face.

title: Teaching Not My Own
subtitle: from dust to the doctrine of the Father
keyVerse: Jesus therefore answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.

passage.text: After these things, Jesus was walking in Galilee, for he wouldn’t walk in Judea, because the Jews sought to kill him.
Now the feast of the Jews, the Feast of Booths, was at hand.
His brothers therefore said to him, “Depart from here and go into Judea, that your disciples also may see your works which you do.
For no one does anything in secret while he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, reveal yourself to the world.”
For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.
Jesus therefore said to them, “My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready.
The world can’t hate you, but it hates me, because I testify about it, that its works are evil.
You go up to the feast. I am not yet going up to this feast, because my time is not yet fulfilled.”
Having said these things to them, he stayed in Galilee.
But when his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly, but as it were in secret.
The Jews therefore sought him at the feast, and said, “Where is he?”
There was much murmuring among the multitudes concerning him. Some said, “He is a good man.” Others said, “Not so, but he leads the multitude astray.”
Yet no one spoke openly of him for fear of the Jews.
But when it was now the middle of the feast, Jesus went up into the temple and taught.
The Jews therefore marveled, saying, “How does this man know letters, having never been educated?”
Jesus therefore answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.
If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself.
He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and no unrighteousness is in him.
Didn’t Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keeps the law? Why do you seek to kill me?”
The multitude answered, “You have a demon! Who seeks to kill you?”
Jesus answered them, “I did one work and you all marvel because of it.
Moses has given you circumcision (not that it is of Moses, but of the fathers), and on the Sabbath you circumcise a boy.
If a boy receives circumcision on the Sabbath, that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me, because I made a man completely healthy on the Sabbath?
Don’t judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”

stationsIntro: Take these verses one at a time and let the Son’s voice carry the Father’s weight. Answer the question before you read the Greek, then let the word press the verse deeper into you.
lifeIntro: Jesus kept the Father’s time all the way to the cross, and He handed you the Father’s teaching without adding a word or holding one back. These five practices put you under that word for one week, and every one of them comes out of verses 1 through 24.
lifePulls: The Son kept the Father’s time, spoke the Father’s teaching, and sought the Father’s glory. Every word He handed you came from the Father’s own mouth, and it will hold your weight.
prayer: Father, You have spoken to me in Your Son, and His teaching is Yours. Lord Jesus, You kept Your Father’s time and went to the cross at the right time for the ungodly. You sought only Your Father’s glory, and no unrighteousness was in You. You carried my unrighteousness, and You cleanse me from all of it. Forgive me for treating Your word as one opinion among many. Forgive me for the whispering faith that goes quiet when men are watching. Bend my will toward Yours, so that I know Your teaching and stand on it. Loosen my tongue to speak of You in the open, since You were never ashamed of me. Teach me to judge with righteous judgment and not by appearance. In Jesus’ name, amen.

bottomLine: His brothers wanted a show. The crowd whispered. The leaders measured Him by His schooling and called His work a demon. Through all of it Jesus kept the Father’s time, spoke the Father’s teaching, and sought the Father’s glory. His doctrine is not opinion; it is God speaking. Stop sizing Him up by appearance. Sit under His word every morning, say His name in the open, and let the Righteous One’s verdict stand over you.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and listen to the Man in the temple court. Listen to a voice with no school behind it and the Father behind every word. Listen to a teacher who never once spoke from Himself, never padded his own name, never shaded the truth to keep a crowd. Listen, because that voice is speaking to you over the noise of your own opinions, and what it says did not start with a man. It started with God, and it came down to the dust to find you.

The dust told you doctrine was just men talking and you could take what fits. It told you to size up Jesus by how He looked — a Galilean, Joseph’s son, a crowd divided over Him. You have done it. You have weighed His word against your own read on things and let your read win. You have gone quiet in the break room. You have judged your own house by its worst day. None of that is hidden from Him, and none of it has turned Him away from you.

But hear what He did with the Father’s time. He would not be hurried by brothers who did not believe Him, and He would not be stopped by leaders who wanted Him dead. When the season came, He went to the cross on the Father’s day — at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. The One in whom there was no unrighteousness took yours and carried it all the way into the grave. Then the Father raised Him on the first day of the week, and the false verdict men had passed on Him was overturned in heaven’s court.

So the word you stand on this week is not your opinion, and it is not the crowd’s. It is the Father’s teaching, given by the Son who sought only His Father’s glory. He has promised to forgive you and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. He judges righteous judgment, and in Him that judgment over you is already spoken. Go to work with it in your pocket. Go home with it on your tongue. Say it to your son. Stand on it when the crowd in your own head starts to whisper again. It will hold, because the One who spoke it has already risen to keep it.
closingVerse: Jesus therefore answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.
carry: If the teaching of Jesus is the Father’s own word, as He said in the temple, where will you let it overrule your own opinion before this week is out?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: There is a kind of dry a man learns to hide. It is not thirst for water. It is the dry that sets in after years of doing the right things — the offering envelope, the Sunday shirt, the prayer before supper said fast so the food stays hot. Nothing is wrong on paper. But inside, the ground has cracked. You read a chapter and feel nothing. You sing and only your mouth moves. You would not say it to your pastor, and you would not say it to your wife, because a Christian man is not supposed to run dry.

The dust has two things to tell you about that. First, it says your thirst is proof you are on the outside — that the Spirit of God is for other men, the ones who pray out loud without notes and never seem to have a gray morning. Second, it says the cure is to dig harder. Read more, give more, get up earlier, and maybe the water will come. One lie shames you for being dry. The other hands you a shovel and points at hardpan.

A dry man does not need a lecture. He needs water, and he needs to know he is allowed to ask for it. A dry man can still pray, even with dust in his mouth: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) John 7 is that word. On the last day of a feast, with officers in the crowd sent to arrest Him, Jesus stood up and called out to anyone who was thirsty. Not anyone who was qualified. Anyone who was dry.

sections.heading: A Feast, a Crowd, and an Hour Not Yet Come
pulls: Your thirst is not proof that you are on the outside. It is the very thing Jesus called out for on the last day of the feast. He did not ask for the qualified. He asked for the dry.
paras: Last week Jesus went up to Jerusalem for the Feast of Booths and taught in the temple in the middle of the feast. Now the city is arguing about Him. Some know the rulers want Him dead and wonder why He is still speaking in the open. Some believe. The chief priests and the Pharisees send officers to bring Him in. And through all of it John keeps repeating one thing: His hour had not yet come. Nobody sets His schedule but His Father.

Read 7:25–52 in one sitting before you go further. Watch how many people are sure they know who He is, and how few of them are right. Then watch Him stand on the last and greatest day of the feast and offer the one thing none of their arguments could give them. This is the week John tells you plainly what the living water is: the Holy Spirit, given to those who believe, once Jesus has been glorified.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: WHERE HE COMES FROM
paras: The people of Jerusalem think they have Jesus figured out. Isn’t this he whom they seek to kill? they ask, and then they wonder whether the rulers have changed their minds. But one thing settles it for them: we know where this man comes from. They know His town. They know His family. A man from up the road cannot be the Christ.

Jesus answers them out loud, right there in the temple. You both know me, and know where I am from. I have not come of myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you don’t know. They know His address. They do not know His Father. That is the gap in every man who takes familiarity for faith. You can know the stories, the hymns, and the name of the church your grandfather helped build, and still not know where Jesus is from.

Then the plain claim: I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me. Jesus is not a good man who climbed up to God. He came down from the Father, sent on a work only He could do. That is why the next line reads the way it does. They sought therefore to take him; but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come. Men with orders and strong arms could not touch Him one hour early. The Father kept the clock.

And in the middle of the threats, John slips this in: But of the multitude, many believed in him. The Father was drawing men to His Son while the rulers were plotting. That has not changed. While the noise rises around you, God is still bringing men to Christ, one at a time.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: YOU WILL SEEK ME
paras: The Pharisees hear the crowd murmuring, and they move. The chief priests and the Pharisees sent officers to arrest him. Men with authority, sending men with orders. It is the way the world handles a problem it cannot answer. If you cannot refute a man, you remove him.

Jesus is not rattled. I will be with you a little while longer, then I go to him who sent me. He is not running from the officers. He is going home to the Father, and He will go when the hour comes and not before. Then He says a hard thing: You will seek me, and won’t find me. You can’t come where I am. There is a door open now that will not stay open forever. The offer is real today, spoken while He is near.

They miss it entirely. Where will this man go that we won’t find him? Will he go to the Dispersion among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks? They meant it as a sneer. Read on into Acts and see where His word went — out past Jerusalem, to Greeks, to men who had never kept a feast in that city in their lives. What they mocked as unthinkable was the plan all along. The Father’s reach was always wider than one temple court.

Do not let that comfort you into delay. A little while longer is a warning as well as a mercy. The same Jesus who will not be hurried by His enemies will not stand waiting at the door forever for a man who means to get around to Him someday. If He is calling you this week, come this week.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: IF ANYONE IS THIRSTY
pulls: Coming and drinking is believing. You do not earn living water by hauling buckets. You receive it from the One who stood up on the last day of the feast and called for the thirsty.
paras: Now on the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out. He stood and raised His voice over the crowd: If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink. Look at the gate He opens. Anyone. The only requirement is thirst, and every man in that crowd had it, whether he knew it or not.

Then He says what drinking is. He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water. Coming and drinking is believing. You do not earn the water by hauling buckets. You receive it by trusting the One who gives it. And it does not end as a cup in your hand. Rivers flow from within you, more than you can hold, running out to others.

John does not leave you guessing what the water is. But he said this about the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive. For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus wasn’t yet glorified. The living water is God Himself, the Holy Spirit, given to live in every man who believes. And He comes by a road. Jesus must first be glorified, and in John that word points to His hour: the cross, the empty grave, the return to the Father. After He rose, Jesus breathed on His disciples and said, Receive the Holy Spirit. Peter preached that the exalted Christ has poured out this, which you now see and hear.

So the Spirit is not a prize for advanced believers. He is the gift Christ died and rose to give. God promised long ago, I will put my Spirit within you, and Christ paid for that promise with His own blood. If you believe in Him, the river is yours now.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: NO MAN EVER SPOKE LIKE THIS
paras: The cry splits the crowd. Some say, This is truly the prophet. Others say, This is the Christ. Others argue from what they think they know: What, does the Christ come out of Galilee? They quote the Scripture that the Christ comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was. John lets the argument stand without stepping in. So a division arose in the multitude because of him. Jesus divides men. You cannot stand near Him for long and stay neutral.

The officers come back empty-handed. Why didn’t you bring him? Their answer is the best line in the chapter: No man ever spoke like this man. Men sent with orders went out to seize Jesus and came back seized by what He said. Nobody laid hands on Him. His words had laid hands on them.

The Pharisees sneer. Have any of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees? Then they say what they think of the people: this multitude that doesn’t know the law is cursed. The men with the most Bible looked out at the crowd and saw a curse. Jesus looked out at the same crowd and called them to drink.

One man speaks up. Nicodemus, he who came to him by night, asks whether the law judges a man before it hears him. They shut him down with a jab about Galilee. But mark Nicodemus. He will come back at the end, carrying myrrh and aloes to bury Jesus. The rulers called the crowd cursed. At the cross Christ took the curse Himself, having become a curse for us, so that cursed men could come and drink.

stations.verse: They sought therefore to take him; but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come.
stations.question: John says no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come — His cross would come on His Father’s time; whose power over me this month do I fear more than I trust that Father?
stations.gloss: to lay hold of; to seize; to take
body: Piazō means to lay hold of, to take, to seize. It can be gentle: Peter took a lame man by the right hand and raised him up. But eight of its twelve New Testament verses fall in John’s Gospel, and most of them say the same thing: men tried to seize Jesus, and could not.

The reason is never their weakness. John gives one reason only: his hour had not yet come. Jesus was keeping His Father’s time. And when the hour did come, He did not wait to be seized. He went out to meet the soldiers and gave Himself up.

The dust says your life is in the grip of whoever has the most power over you this month — the boss, the bank, the man suing you. Piazō says hands reach only as far as the Father allows. The same word closes the book, where men who caught nothing all night are fed by the risen Christ.
stations.live: Name the person or pressure that feels like it has its hands on your life this week. Write it down, and under it write: ‘My times are in my Father’s hand, not in theirs.’

stations.verse: He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.
stations.question: Jesus promised that from the inmost part of the man who believes in Him will flow rivers of living water, meaning the Spirit; what am I still pouring into that inner place instead of coming to Christ to drink?
stations.gloss: belly; womb; the inmost part of a man
body: Koilia comes from a word for hollow: the belly, the stomach, the womb. John uses it once before this, when Nicodemus asks whether a man can enter a second time into his mother’s womb. Here it is used of the heart, the inmost part of a man; the WEB gives it as from within him.

A man is hollow at the center, and every man feeds that hollow with something — work, the bottle, the screen, the nod of men he respects. None of it fills. It runs through and leaves the hole wider. Jesus does not shame the hollow. He fills it with the Spirit until it becomes a spring.

The dust says the empty place in you is proof you are a fraud. Koilia says it is the very place God means to fill. Paul could say God separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace. The God who shaped you in the womb has a river for that hollow.
stations.live: When you reach for something this week to fill the empty place — the drink, the phone, the second plate — stop with it in your hand and pray: ‘Jesus, I am thirsty. I believe You. Fill me.’

stations.verse: He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.
stations.question: Jesus promised a believer not a cup to guard but rivers of living water running out of him; who near me has been getting only the trickle I can spare, as if the Spirit Christ gives were rationed?
body: Hrheō is a plain word: to flow. It appears in only one New Testament verse, this one. In the Greek Old Testament it mostly stands for a Hebrew word for flowing. It is water on the move.

Jesus could have promised a full cup. He promised rivers of living water. The Spirit given to a believing man does not sit in him like a reserve. He flows. A forgiven father starts to forgive. A man given patience finds it running out of him toward a slow son or a sharp-tongued neighbor. The water does not stop at you.

The dust says you have to ration grace and give only to the ones who earn it. Hrheō says the source is not in you. The river runs because Christ keeps giving the Spirit, not because you keep the level up. You cannot run dry giving away water you did not make.
stations.live: Pick one person this week who has drained you. Do one kind thing for that person that costs you something, and before you do it, pray: ‘This is not from my well. Let it flow.’

stations.verse: So a division arose in the multitude because of him.
stations.question: The crowd split over one question — is this the Christ, or only a man from Galilee — and a division arose in the multitude because of him; what answer to that question would the men I work beside say my life gives?
stations.gloss: a tear; a split; a division
body: Schisma is a tear. Jesus used it of an old garment patched with unshrunk cloth, where a worse hole is made. From there it came to mean a split among people. Three of its eight New Testament verses are in John, and each time the tear runs through a crowd because of Jesus.

Read verse 43 again: a division arose in the multitude because of him. Not because of a policy or a preacher. Because of Him. Some heard Him and said, This is the Christ. Others stood in the same court and argued about Galilee. Same feast, same voice, two directions.

The dust tells you peace means keeping Jesus quiet at the supper table. Schisma says He divides men anyway, and the tear is not yours to prevent. Yet among His own people Paul pleads that there be no divisions among you. Christ divides men from the world so He can join them to one another.
stations.live: Name one relationship where you have kept quiet about Christ to keep the peace. Ask God for one plain, kind sentence about what Jesus has done for you, and say it to that person this week.

stations.verse: But this multitude that doesn’t know the law is cursed.
stations.question: The Pharisees, sure of their learning, dismissed the people listening to Jesus as a crowd that doesn’t know the law; where does my own Bible knowledge make me look down on plain men Christ is calling to Himself?
stations.gloss: accursed; under a curse called down
body: Eparatos means accursed. It comes from a verb for calling down a curse on someone. John 7:49 is its only New Testament use, and it comes from the mouth of the Pharisees: this multitude that doesn’t know the law is cursed. It is a verdict, handed down by the men who claimed to know the law best.

Look at who they cursed. The crowd — the people without the rulers’ learning, who had listened to Jesus and wondered out loud whether He was the Christ. The rulers saw a curse. Jesus had already stood up and called those same people to come and drink.

The dust may have cursed you the same way — not enough schooling, not enough Bible, too far gone. Hear the answer of the gospel: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. He carried the curse itself to the cross, so that cursed men could be welcomed to the water.
stations.live: Think of a man you have quietly written off — at work, at church, in your own family. Pray for him by name every day this week: ‘The water is offered to him too. Lord, draw him.’

practices.title: ADMIT THE THIRST
practices.body: Jesus called out to anyone who is thirsty, and the only way to answer Him is to admit you are. Sit down early one morning this week and write one plain sentence about where you are dry: no joy in prayer, no patience at home, no hunger for the Word. Then read 7:37 out loud over it. You have not shut yourself out by writing that sentence. You have just met His one requirement. Thirst does not keep you from Him. He called for it.

practices.title: DRINK BY BELIEVING
practices.body: In this chapter, coming and drinking is believing. Each morning this week, before the coffee is done, tell Jesus one thing you believe about Him from John 7: that the Father sent Him, that His hour was never in men’s hands, that He gives the Spirit to all who believe in Him. Say it slowly, out loud. You are not priming a pump. You are taking a drink from the One who offered it, and His well does not run dry.

practices.title: THANK HIM FOR THE SPIRIT IN YOU
practices.body: The Spirit was not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified. Now He has been — crucified, raised, and gone up to the Father — and the Spirit has been poured out. If you believe, He lives in you. Once a day this week, stop what you are doing, put your hand flat on your chest, and thank God out loud that His Spirit lives there. Not because you feel Him. Because Christ promised Him, and Christ keeps His word.

practices.title: LET ONE THING FLOW OUT
practices.body: Rivers flow out, not in. Pick one person in your house who has been getting the dry end of you — the short answers, the sighs, the silence at the end of the day. Ask the Spirit for one specific grace toward that person, and then give it: an apology, an hour of listening, a chore done before anyone asks. What He gives you is not yours to dam up. It was given to run, and there is more where it came from.

practices.title: STAND WITH THE CROWD
practices.body: Jesus called the very crowd the rulers had cursed. Nicodemus was one of those rulers, and he still said the hard thing in the room: hear a man before you judge him. This week, when someone near you is being written off — a coworker, a man at church, a kid down the road — be the voice that asks for fairness. You may get mocked for it, as he was. Christ was not ashamed of that crowd, and He is not ashamed of you.

title: Rivers of Living Water
subtitle: from dust to the Spirit poured out
keyVerse: He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.

passage.text: Therefore some of them of Jerusalem said, “Isn’t this he whom they seek to kill?
Behold, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Can it be that the rulers indeed know that this is truly the Christ?
However we know where this man comes from, but when the Christ comes, no one will know where he comes from.”
Jesus therefore cried out in the temple, teaching and saying, “You both know me, and know where I am from. I have not come of myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you don’t know.
I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.”
They sought therefore to take him; but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come.
But of the multitude, many believed in him. They said, “When the Christ comes, he won’t do more signs than those which this man has done, will he?”
The Pharisees heard the multitude murmuring these things concerning him, and the chief priests and the Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.
Then Jesus said, “I will be with you a little while longer, then I go to him who sent me.
You will seek me, and won’t find me. You can’t come where I am.”
The Jews therefore said among themselves, “Where will this man go that we won’t find him? Will he go to the Dispersion among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks?
What is this word that he said, ‘You will seek me, and won’t find me;’ and ‘Where I am, you can’t come’?”
Now on the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!
He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.”
But he said this about the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive. For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus wasn’t yet glorified.
Many of the multitude therefore, when they heard these words, said, “This is truly the prophet.”
Others said, “This is the Christ.” But some said, “What, does the Christ come out of Galilee?
Hasn’t the Scripture said that the Christ comes of the offspring of David, and from Bethlehem, the village where David was?”
So a division arose in the multitude because of him.
Some of them would have arrested him, but no one laid hands on him.
The officers therefore came to the chief priests and Pharisees, and they said to them, “Why didn’t you bring him?”
The officers answered, “No man ever spoke like this man!”
The Pharisees therefore answered them, “You aren’t also led astray, are you?
Have any of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees?
But this multitude that doesn’t know the law is cursed.”
Nicodemus (he who came to him by night, being one of them) said to them,
“Does our law judge a man, unless it first hears from him personally and knows what he does?”
They answered him, “Are you also from Galilee? Search, and see that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee.”

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE LIVING WATER
stationsIntro: These five words run from the hands that could not seize Jesus to the curse the rulers spoke over the crowd. Read each verse slowly, answer it as yourself, and let the Greek open a little more of the river He promised.
lifeIntro: On the last day of the feast Jesus stood and called every thirsty man to come and drink, and He was glorified so that the Spirit could be poured out on all who believe. The river is His gift, not your project. The five practices below are ways to keep coming back to drink.
lifePulls: The rulers looked at the crowd and saw a curse. Jesus looked at the same crowd and called them to drink. Christ became a curse so that thirsty, cursed men could come to Him and never go dry.
prayer: Father, You sent Your Son, and no hand could touch Him until His hour came. Thank You that Jesus stood up on the last day of the feast and called for the thirsty. I am dry, and I have tried to hide it and to fix it myself. I come to Him now, and I believe Him. Thank You that He was glorified, and that the Spirit He promised has been poured out. Fill the hollow place in me with Your Spirit. Let what You give flow out to the people in my house and the men I work beside. Keep me from cursing anyone You are calling to drink. Hold my days in Your hand, as You held His. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You sent Your Son, and no hand could touch Him until His hour came.
Thank You that Jesus stood up on the last day of the feast and called for the
thirsty.
I am dry, and I have tried to hide it and to fix it myself.
I come to Him now, and I believe Him.
Thank You that He was glorified, and that the Spirit He promised has been
poured out.
Fill the hollow place in me with Your Spirit.
Let what You give flow out to the people in my house and the men I work beside.
Keep me from cursing anyone You are calling to drink.
Hold my days in Your hand, as You held His.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Jesus stood on the last day of the feast and called every thirsty man to come and drink. Coming is believing. The water is the Holy Spirit, given because Christ was glorified — crucified, raised, and returned to the Father. No hand could seize Him early, and no curse the rulers spoke could shut the crowd out. Stop hiding your thirst. Stop digging your own well. Come to Him and drink.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and hear who is calling. He is the One the officers could not bring in. He is the One whose hour no ruler could hurry. He is the One who stood on the last and greatest day of the feast, with men sent to arrest Him standing in the crowd, and raised His voice for you. He did not call for the strong, or the learned, or the men who had kept the feast best. He called for the thirsty: If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink.

The dust has told you that your dryness shuts you out. It has told you the Spirit belongs to other men, and that if you want water you had better start digging. And it has told you the rulers have the last word — that men who know more and pray better have looked you over and called you cursed. But the rulers did not have the last word in John 7, and they do not have it over you. The officers came back with empty hands and full ears. No man ever spoke like this man.

Then He went to His hour. The One no hand could seize gave Himself up. He was lifted on a cross, and the curse the rulers were so quick to speak fell on Him. He was laid in a new tomb in a garden, and He came out of it alive, and He went up to the Father glorified. From the Father’s right hand He has poured out the Spirit He promised — not a ration, not a trickle, but rivers. He did not hold back the best gift until you proved yourself. The water that was not yet given on the day of the feast has been given now.

So carry this into the week. If you believe in Him, the Spirit of God lives in you, and He is not leaving. You will have dry mornings. Come to Him on those mornings and drink again, as many times as it takes, because He does not run out and He does not turn away the man who comes. The hollow place in you that the dust called proof of failure is the very place Christ has made a spring. Out of it, by His own promise, will flow rivers of living water.
closingVerse: He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.
carry: Jesus said that out of the man who believes in Him will flow rivers of living water, and He meant the Spirit; what dry place will you bring to Him this week to drink, instead of digging at it on your own?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man has a night he would not want read out loud. Maybe it is one night. Maybe it is a whole year. The search history, the money moved where it should not have gone, the woman who was not his wife, the words he said to his son that he cannot take back. He keeps it locked away. And the fear he carries is simple: if anyone ever drags it into the light, he is finished. So he keeps the door shut and his voice low, and he never quite looks anyone in the eye.

The dust tells you that your worst night is who you are. It says that once your sin is out, there is nothing left for you but stones. Then it tells a second lie, quieter and more pleasant. It puts a stone in your hand and stands you in the circle. It points at the other man — the one who got caught, the one whose marriage came apart in public, the one everybody at church is talking about — and lets you feel clean by comparison. Most men have lived inside both lies, sometimes in the same afternoon.

Both lies keep you face down. The man who is caught lies in the dust in shame. The man with the stone is just as low; he only cannot see it yet. Both men need the same mercy, and both can ask for it in the same words: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) John 7:53–8:11 gives that word in a temple court at dawn. It is spoken by the only man present who had the right to throw, and it is this: Neither do I condemn you.

sections.heading: Early Morning in the Temple
pulls: The dust says your worst night is who you are, and then it hands you a stone for the other man. Christ stands in the middle of the circle with the only clean hands there, and He does not throw.
paras: Last week ended with the rulers arguing, and then Everyone went to his own house. Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Now very early in the morning, he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him. He sat down and taught them. The earliest manuscripts of John do not contain this account; the WEB prints it, and this study teaches it as printed.

Into that morning class walk the scribes and the Pharisees with a woman and a question. Jesus is sitting, teaching the people who came to Him. He has not gone looking for a fight. The fight is carried in to Him. These men are not asking to be taught. John tells you they were testing him, that they might have something to accuse him of. Read the passage twice before you go on. The first time, stand where the woman stands. The second time, look down at your own hand and see what is in it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: SET IN THE MIDDLE
paras: The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery. Having set her in the middle, they put their case to Jesus. John does not soften what she did. Adultery is the breaking of the marriage covenant, and she was caught in it — in the very act, they say. There is no talk of a misunderstanding. She was guilty, and no one in the court disputed it.

Notice what they do with her. They set her in the middle, in front of everyone, while Jesus is teaching. Her sin is real, but to them she is not a soul to be won. She is the bait for a trap. Then they reach for the law: Now in our law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. What then do you say about her? The law of Moses did name death for adultery. It named it for both — the adulterer and the adulteress. John says nothing about the man. He was not brought.

Do not look for yourself only among the Pharisees. Some men reading this have been the one set in the middle — found out, named in front of the people whose good opinion mattered most. If that is you, look at where they set her. In the middle of the court, yes. But also right in front of Jesus. They meant it as a trap. It turned out to be the one place in Jerusalem that morning where mercy was standing.

And mark this before you go further. The law was not wrong. Her sin was not small. Whatever Jesus does next, He will not do it by pretending adultery is nothing. He is about to show a better way through than the stones.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: HE STOOPED DOWN
paras: Jesus does not answer right away. But Jesus stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger. John does not tell you what He wrote, and you do not need to know. What you need to see is the posture. The accusers stand over the woman. Jesus bends low, toward the dust. Men who want a verdict stand tall. He gets low.

They keep pressing Him, and he looked up and said to them: He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her. He does not set the law aside. He does not say adultery is nothing. He agrees that sin deserves judgment — and then He asks who is fit to carry it out. The question lands on every man in the circle at once.

Again he stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger. He gives them time. Their trap has not touched Him. He does not stand over them glaring. He lets one question do its work while He bends to the ground again. That is how He deals with your sin too. He does not pile on. He asks one true question and gives you room to hear it.

Now look at your own hand. The stone is the side comment about the man who left his wife. It is the grudge you have kept polished for eleven years. It is the quiet satisfaction you felt when the other man’s sin came out and yours did not. Jesus has not asked you whether that man deserves it. He has asked whether you are without sin. He has not asked whether you would ever do what that man did.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ONE BY ONE
pulls: Only one man in that court was without sin, and He was the one standing in front of her. The only One with the right to throw the stone is the One who came to bear its weight.
paras: They, when they heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last. No one argued. Not one man claimed to be clean. Not one stone left a hand. A single question from Jesus emptied the court of accusers, and John records the order: the oldest first, and so on down to the last.

John does not tell you why the oldest went first. He only writes it down. But any man with gray in his beard knows that the longer you live, the longer the list you carry. Years do not make a man cleaner. They give him more time to learn what is in him. The young man with a stone has the same heart; he only has fewer years of evidence.

Then comes the line to stop on: Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle. The crowd of accusers thinned until two people were left in the middle of the court — the guilty woman and the one man who was without sin. He had said the sinless man should throw first. Only one man there qualified. He was the one standing in front of her.

Hold on to that. The one man with the right to condemn you is the same man who came to save you. God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him. The stones went out of the court one by one in the hands of the men who carried them. His hands stayed empty — and before long they would be nailed open for sinners like her, and like you.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: FROM NOW ON
paras: Jesus, standing up, saw her and asked, Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you? She answers, No one, Lord. It is the only thing John records her saying. Three words, and one of them is Lord.

Then Jesus speaks, and the order of His words matters more than anything else in this passage. Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more. Pardon first. Then the command. He does not say, stop sinning and then I will not condemn you. He says, I do not condemn you — now go, and sin no more. The mercy is not a reward for her change. It is the ground she will stand on to change.

How can He say it? Not because adultery is small. Not because He is soft. He can say Neither do I condemn you because He was going to be condemned in the place of sinners like her. For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf; so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. The sinless man did not throw the stone. He bore the blow. The verdict she earned fell on Him at the cross, and He was raised from the dead with the debt settled.

So hear both words, in that order, if you have believed in Him. There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus. That is no permission to go back to the old sin. Sin no more is real, and it is hard. But it is spoken to a forgiven woman, not a woman on trial. You fight your sin this week as a man already let go, not to earn the pardon but because you have it.

stations.verse: The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery. Having set her in the middle.
stations.question: Her accusers set a woman taken in adultery in the middle, her sin out in front of everyone and in front of Jesus; what sin have I hidden from Him because I expect Him to treat me as they treated her?
body: Moicheia is adultery, the breaking of the marriage bond. The Greek Old Testament uses it in Hosea and Jeremiah, where the prophets charge God’s own people with it. In John 8 it is the charge against the woman, and it was true.

But listen to Jesus elsewhere: out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries. Adultery does not start in a bed. It starts in the place every sin starts, and every man in that court had that place in him. The Pharisees held up her sin as if it belonged to another kind of person. Jesus traces it to a heart like theirs.

The dust tells the man who has fallen here that he is past washing. It tells the man who has not that he is safe. In John 8, moicheia is named plainly and then met by a Savior who does not condemn the woman caught in it. Paul could write to men who had done this very thing: you were washed.
stations.live: If this sin is in your past or your present, name it to God plainly this week, without a softer word. Then read His answer back to yourself: ‘Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.’

stations.verse: They said this testing him, that they might have something to accuse him of. But Jesus stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger.
stations.question: The scribes used a guilty woman as bait that they might have something to accuse him of; when another man’s sin comes to light near me, what do I tend to use it for?
stations.gloss: to bow the head; to stoop down
body: Kyptō means to bow the head, to stoop down. Outside John 8 it appears once, on the lips of John the Baptist, who said he was not worthy to stoop down and loosen the strap of Christ’s sandals. To stoop is to go low.

Now look at the temple court. John the Baptist said he was not fit to bend down at Jesus’ feet. Here Jesus Himself bends down, twice, in front of a woman caught in sin and the men who wanted her dead. The One John was unworthy to serve stoops. He goes low first. He does not wait for sinners to climb up to Him.

The dust says God looks down on you from a height, arms folded. Kyptō says He bends. Christ humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. The stooping in the temple court was a small picture of the great one. He came all the way down to where you lie.
stations.live: When you pray this week about the sin you are most ashamed of, picture Him bending low, not standing over you. Then say: ‘You came down to where I am. I will not hide from You.’

stations.verse: They said this testing him, that they might have something to accuse him of. But Jesus stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger.
stations.question: Pressed for a ruling, Jesus stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger and gave the accusers no quick verdict; where have I been quicker than Christ to pass a verdict on another man’s sin?
stations.gloss: to write down; to inscribe; to record
body: Katagraphō is a word about marks. In wider Greek it could mean to scratch, to engrave laws, to fill a tablet with writing, to write something down as a record. It appears in no other New Testament verse. Here it is Jesus’ finger moving on the ground.

John does not tell you what He wrote. Any guess goes past the text, so leave it there. What the text does show is this: the accusers came with a charge already drawn up, and Jesus answered with His finger in the dust and one question. They came holding a record against her. They went out convicted by their conscience.

The dust keeps a record against you and reads it back every night. It keeps one against the other man too, so you can feel better. If you, Yah, kept a record of sins, Lord, who could stand? No one could. But there is forgiveness with you. Whatever His finger wrote that morning, the woman walked away uncondemned.
stations.live: Write down one grudge or one record you have been keeping on another man. Pray over it, tear it up, and say: ‘Lord, You do not keep this list on me. I will not keep it on him.’

stations.verse: But when they continued asking him, he looked up and said to them, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.
stations.question: Jesus did not deny the woman’s guilt; He turned every accuser to his own heart with He who is without sin among you; what stone am I holding right now that this sentence tells me to put down?
body: Anamartētos is formed from the verb for sinning, and it means without sin, faultless. In other Greek writing it could mean unerring, a man who does not miss. The New Testament has it nowhere else. Jesus sets it in the center of the court as a test: He who is without sin among you.

That one word cleared the court. No man there could claim it. No man reading this can either. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. The stone in your hand needs a clean hand to throw it, and you do not have one.

But the word does fit one man. Scripture says Christ was tempted in all points like you, yet without sin. The dust says the only answer to sin is a stone. Anamartētos points you to the only sinless man who ever lived — and He used His clean hands to save, not to throw.
stations.live: The next time you feel the stone in your hand this week — the comment, the look, the story about another man — stop and say under your breath: ‘I am not without sin. He is, and He did not throw.’

stations.verse: They, when they heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last. Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle.
stations.question: The accusers, convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, and left the woman alone with Jesus; when my conscience convicts me, what keeps me from staying where she stayed?
body: Presbyteros is the comparative of a word for an old man: older, elder. It can mean simply the older of two, as with the father’s elder son in Luke 15. It can mean a man of rank — the elders of the people, and later the elders of the church. In John 8 the WEB gives it as the oldest.

John says the accusers left beginning from the oldest, even to the last. He gives no reason. He simply records that the men with the most years were the first to drop their stones. A long life gives a man a great deal to answer for.

The dust tells an older man that his years have made him respectable, that age has cleaned him. Presbyteros in this verse says otherwise. But there is hope here for old and young alike. Every accuser walked out. The one who stayed in the middle with Jesus is the one who heard Neither do I condemn you.
stations.live: If you are older, ask a younger man to breakfast this week and tell him one thing God has forgiven you. If you are younger, ask an older man of faith to tell you his.

practices.title: DROP THE STONE YOU ARE HOLDING
practices.body: Jesus asked one question and the court emptied. Name the person you have been holding a stone for — the brother who wrecked his marriage, the pastor who fell, the neighbor everyone talks about. Write the name down. Under it, in your own hand, write: I am not without sin. Pray for that person by name every day this week, and do not tell one more soul what they did. Christ did not broadcast her sin. You have no call to broadcast theirs.

practices.title: STAY IN THE MIDDLE WITH JESUS
practices.body: The accusers walked out, but the woman stayed where she was and was left alone with Jesus. If your sin has come out, or you are afraid it will, do not run from Him. Go to Him first this week, before you go to anyone else, and tell Him plainly what you did. Then hear what He says to everyone who believes in Him: no condemnation. He has already borne the verdict, and He does not hand it back.

practices.title: HEAR THE WORDS IN ORDER
practices.body: Christ spoke pardon before command. Write 8:11 on a card: Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more. Keep it in your shirt pocket or your lunch pail. Read it every time you are tempted this week, and read it in order. A man who fights sin to earn the first sentence will lose. A man who fights from the first sentence fights as one already set free. Start every fight this week with His first word.

practices.title: SHUT THE DOOR SIN USES
practices.body: Sin no more is a real command, and it was given to a forgiven woman. Name the one place your sin keeps happening — the phone after eleven, the bar on the drive home, the private conversation that should not be private. Make one concrete change this week that cuts off the way in: a password handed to your wife, a different road home, a conversation ended. You do this not to stay forgiven. You do it because you are. Tell one brother what you changed, and let him ask you about it.

practices.title: GO LOW TOWARD THE CAUGHT
practices.body: Christ stooped toward a woman everyone else stood over. When a man near you is caught in sin this week — at work, at church, in your own family — go low toward him, not over him. Paul says you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted. Call him. Sit with him. Do not lecture him. Tell him where mercy stood that morning. He may be lying where you once lay.

title: Neither Do I Condemn You
subtitle: from dust to mercy at the feet of Christ
keyVerse: She said, “No one, Lord.” Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.

passage.text: Everyone went to his own house,
but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.
Now very early in the morning, he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him. He sat down and taught them.
The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery. Having set her in the middle,
they told him, “Teacher, we found this woman in adultery, in the very act.
Now in our law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. What then do you say about her?”
They said this testing him, that they might have something to accuse him of. But Jesus stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger.
But when they continued asking him, he looked up and said to them, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.”
Again he stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger.
They, when they heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last. Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle.
Jesus, standing up, saw her and said, “Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?”
She said, “No one, Lord.” Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.”

stationsIntro: These five words follow one morning from the charge of adultery to the oldest accuser walking away. Take each verse slowly, answer it as yourself, and let the Greek put you in that court — with the stone, and with the woman.
lifeIntro: This week is not about learning to throw straighter or duck faster. Jesus has already stooped, stood, cleared the court, and spoken the word that settles the case: Neither do I condemn you. Here are five ways to live as a man who has heard it.
lifePulls: Pardon first, then the command. Jesus did not tell her to stop sinning so that He would not condemn her. He refused to condemn her, and then He sent her out to sin no more.
prayer: Father, You sent Your Son into the world not to judge it, but to save it. I confess I have stood in the circle with a stone in my hand. I confess I have also lain in the dust, afraid of being found out. Thank You that Jesus stooped down to where sinners lie. Thank You that the only One without sin did not throw, but bore the judgment I deserved. Let me hear Him say, Neither do I condemn you, and let me believe it. Then give me grace to go my way and sin no more. Make me gentle with every man caught in what I could have done. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You sent Your Son into the world not to judge it, but to save it.
I confess I have stood in the circle with a stone in my hand.
I confess I have also lain in the dust, afraid of being found out.
Thank You that Jesus stooped down to where sinners lie.
Thank You that the only One without sin did not throw, but bore the judgment I
deserved.
Let me hear Him say, Neither do I condemn you, and let me believe it.
Then give me grace to go my way and sin no more.
Make me gentle with every man caught in what I could have done.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: They brought a guilty woman and a stone for every hand. Jesus stooped, asked one question, and the court emptied from the oldest to the last. Only the sinless man remained, and He did not throw. Neither do I condemn you came first; sin no more came second. He could say it because He would be condemned in the place of sinners like her. Drop your stone. Stand before Him. Go, forgiven, and sin no more.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, past the circle and the stones, to the one man still in the court with her. Not the scribes. Not the Pharisees. Not the oldest man with the heaviest stone, and not the last man out with his arm still cocked. Every accuser has gone, one by one, and only Jesus remains — the One who stooped to the ground, the One who asked the question no man could answer, the One without sin. He is the only one who could have thrown. And He is looking at you.

The dust has kept you on both sides of that circle. Some days you stood with the stone and felt clean because the other man got caught. Other days you lay in the middle of the court of your own mind, sure that if the truth came out you were finished. Both places are low. Both are dust. You were never meant to live in either one. And Jesus walked into the middle of all of it, bent down, and would not let the stones decide the morning.

Then He did what no one in that court yet understood. He went to the cross and stood where she stood — in the middle, condemned, with the whole weight of the law against Him. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree. The judgment due to every sinner who comes to Him — the caught and the stone-holders alike — fell on Him instead. He did not cast the first stone. He took the full weight of every one. And on the first day of the week the Father raised Him from the dead, the debt paid in full, so that the pardon He spoke would stand forever.

So here is what you carry into this week. If you have believed in Him, He has already said it to you, and He will not take it back: Neither do I condemn you. There is no court left that can try you. Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, and He has spoken for you. Tomorrow morning, when the old shame wakes up before you do, answer it with His words, not your own. Stand up out of the dust a pardoned man. Go your way. And from now on, by the same grace that let you go, sin no more.
closingVerse: She said, “No one, Lord.” Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.
carry: Jesus told the woman Neither do I condemn you before He told her From now on, sin no more; which sin will you fight this week as a man already pardoned rather than a man still on trial?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men do not think they live in the dark. They think the light is a little low. A dim stretch, a hard year, a season when things are tough to make out. You can still find the door. You still get to work, pay the fuel bill and keep the books close to square. A man who can do all that does not feel blind. He feels tired. So he reaches for what tired men reach for — a better plan, stronger coffee, a few more hours of sleep — and calls that seeing.

The dust is good at this lie because darkness does not announce itself. A man who has worked his whole life underground does not miss the sun. He learns the tunnels by feel. He knows where the low beams are. He can cross his own house with the lights off, and takes that for knowing the way to God. In this passage men stand within arm’s reach of the Light of the world and ask Him, Where is your Father?

A second lie runs underneath the first. It tells you death is far off and sin is a habit to keep out of sight. Jesus says something harder. He says a man can die in his sins: carry them all the way to the grave, and through it, still wearing them. The dust would rather you never heard that sentence. But it is the sentence that puts a man on his knees, and a man on his knees has one prayer left, which is enough: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) John 8:12–30 is that reviving word. Jesus says He is the light of the world, and that whoever follows Him will have the light of life.

sections.heading: Light Spoken in a Hostile Room
pulls: The dust tells you the light is only a little low. Jesus tells you the truth: without Him a man walks in darkness and dies in his sins. Then He says, I am the light of the world.
paras: The scene is still the temple, in the wake of the Feast of Booths. In John 7 the crowd split over Jesus. Some said he leads the multitude astray. The officers sent to seize Him came back empty-handed, and the rulers sneered at anyone who believed. Then, very early in the morning, He was back in the temple teaching. Verse 12 opens with a small word: Again. He had been plotted against and shouted down, and He spoke again anyway. The Light does not wait for a friendly crowd.

John tells you exactly where He stood: in the treasury, as he taught in the temple. What follows is no calm lesson. It is a contest of witnesses, then a warning, then a word about a cross.
