Read 8:12–30 aloud before you go further. Mark how often Jesus says the Father who sent me. Watch how it ends — not with the whole court won over, but with John’s plain report: many believed in him. He wrote his whole book for that sentence, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD
paras: I am the light of the world. Jesus does not say He has some light, or that He will point you toward it. He says He is it. The world is the dark room, and He is the lamp. John told you so at the head of his book: In him was life, and the life was the light of men. Now the man from Nazareth stands up in the temple and says it in the first person.

Israel had a picture for it. When God brought His people out of Egypt, He went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light. They did not plot the route. They watched the fire and moved when it moved. That is the shape of what Jesus offers. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness. Following is not one decision made once and filed away. It is a man walking behind someone, step after step.

Look at the two promises. First, the follower will not walk in the darkness. The dark is still out there. But the man behind Jesus is not walking in it any longer. Second, he will have the light of life. Not borrowed light. The life of God Himself, given to a man made of dust.

This comes first, before anything is asked of you. Jesus does not say, Find enough light and then you may follow Me. He says, I am the light. The light is already burning. Your part is the part of a man lost in a dark field who sees a lantern and walks toward it.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: TWO WITNESSES
paras: The Pharisees answer with a point of order. You testify about yourself. Your testimony is not valid. It is a fair rule: one man’s word about himself does not settle a case. Jesus grants their law and then shows them who is in the witness box. My testimony is true, for I know where I came from, and where I am going. He came from the Father. He is going back to the Father. They know neither end of His road, so they judge Him the way they judge any man — according to the flesh.

Then He calls His second witness. I am not alone, but I am with the Father who sent me. The law asked for two. Here they are: the Son who speaks and the Father who sent Him. Their reply shows how dark it is in that court. Where is your Father? They want a man they can summon. Jesus tells them plainly, If you knew me, you would know my Father also. There is no going around the Son to get to God.

You do the same thing in your own way. You want God to step into court on your terms — sworn in, cross-examined, made to answer for the year you had. But God has already testified. He sent His Son. The witness you are waiting for has been standing in front of you the whole time.

John closes the scene quietly. Jesus said all this in the treasury, within reach of every man who hated Him. Yet no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come. The Father set the hour — not the crowd, not the rulers, not the officers. Your hours rest in the same hand.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: DIE IN YOUR SINS
pulls: No man climbs from beneath to above. The One from above came down, spoke God’s own name in the temple court, and let Himself be lifted up on a cross — so that you would not die in your sins.
paras: Now Jesus says the hardest thing in the passage. I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sins. Where I go, you can’t come. He says it twice more by verse 24. He does not throw it in anger. He says it the way a doctor reads a scan to a man who will not look at it. Left alone, sin is the clothing a man is buried in.

His hearers cannot follow Him. They wonder aloud whether He means to kill Himself. Jesus answers by naming the distance. You are from beneath. I am from above. You are of this world. I am not of this world. That is where the whole race stands — below, of this world, with no ladder long enough. No man climbs out of the dust by his own grip.

Then He opens the door. Unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins. The way out is a Person. The WEB adds he; the words Jesus spoke are simply I am. They echo what God said to Moses at the burning bush: I AM WHO I AM. The Man from above is taking the name of the God who brought Israel out of slavery.

So the hard word has a door in it. The way not to die in your sins is not to scrub them out. It is to believe in Him — to rest your whole weight on the One from above who bears God’s own name. The same breath that warns you tells you how not to.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: WHEN YOU HAVE LIFTED UP
paras: Who are you? they ask. It is the right question asked with arms folded. Jesus gives them nothing new. Just what I have been saying to you from the beginning. He has said it at Cana, at the well, on the hillside with the bread. He has nothing to take back. And John adds a sad line: They didn’t understand that he spoke to them about the Father.

So Jesus tells them when they will understand. When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he. Lifted up is John’s cross word. He used it with Nicodemus about the serpent on the pole, and later John explains it: he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die. The darkest thing men ever did — nailing the Light to a beam — became the place the Light shone clearest. At the cross you see who He is. The I AM let Himself be lifted up for men from beneath.

See what held Him steady through it. He who sent me is with me. The Father hasn’t left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him. Always. Not most days. Every word and act of the Son pleased the Father, and that whole obedience is what God counts to the man who believes. You have not always done what pleases God. He has, in your place.

And the passage ends where John wants every chapter to end. As he spoke these things, many believed in him. The same words that hardened some men opened others. The Light did not change. What opened their eyes was the mercy of God. Ask Him for that mercy, and then walk behind Him.

stations.verse: The Pharisees therefore said to him, “You testify about yourself. Your testimony is not valid.
stations.question: The Pharisees heard Jesus say I am the light of the world and answered, Your testimony is not valid; where am I still waiting for more proof before I take Him at His word about Himself?
stations.gloss: true; real, conforming to what actually is
body: Alēthēs is tied to a verb for escaping notice. At root it means unconcealed, out in the open — and so actual, real, true to fact. Of words it means true; of persons, truthful. It appears in 25 New Testament verses, and more than half of them are in John’s Gospel.

The Pharisees use it to throw Jesus out of court: Your testimony is not valid. One verse later He picks up the same word and hands it back to them: my testimony is true. They meant His word had not been proved. He meant it matched what is. He stood in open daylight telling them what is.

The dust wants the truth about you kept covered — the second drink, the money, the coldness at home — and wants Jesus kept on trial so His word never lands. Alēthēs says the Light hides nothing. And the truth He tells about your darkness comes bound to the truth that He came to save you from it.
stations.live: Take one thing Jesus says about you in this passage — that without Him you walk in darkness — and stop cross-examining it. Agree with Him out loud: ‘You are true. I am in the dark without You.’

stations.verse: Even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for I am not alone, but I am with the Father who sent me.
stations.question: Jesus said His judgment is true because I am not alone, but I am with the Father who sent me; which hard word of His about my sin have I treated as less than the Father’s own word?
body: Pempō is the plain verb for sending — a man, a message, a gift. In the Greek Old Testament it chiefly stands for the Hebrew shalach. In the New Testament it is used of teachers sent by God. Of its 78 New Testament verses, 31 are in John’s Gospel, most of them in the phrase Jesus will not stop saying: him who sent me.

In verse 16 the sending is His defense. I am not alone, but I am with the Father who sent me. Jesus never speaks on His own account. Every word in the temple court comes with the Father behind it. And the One who sent Him does not drop Him off and drive away: He who sent me is with me.

The dust says God is waiting for you to come find Him, and will grade you on how hard you looked. Pempō says the Father moved first. He sent His Son into the dark after you. And the Son, risen, sends His own: As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.
stations.live: Each morning this week, before you head out, say the sentence Jesus kept saying and make it yours: ‘The Father sent His Son for me. I did not find Him. He was sent.’

stations.verse: Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, as he taught in the temple. Yet no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.
stations.question: Jesus said these things openly, in the treasury, as he taught in the temple, a few steps from men who wanted Him seized; where have I kept my faith in Him quiet because I fear what people could do?
stations.gloss: a treasury; the temple’s store of offerings
body: Gazophylakion is a treasury. In the Greek Old Testament it names the temple’s treasure chambers. The New Testament has it in only four verses. Three are in Mark and Luke, where Jesus watches the rich people who were putting their gifts into the treasury, and a poor widow drops in two small coins. The fourth is here.

So the Light of the world spoke His great word about light in the place where giving was done. Men brought what they had and dropped it in. Jesus stood among them giving what no one could pay for. And John adds that no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come. In the place where everything was counted, the Father was keeping a different count.
The dust keeps books on you: what you have given, what you have done, what God owes you for it. Gazophylakion says the light was handed out in the treasury, free, and not one coin was asked for it.
stations.live: Write down what you have been quietly counting as your deposit with God — the years, the tithe, the help you gave. Then pray over the list: ‘None of this bought the light. You gave it to me free.’

stations.verse: Jesus said therefore again to them, “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sins. Where I go, you can’t come.
stations.question: Jesus warned the men around Him, you will die in your sins, and then named the only way out — believing that He is I AM; what am I trusting, besides Him, to keep me from dying in mine?
body: Apothnēskō means to die. The New Testament uses it of natural death, of violent death — above all the death of Christ — and of the spiritual death of a man cut off from God. It appears in 100 New Testament verses. In John 8:21 and 8:24 it stands with the small word en: to die in your sins.

The same verb stands with another small word, the one English renders for, to say what Christ did. Christ died for us. Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures. One verb, two little words, and between them the whole gospel. Either a man dies in his sins, or Christ dies for them.

The dust says the grave is a long way off and your sins are light enough to carry. Apothnēskō will not let you sleep on that. But it does not leave you there either. The sins you would have died in, Christ died for — once, in your place, and it is finished.
stations.live: Name before God one sin you have been treating as too small to matter. Then lay it at the cross by name: ‘I will not die in this. Christ died for this.’

stations.verse: He said to them, “You are from beneath. I am from above. You are of this world. I am not of this world.
stations.question: Jesus told His hearers, You are from beneath. I am from above; where am I still trying to close that distance by my own effort instead of trusting the One who came down?
body: Katō is a plain word of direction: down, downward, below, beneath. Here Jesus sets the things below against the things above: You are from beneath. I am from above. It appears in eight New Testament verses. In two of them the devil sets Jesus on the temple and tells Him to throw Himself down.

The line between below and above is the line no man crosses on his own. You were born below. So was every man you know. But mark where else the word turns up. When Jesus died, the veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom. From above to below. God tore the way open from His side.

The dust tells you to build a ladder — more effort, more church, more control. Katō says you are below, and no ladder reaches. Then the torn veil says the One from above came all the way down to where you are, and opened the way from the top.
stations.live: When you catch yourself trying to earn your way upward this week, stop and read Mark 15:38. Then say it plainly: ‘You tore it from the top. I come in through what You opened.’

practices.title: WALK BEHIND HIM
practices.body: Jesus did not say, Whoever studies me, or whoever admires me. He said, He who follows me will not walk in the darkness. Pick one decision you have been making in the dark — the money, the job offer, the talk you owe your wife. Before you settle it, read John 8:12 and ask one plain question: where is Jesus walking in this? Then take the next step behind Him, not out ahead of Him. Light for one step is enough to walk by.

practices.title: STOP PUTTING HIM ON TRIAL
practices.body: The Pharisees put Jesus in the witness box. Men still do. Notice where you do it — the prayer you will not believe until God proves Himself, the promise you hold at arm’s length. Write down one promise Jesus makes in this passage and carry it in your shirt pocket all week. Each time you pull it out, drop the cross-examination and agree with what He said of Himself: my testimony is true.

practices.title: NAME THE SINS YOU WOULD DIE IN
practices.body: Jesus said it three times: you will die in your sins. Sit down one evening with a sheet of paper and write out the sins you have been treating as small — the grudge, the screen at midnight, the sharp word to your son. Do not dress them up. Then write across the top of the page: Christ died for these. Burn the sheet in the stove or the burn barrel, and let the fire say what the cross already said.

practices.title: SAY HIS NAME RIGHT
practices.body: On one morning this week, read Exodus 3:13–15 and then John 8:24 and 8:28. Mark the words I AM. The Man who stood in the temple court is the God who spoke from the bush. When you pray this week, do not speak to Jesus as a helpful teacher or a good example. Speak to Him as the Lord from above. Then watch what it does to your fear to remember who is listening.

practices.title: GO TO THE CROSS FOR THE ANSWER
practices.body: Jesus said, When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he. When the question of who He is goes cloudy for you — after a funeral, in a long dry spell, on the night shift with nothing but your own thoughts — do not go looking for a new sign. Read John 19:16–30 slowly. That is where the Light shows you who He is, and how far down He came for you.

title: The Light of Life
subtitle: from dust to light that darkness cannot hold
keyVerse: Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.

passage.text: Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.”
The Pharisees therefore said to him, “You testify about yourself. Your testimony is not valid.”
Jesus answered them, “Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from, and where I am going; but you don’t know where I came from, or where I am going.
You judge according to the flesh. I judge no one.
Even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for I am not alone, but I am with the Father who sent me.
It’s also written in your law that the testimony of two people is valid.
I am one who testifies about myself, and the Father who sent me testifies about me.”
They said therefore to him, “Where is your Father?” Jesus answered, “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also.”
Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, as he taught in the temple. Yet no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.
Jesus said therefore again to them, “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sins. Where I go, you can’t come.”
The Jews therefore said, “Will he kill himself, because he says, ‘Where I am going, you can’t come’?”
He said to them, “You are from beneath. I am from above. You are of this world. I am not of this world.
I said therefore to you that you will die in your sins; for unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins.”
They said therefore to him, “Who are you?” Jesus said to them, “Just what I have been saying to you from the beginning.
I have many things to speak and to judge concerning you. However he who sent me is true; and the things which I heard from him, these I say to the world.”
They didn’t understand that he spoke to them about the Father.
Jesus therefore said to them, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and I do nothing of myself, but as my Father taught me, I say these things.
He who sent me is with me. The Father hasn’t left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him.”
As he spoke these things, many believed in him.

stationsIntro: Five words from an argument in the temple, spoken a few steps from the treasury. Read each verse slowly, let the question find the dark place it was meant for, and let the Greek bring the light a little closer.
lifeIntro: The Father sent His Son into the dark. The Son spoke God’s own name in the temple, always did what pleased the Father, and was lifted up on a cross for men from beneath. A man handed a light he did not kindle has one thing to do with it: follow.
lifePulls: Jesus is the light of the world, and the man who follows Him will not walk in darkness. You do not make the light. You walk behind the One who is the light, step after step, all the way home.
prayer: Father, You sent Your Son into a dark world, and He came into mine. I confess that I have walked in the dark and called it daylight. I have kept sins I could have died in and called them small. Thank You that Jesus is the light of the world, and that the man who follows Him will not walk in darkness. Thank You that He always did what pleased You, and that He was lifted up for men from beneath. I believe that He is I AM, from above, and I rest my whole weight on Him. When the day goes dark, keep my eyes on Him and my feet behind His. Open the eyes of the men I love who still cannot see. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You sent Your Son into a dark world, and He came into mine.
I confess that I have walked in the dark and called it daylight.
I have kept sins I could have died in and called them small.
Thank You that Jesus is the light of the world, and that the man who follows Him
will not walk in darkness.
Thank You that He always did what pleased You, and that He was lifted up for
men from beneath.
I believe that He is I AM, from above, and I rest my whole weight on Him.
When the day goes dark, keep my eyes on Him and my feet behind His.
Open the eyes of the men I love who still cannot see.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Jesus stood in the temple treasury, among men who wanted Him dead, and said, I am the light of the world. Without Him you walk in the dark and die in your sins, however well you know your way around. With Him you have the light of life. He is from above, He bears God’s own name, and He was lifted up so that you would not die where you lie. Follow Him.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, because the Light has spoken in the dark room. He spoke where men were plotting to take Him. He spoke where men were counting coins. He spoke to men who would not hear Him, and then He spoke again. He did not wait for the crowd to warm to Him, and He did not wait for you to come looking. The Light came to the place where you were standing, said His own name, and did not go out.

The dust told you the light was only a little low — that you could find your way with what you had, and that death was a long road off. It lied twice. You were from beneath, and the dark went all the way down. But the One from above did not call directions down from the top of the well. He came down into it. He took the name God gave Moses at the bush, and He stood in the temple court where any man could have laid hands on Him, and no man could, because His hour was His Father’s to name.

Then the hour came. They lifted up the Son of Man, just as He said they would. The Light of the world was nailed to a beam and raised up at the Place of a Skull, near the city. And there, in the darkest thing men ever did, you can see who He is. He always did the things that pleased His Father. He died for the sins you would have died in. The veil tore from the top, and the way to God stands open from His side.

So follow Him this week, one step at a time, in whatever light you are given. The dark is still out there — on the job site, in the news, in your own heart at two in the morning. But you are behind the Lamp now. Mary went to His tomb while it was still dark, and before that morning was over she had seen Him alive. That is the Light you follow, and here is the promise to carry into Tuesday: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.
closingVerse: Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.
carry: Jesus said, He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life; what decision this week will you walk through behind Him instead of by your own dim light?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Ask a man whether he is free and he will look at you as if you asked whether he can read. Of course he is free. Nobody owns him. He picks his own job, his own church, his own way to spend a Saturday. He pays his own way at the feed store and answers to no one when he locks the shop at night. He says it the way the men in this passage said it: We are Abraham’s offspring, and have never been in bondage to anyone.

Then watch him for a week. Watch him reach for the phone after the house is asleep, against everything he promised himself that morning. Watch the temper come up out of him at supper before he can stop it. Watch him hold the same grudge for ten years, shade the same small truths, and promise again on Sunday to be different. A free man would stop. He has the reasons and the will to stop, and still he does not stop. He is not choosing these things anymore. They are choosing him.

That is the lie of the dust: that you are free because no one holds the rope but you. Jesus says the rope runs the other way. Everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin. The man who thinks he owns his appetites is the man they own. A held-down man does not need more willpower. He needs life, and the old prayer asks for it: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) John 8:31–59 is the word that answers him: If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.

sections.heading: Believers Who Picked Up Stones
pulls: A man can nod along with Jesus, count himself a believer, and still be a slave who has never been set free. Freedom is not something you claim for yourself. It is something the Son gives.
paras: The passage opens on a hopeful note. Verse 30 told you that many believed in him, and now Jesus turns to those Jews who had believed him. He does not pat them on the back. He tells them what real disciples look like. Within minutes they are calling Him a Samaritan with a demon, and by the last verse they took up stones to throw at him.

Read the whole of 8:31–59 at one sitting and feel how fast it turns. Men who began by believing Him end by trying to kill Him. John tells you this not so you can sneer at them, but because a man can nod along with Jesus, count himself a believer, and never be made free. Every man who argued with Jesus that day was a son of Abraham. So was Jesus. So was John, who wrote it down. The line this chapter draws does not run between nations. It runs through every human heart, yours included.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE SLAVE AND THE SON
paras: Jesus starts with His word. If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free. Mark the order: His word, then knowing, then freedom. Freedom does not start in you. It comes from outside you, through what Jesus speaks — and in this Gospel the truth has a face: the Man who will say, I am the way, the truth, and the life.

The men bristle. How do you say, ‘You will be made free’? They have forgotten Egypt, where their fathers made bricks for Pharaoh. They have forgotten the exile. And that is how sin’s bondage works: the chain is hardest to feel on the man most sure he is not wearing one.

So Jesus says it straight. Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin. Not every man who once slipped. Every man who goes on doing it. Sin is not a tool a man picks up and sets down at the end of the day. It is a master, and it works him from first light to long after dark, and pays him nothing.

Then Jesus shows them a house. A bondservant doesn’t live in the house forever. A son remains forever. A slave can be sold off or sent away; he has no place that is his. The son belongs. And the Son of this house is the One talking. If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed. He does not hand you a key and tell you to work the lock. He opens the door Himself and gives you a place in the house with Him.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: WHOSE CHILDREN ARE YOU
paras: I know that you are Abraham’s offspring, Jesus says, yet you seek to kill me, because my word finds no place in you. Blood was never the point. Abraham believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness. He trusted God’s word. These men want God’s Son dead. A family name on paper does not make a man a son.

Then comes the hardest line in the chapter. You are of your father, the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. Read it slowly, and read it about yourself before you read it about anyone else. Jesus is not fencing off a people. He is pulling back the curtain on every human heart outside of Him. Paul, a son of Abraham himself, says that we also all once lived that way, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest. Every man is born on the wrong side of this line. You were.

Look at the family likeness. The devil was a murderer from the beginning, and he is a liar, and the father of lies. Hatred that wants a man gone, and words bent to get there. You have seen both in yourself — the grudge you feed, the story you shade, the anger that wishes a certain man would just disappear.

Why don’t you understand my speech? Because you can’t hear my word. Can’t, not won’t. A deaf man does not decide to hear. He needs ears. So the hope of this chapter lies in the One speaking, not in the men listening. He who is of God hears the words of God — and God gives new birth to men who could not hear.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: WHO CONVICTS ME OF SIN
pulls: Jesus looked around a court full of enemies and asked, Which of you convicts me of sin? No one could answer. Only a Son with no debt of His own could pay the debt of slaves.
paras: Then Jesus asks a question no other man could ask. Which of you convicts me of sin? He looks around a court full of enemies — men who want something on Him badly enough to kill for it — and invites them to name one thing. No one does. You could not ask that question in your own house for one afternoon. He asked it of His enemies and stood.

They answer with insults. Don’t we say well that you are a Samaritan, and have a demon? Jesus does not answer with heat. I don’t have a demon, but I honor my Father and you dishonor me. He is not guarding His reputation. I don’t seek my own glory. There is one who seeks and judges. He leaves His name in His Father’s hands. That is the freedom the Son shares with every man He sets free — the freedom of a man who does not need to win the argument.

And right there, in the middle of the insults, He makes an offer. Most certainly, I tell you, if a person keeps my word, he will never see death. They call Him demon-possessed, and He answers with life that death cannot touch. That is the Son who makes men free. The sinless One takes the dishonor and holds out life to the men heaping it on Him.

This is why His freedom is real. One slave cannot buy another out of the market. Only a Son with no debt of His own could pay the debt of slaves. That is why the question Which of you convicts me of sin? matters to you. If one charge had stuck, He could not have stood in your place. None did. He had nothing of His own to answer for, so He could answer for you.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: BEFORE ABRAHAM, I AM
paras: Now they think they have Him. Abraham died, as did the prophets. If the greatest men of Israel went into the ground, who is this man to promise anyone that he will never taste death? Who do you make yourself out to be?

Jesus answers with Abraham himself. Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day. He saw it, and was glad. Abraham lived in tents and died looking ahead. God had promised him, All the families of the earth will be blessed through you. On the mountain he told his son, God will provide himself the lamb. He did not see the whole of it. He saw enough to be glad, and the day he was looking toward was the day of Christ.

They scoff. You are not yet fifty years old, they say. Have you seen Abraham? And Jesus gives the answer of the chapter: Most certainly, I tell you, before Abraham came into existence, I AM. Not I was. I AM. Abraham came into being; the Son simply is. He speaks the name God gave at the bush, and they understood Him well enough. They took up stones to throw at him.

But Jesus was hidden, and went out of the temple, having gone through the middle of them. His hour had still not come. When it did, He would not slip through the crowd. He would let them take Him and lift Him up, and the I AM would die the death of a slave to make slaves into sons. Then He would walk out of the grave as freely as He walked out of the temple. That is the freedom He gives. It is freedom indeed.

stations.verse: If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.
stations.question: Men who said they had never been in bondage to anyone heard Jesus say only the Son makes a man free indeed; what sin have I been calling a habit when it is a master only He can break?
body: Ontōs is an adverb built on the participle of the verb to be. It means really, actually, truly — a thing as it is. It appears in ten New Testament verses. On the evening of the first day of the week, the disciples in Jerusalem greet the two men back from Emmaus with it: The Lord is risen indeed.

That is the weight Jesus puts on freedom. If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed. Not free in theory. Not free on good days. Free the way the empty tomb is real. Feelings rise and fall like weather over the back field. The fact under them does not move.

The dust says your freedom is only a word — that you are the same slave with a new label, and the old master will have you back by Friday. Ontōs says the Son has made you free as surely as the Lord is risen. Both are facts, and neither one hangs on you.
stations.live: When the old pull comes back this week and tells you nothing has changed, answer it out loud with the Son’s word: ‘The Son made me free. I am free indeed.’

stations.verse: You are of your father, the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and doesn’t stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks on his own; for he is a liar, and the father of lies.
stations.question: Jesus called the devil a liar, and the father of lies, then said, because I tell the truth, you don’t believe me; which word of Christ have I been slow to believe because a lie sounds easier to live with?
body: Pseustēs is a liar, from the verb meaning to lie. The Greek Old Testament uses it in Psalm 116: All people are liars. John uses it seven times, two of them here.

Jesus calls the devil a liar, and the father of lies. His lies seldom sound loud. They sound reasonable. Then in verse 55 Jesus uses the word of Himself. If He denied knowing the Father, I would be like you, a liar. He would not lie to save His life.

The dust speaks the devil’s tongue, and you learned it young. Pseustēs sets every voice beside the One who cannot lie. Paul says it plainly: let God be found true, but every man a liar. Your feelings, your record, the voice at night — let them be the liars. God tells you the truth.
stations.live: Write down the lie about God you hear most — that He is tired of you, that He is holding back. Under it write John 8:36. Read both each morning, and say out loud which one is true.

stations.verse: You are of your father, the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and doesn’t stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks on his own; for he is a liar, and the father of lies.
stations.question: Jesus told the men plotting His death, you want to do the desires of your father, and named that father the devil; which of my wants this month bears the liar’s likeness more than the Son’s?
body: Epithymia means desire or longing. Most often in the New Testament it points to desire for forbidden things — lust in the full sense. Here Jesus speaks of men who want to do the desires of the devil.

Mark the shape of it: desire, then doing. A man does not drift into sin with no wanting. He wants, and then he does what the wanting tells him. That is a bondservant — a man whose desires give the orders.

The dust says your desires are you. But the same word has another use. Jesus told His disciples, I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. The Son’s desire ran toward you, all the way to the cross, and it is stronger than yours.
stations.live: Name the desire that has been running you. Each time it rises this week, answer it with the desire of Christ: ‘He earnestly desired to suffer for me. I belong to Him, not to this.’

stations.verse: Jesus answered, “I don’t have a demon, but I honor my Father and you dishonor me.
stations.question: Called a Samaritan with a demon, Jesus answered, I honor my Father and you dishonor me, and left His glory to the Father; whose insult am I still carrying because I want to set the record straight myself?
body: Atimazō means to dishonor, to insult, to treat a man with contempt. It appears in seven New Testament verses. In Mark and Luke it is the word for what the wicked tenants in Jesus’ parable did to the owner’s servants: they beat them and sent them away shamefully treated. Then the owner sent his son.

Now the Son stands before the tenants. I honor my Father and you dishonor me. He does not hit back. He does not demand His rights. I don’t seek my own glory. He takes the insult and hands His name to the Father to keep. That is the freedom of a Son who does not need to win.

The dust says your name is yours to defend — every slight answered, every side comment paid back. Atimazō says Christ was dishonored for you. Later His apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name. A man the Son has freed can afford to lose face.
stations.live: When someone slights you this week, let it lie. Do not answer it, and do not rehearse it on the drive home. Pray instead: ‘Jesus bore worse for me. My Father keeps my name.’

stations.verse: Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day. He saw it, and was glad.
stations.question: Jesus said Abraham rejoiced to see my day, though he saw it only from far off; what has crowded out my gladness in Christ when I stand on the near side of His cross and empty tomb?
body: Agalliaō means to exult, to rejoice greatly. It is a later form of an older verb meaning to glorify, and in the Greek Old Testament it is found most often in the Psalms. It appears in eleven New Testament verses. This is not a polite smile. It is gladness that spills over.

Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day. Abraham lived in tents and died before the promise was in his hands. He saw it from far off and was glad. Peter uses the same word of you: believing, you rejoice greatly with joy that is unspeakable. Abraham was glad looking forward. You look back on a finished cross and an empty tomb.

The dust says joy belongs to men whose lives are going well. Agalliaō says the gladness comes from His day, not from yours. Even Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit that the Father shows these things to little children. The joy starts in Him, and He shares it.
stations.live: Set aside ten minutes one evening to do nothing but thank God for the day of Christ — His birth, His cross, His rising. No requests. Then say it: ‘I have seen His day, and I am glad.’

practices.title: REMAIN IN HIS WORD
practices.body: Jesus said the way to know the truth that frees is to remain in my word. Not visit it. Stay in it. Read John 8:31–59 every morning this week, start to finish, before the phone and before the news. On the fourth morning, write down one sentence Jesus said that you missed the first three times. Freedom comes through the word He speaks, so keep your ear where He is talking, even on the mornings it feels like nothing is happening.

practices.title: NAME YOUR MASTER
practices.body: Everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin. Pick the one sin you keep promising to quit. Write it at the top of a page, and under it write: This is a master, not a habit. Under that, copy out John 8:36. Bring the page to God on your knees, or at the tool bench if that is where you pray, and tell Him plainly what has been owning you. You cannot free yourself by trying harder. You can tell the Son the truth, and the Son makes free.

practices.title: CATCH THE LIE
practices.body: The father of lies rarely sounds like a liar. Most of what he says passes for common sense. For one week, listen for it: God is tired of you; you can have Him and keep your sin; you are on your own. Each time you catch one, answer it with something Jesus said in this chapter. Keep a short list in your lunch pail or your wallet. By Saturday you will know which lie you have been living under.

practices.title: LET YOUR NAME GO
practices.body: Jesus was called a Samaritan with a demon, and He answered, I don’t seek my own glory. This week, when you are slighted — on the job site, at church, in your own family — do not defend yourself. Not once. Let the comment lie where it fell, and do not replay it at the fence line that evening. Then do one quiet good turn for the man who said it. A son whose Father keeps his name does not need to win the argument.

practices.title: REJOICE IN HIS DAY
practices.body: Abraham saw Christ’s day from a long way off and was glad. You stand on the near side of it. Before worship on Sunday, read Genesis 22:1–14 and then John 8:56–58. See how the lamb God promised to provide points to the I AM who stood in the temple. Then go and sing with the gladness of a man who has seen the day Abraham waited for. If your heart is cold, sing anyway; the joy is in His day, not in your mood.

title: Free Indeed
subtitle: from dust to the freedom the Son gives
keyVerse: If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.

passage.text: Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples.
You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.”
They answered him, “We are Abraham’s offspring, and have never been in bondage to anyone. How do you say, ‘You will be made free’?”
Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin.
A bondservant doesn’t live in the house forever. A son remains forever.
If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.
I know that you are Abraham’s offspring, yet you seek to kill me, because my word finds no place in you.
I say the things which I have seen with my Father; and you also do the things which you have seen with your father.”
They answered him, “Our father is Abraham.” Jesus said to them, “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham.
But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from God. Abraham didn’t do this.
You do the works of your father.” They said to him, “We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father, God.”
Therefore Jesus said to them, “If God were your father, you would love me, for I came out and have come from God. For I haven’t come of myself, but he sent me.
Why don’t you understand my speech? Because you can’t hear my word.

You are of your father, the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and doesn’t stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks on his own; for he is a liar, and the father of lies.
But because I tell the truth, you don’t believe me.
Which of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?
He who is of God hears the words of God. For this cause you don’t hear, because you are not of God.”
Then the Jews answered him, “Don’t we say well that you are a Samaritan, and have a demon?”
Jesus answered, “I don’t have a demon, but I honor my Father and you dishonor me.
But I don’t seek my own glory. There is one who seeks and judges.
Most certainly, I tell you, if a person keeps my word, he will never see death.”
Then the Jews said to him, “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, as did the prophets; and you say, ‘If a man keeps my word, he will never taste of death.’
Are you greater than our father, Abraham, who died? The prophets died. Who do you make yourself out to be?”
Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say that he is our God.
You have not known him, but I know him. If I said, ‘I don’t know him,’ I would be like you, a liar. But I know him and keep his word.
Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day. He saw it, and was glad.”
The Jews therefore said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old! Have you seen Abraham?”
Jesus said to them, “Most certainly, I tell you, before Abraham came into existence, I AM.”
Therefore they took up stones to throw at him, but Jesus was hidden, and went out of the temple, having gone through the middle of them, and so passed by.

stationsIntro: Five words from the day Jesus told believing men they were still slaves. Read each verse slowly, let the question find the chain you have stopped noticing, and let the Greek show you the Son who breaks it.
lifeIntro: The Son came into a house of slaves. He kept His Father’s word without a single sin, bore dishonor without hitting back, and went to the cross to make slaves into sons. He paid the whole price, and nothing is left owing. These five practices are not how you get free. They are how a free man walks out through a door already opened.
lifePulls: The Son does not hand you a key and tell you to work the lock. He opens the door Himself, and the man He sets free is free indeed — as surely as the Lord is risen.
prayer: Father, I have called myself free while my sins held the rope. I have wanted what the liar wants and called it my own choice. Thank You for sending Your Son into the house of slaves. Thank You that He never sinned, and that no one could convict Him. Thank You that He bore dishonor for me and did not hit back. Make me free indeed, and keep me in His word. Teach me to hear the lie and to answer it with the truth. Give me Abraham’s gladness in the day of Christ. When the old master calls me back, remind me that the Son remains in the house forever, and so do I. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have called myself free while my sins held the rope.
I have wanted what the liar wants and called it my own choice.
Thank You for sending Your Son into the house of slaves.
Thank You that He never sinned, and that no one could convict Him.
Thank You that He bore dishonor for me and did not hit back.
Make me free indeed, and keep me in His word.
Teach me to hear the lie and to answer it with the truth.
Give me Abraham’s gladness in the day of Christ.
When the old master calls me back, remind me that the Son remains in the house
forever, and so do I.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: You are not as free as you think. Everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin, and the chain is hardest to feel on the man who swears he is not wearing one. But the Son remains in the house forever, and He sets slaves free. He had no sin of His own. He bore dishonor and death in your place, and He is the I AM who was before Abraham. Whom He frees is free indeed.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul; the Son has come into the house. He came where the slaves were kept. He came to men who called Him a Samaritan with a demon. He came to men who laughed at His age and could not hear His word. He came to men who believed Him in one breath and reached for stones in the next. And He came to you, while you were still telling yourself you had never been in bondage to anyone, and He did not leave when you argued with Him.

The dust told you that you were free because no one held the rope but you. But you could not put down what you kept promising to put down. You wanted what the liar wanted and called it your own taste. That is how a slave lives, and you lived it. No slave buys his own way out. He has nothing to pay with. He needs the Son of the house to stand up for him, to pay what he owes, and to walk him out through the front door in daylight where every man can see he has been let go.

That is what the Son did. He had no sin any man could name. He took the insults and handed His name to His Father to keep. Then, when His hour came, He did not slip through the crowd. He let them lift Him up. The I AM, who was before Abraham came into existence, died the death of a slave so that slaves could be made sons. He did not stay dead. On the first day of the week the grave stood empty, and the men who had run from Him said it plainly: the Lord is risen indeed. Your freedom is as solid as that empty grave.

So go free this week. Not free to do as you please; no man was ever free that way. Free to remain in His word. Free to hear the lie and call it a lie. Free to let your name go. Free to be glad in His day. The bondservant does not live in the house forever, but you are not a bondservant now. You are in the house because the Son brought you in, and here is the promise to carry into Tuesday: A son remains forever.
closingVerse: If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.
carry: Jesus said, If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed; what chain will you name to the Son this week, trusting Him to break what you never could?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust keeps books. Something breaks in your life, and the first thing it does is hunt for the line where the debt was written. Your boy goes wrong, and you go back over every hard word you ever said to him. Your back gives out, and you wonder what you did to earn it. The marriage goes cold, and you trace it to a sin from twenty years ago that you never told anyone. Somebody sinned. Somebody always sinned. Find the name and you have the reason.

That lie has a twin. It says what you were born with is what you will die with. Your father’s anger. The dark moods that run down the family line. The hand you were dealt before you could walk. The dust calls it fate and tells you to sit down by the road and make the best of it. Hold out a hand for small change, it says, and stop asking for anything bigger.

A man can sit by that road for years. He learns which footsteps pass without stopping and which might drop a coin. He stops hoping for sight and hopes for enough to get through the day. When he has nothing left to bargain with, he is down where the old psalm finds him: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)

John 9 opens on a man sitting exactly there, and it will not let the dust run the numbers. Jesus will not answer the question of who sinned. He answers a better one: this man’s darkness is the place the works of God might be revealed. Then the Light of the world spits on the ground, works the dirt into mud, and puts it on blind eyes. What the dust could never do for a man, the Lord does with the dust in His hands.

sections.heading: A Beggar by the Road
pulls: The disciples asked who sinned. Jesus answered a better question: what will God do here? The answer came in a pair of hands, a little mud, and a pool called Sent.
paras: Chapter 8 ended with stones in men’s hands. They meant to kill Him, but Jesus went out of the temple, having gone through the middle of them, and so passed by. Chapter 9 picks up with the same words: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. He has just been called a Samaritan and a man with a demon. He is walking out of reach of men who want Him dead. And He stops for a beggar.

This week covers the first twelve verses: the question, the mud, the pool, and the neighbors. Next week follows the man into the hearings that come after. Read all forty-one verses through at one sitting before you go further. John spends a whole chapter on one blind man, and he does it for the reason he gives near the end of his book: that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: WHO SINNED?
paras: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. Mark the order. Jesus sees first. The man does not call out to Him or ask Him for anything. He cannot see who is passing, so he cannot know whom to ask. The whole thing starts with the eyes of Christ on a man who could not look back.

The disciples see him too, but they see a puzzle. Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind? They have already decided someone is to blame. The only thing left to settle is whose name goes on the bill. It is a question asked from a safe distance. Nobody asks the man anything. Nobody asks what can be done for him. To them he is a case. To Jesus he is a man.

Jesus refuses both answers. This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents; but, that the works of God might be revealed in him. He is not saying the man and his parents were without sin. He is saying this blindness is not a payment on some debt they owe. And He does not hand the disciples a theory of why every man suffers. He tells them what God is about to do with this one.

That is where you have to stand with your own trouble. Christ has not handed you a key to every hard thing in your life, and He will not let you write a verdict on yourself out of it either. What He gives you is better than an explanation. He gives you His eyes on you, and His word that the dark place is where God means to work. Stop asking who is to blame. Ask what God will show of Himself there.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: WHILE IT IS DAY
paras: Then Jesus says, I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. He is under orders. The Son who was sent has work to finish, and He will not be turned off it by stones in the temple or by a theology class along the way. A blind beggar is not an interruption to His day. He is the day’s work.

The night is coming, when no one can work. Jesus knows His hours on earth are counted. Twice already John has told you that his hour had not yet come, and every step in this Gospel moves toward it. When Judas walks out of the upper room in chapter 13, John writes three words: It was night. Jesus works while He walks toward that night, and nothing ahead of Him slows His hands.

While I am in the world, I am the light of the world. He said it in the temple; now He shows it. Light is not an idea He teaches. It is what He is, and here it falls on a man who has never seen light at all. John told you at the start: In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The life that made the sun is standing beside a man who has sat in the dark since the day he was born.

This is the ground under every command He will give the man. Before there is go or wash, there is I am. Christ does not ask a blind man to find the light. He comes and stands in front of him as the light. The same holds for you. Your faith did not light the lamp. You believe because the Light came first and stood in your dark.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: DUST IN HIS HANDS
pulls: The dust is what you are and where you lie. It is also the very stuff the Lord takes up when He means to make something of a man. He does not wait for you to climb out of it. He puts His hands into it.
paras: He spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, anointed the blind man’s eyes with the mud. John does not say why. He has healed with a word from miles away before. Here, instead, He spits on the ground and makes mud. Then He presses it onto the man’s eyes. The man feels the hands of Christ on his face before he ever sees them.

Do not make the mud say more than John makes it say. He gives no lesson on it, and you should not invent one. But you cannot watch it and forget where you came from. Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. And John opened his Gospel by telling you who was there: All things were made through him. The hands in the dirt are the hands through which the first man was made. The dust has never been out of His reach.

Here is the turn for a man who clings to the dust. The dust is what you are. He remembers that we are dust. The dust is where you lie. And the dust is the very stuff the Lord takes up when He means to do something with a man. He does not wait for you to climb out of it. He puts His hands into it.

Mud on the eyes did not heal anyone by itself. It was still dirt. For a while the man was more covered than before, not less. Christ’s hands on your life may feel like that at first: something pressed on you, heavy and messy, before anything is clear. The hands that put it there know what they are making.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: GO, WASH
paras: Then comes a word: Go, wash in the pool of Siloam. John stops to tell you what the name means: Sent. A moment ago Jesus spoke of him who sent me. Now the man is sent to a pool called Sent by the One the Father sent. He does not get his sight at Jesus’ feet. He gets it at the end of a walk he has to make blind, with mud drying on his face, on nothing but a word.

So he went away, washed, and came back seeing. No speech, no fuss. He does not argue the method. He does not ask how mud and pool water could do what nothing else had done. He goes because he was told, and the power is in the One who told him. The washing did not earn the sight. It was the road the gift came down. Faith in John looks like that: a man takes Christ at His word and goes. Back home, the neighbors cannot agree on who he is. Isn’t this he who sat and begged? Some say yes. Others say, He looks like him. The man settles it: I am he. Same man, new eyes. That is what grace does. It does not trade the beggar for a better man. It finds the beggar and opens the beggar’s eyes.

They ask how, and he tells them plainly: A man called Jesus made mud, anointed my eyes, and sent him to wash. He does not know much yet. When they ask where Jesus is, he says, I don’t know. But he knows who did it, and he puts that name first. He gives himself no credit at all. In his telling he is only the man who went where he was sent.

stations.verse: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth.
stations.question: Jesus was walking away from men with stones in their hands, yet He stopped and saw a man blind from birth who could not see Him; what does it mean for me that Christ saw me before I ever looked for Him?
stations.gloss: birth; the start of a life
body: Genetē means birth. John uses it in one phrase, ek genetēs, from birth, and this is the only verse in the New Testament where the word appears. The man was not blinded by an accident or a fever. He came into the world without sight and had never known anything else.

That detail carries the whole chapter. Later the man will say that no one since the world began has opened the eyes of someone born blind (9:32). There is no before to go back to and no memory of light to restore. Whatever Jesus does for this man, it has to be a new making.

The dust says what you were born with is what you are stuck with: your father’s anger, the dark moods, the bent you inherited. Genetē marks where the man’s darkness began, and Christ reaches back past it. He made the first man from dust. He is not stopped by how you started.
stations.live: Name the one thing in you that you have always called “just the way I am.” Bring it to Christ by name this week and say it plainly: ‘You saw me from birth. You are not stopped by how I started.’

stations.verse: When he had said this, he spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, anointed the blind man’s eyes with the mud.
stations.question: Having just said I am the light of the world, Jesus spat on the ground and touched a blind beggar’s face; what part of my life do I keep from Christ as too low for Him to touch?
body: Ptyō simply means to spit. It is a plain, low, bodily word, and it appears in only three New Testament verses. All three are Jesus healing: a deaf man in Mark 7:33, a blind man in Mark 8:23, and this man in John 9.

In the Greek Old Testament it shows up in Numbers 12:14, where spitting in a face is a mark of shame. In Christ’s hands the same act begins a man’s sight. And the night He was tried, men spat on Him and covered His face (Mark 14:65). The One whose spittle opened a beggar’s eyes stood still and took that shame for beggars.

The dust wants you to think Christ keeps a clean distance from what is low and bodily in you. Ptyō says otherwise. He came close enough to touch a beggar’s face, and He did not flinch at the dirt on the ground. He will not flinch at yours, and He did not turn back from the cross.
stations.live: Pick the part of your life you keep furthest from Christ because it feels too low to bring up. Bring it up this week, out loud and in plain words, and let Him come that close.

stations.verse: When he had said this, he spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, anointed the blind man’s eyes with the mud.
stations.question: Before the man could see, Jesus pressed mud onto his eyes, and he walked off more covered than before; where is Christ’s hand on my life right now pressing on me in a way I do not yet understand?
body: Pēlos is clay or mud. Paul uses it for a potter’s clay in Romans 9:21, the lump the potter has every right to shape. In John 9 it means wet earth, mud made from the ground. Four of its five New Testament verses sit in this one chapter, and the word keeps coming back as the story is told.

Scripture already knows what clay in the Lord’s hand means. We are the clay and you our potter, Isaiah prays. Here the Potter stands on the ground He made and works it with His own fingers. The mud has no power in itself. The power is in the hands.

The dust tells you that dirt is all you are and all you will be. Pēlos answers that dirt is what the Lord takes up when He means to make something. Through Jeremiah He says, As the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand. You are not lying in the dust alone. You are in His hands.
stations.live: When the dust tells you this week that you are worthless, answer with whose hands you are in: ‘I am clay, and He is the Potter. He has not set me down.’

stations.verse: And said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So he went away, washed, and came back seeing.
stations.question: The blind man walked to Siloam with mud on his face and nothing but Jesus’ word, and he came back seeing; what plain word of Christ am I waiting to understand before I will act on it?
stations.gloss: to wash, usually a part of the body
body: Niptō means to wash, usually a part of the body: the hands, the face, the feet. In John 9 it is used of washing oneself, and it comes three times in the chapter (9:7, 11, 15). The man washes his own face at the pool, because Jesus told him to.

The same word shows up again in John 13, when Jesus takes a basin and washes His disciples’ feet. Peter refuses, and Jesus tells him, If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me. The beggar washed his face at Siloam. But the One who sent him to the pool is the One who does the washing that counts, and in John 13 He does it with a basin and a towel.
The dust says you have to clean yourself up before you come. Niptō says Christ sends you to the water and then stoops to wash you Himself. The cleaning is His work, and the part with Him is His gift.
stations.live: Name the stain you keep scrubbing at. Stop scrubbing this week. Bring it to Christ in plain confession and say it: ‘If You don’t wash me, I have no part with You. Wash me.’

stations.verse: The neighbors therefore, and those who saw that he was blind before, said, “Isn’t this he who sat and begged?
stations.question: When the neighbors argued over whether this was the beggar, he settled it with I am he; how ready am I to own what I was before Christ found me, so that the credit lands on Him?
body: Prosaitēs means a beggar. It appears in only two New Testament verses: here, and Mark 10:46, where Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, sits by the road outside Jericho. In both places a blind beggar gets his sight from Jesus.

The neighbors knew this man by one thing: he who sat and begged. That was his name in town. A beggar brings nothing to the deal but his need. He holds out his hands, takes what is given, and cannot pay it back. That is the only way any man has ever received sight from Christ.

The dust wants you ashamed to be a beggar before God, and eager to show Him what you have brought. Prosaitēs tells you the beggar is the one who went home seeing. Empty hands are no disgrace before Christ. They are the hands He fills, and He has never sent a beggar away from Him empty.
stations.live: This week, pray one prayer with nothing in it about what you have done for God. Ask the way a beggar asks: ‘I have nothing to give You. Open my eyes.’

practices.title: SHUT THE BOOK ON WHO SINNED
practices.body: Pick the trouble you keep tracing back to a cause: your own failure, your father’s, a choice from years ago. Stop running the numbers this week. Jesus refused that question in John 9:3. Bring the trouble to Him and ask the question He answered instead: what will God show of Himself here? Write it on a card and pray over it each morning. You may not get an explanation. You will have the One who saw the beggar first, and He sees you.

practices.title: LET HIM COME CLOSE
practices.body: Christ did not heal this man from a distance. He spat, worked the mud with His fingers, and touched the man’s face. Read John 9:6 slowly on three mornings this week. Then bring Him the part of your life you keep at arm’s length, the low and bodily things you would rather not name. Name them to Him plainly. He has never been afraid of dirt, and He is not afraid of yours. Let Him put His hands on it.

practices.title: GO WHERE YOU ARE SENT
practices.body: The man walked to the pool on nothing but a word, with mud still on his face. Christ’s word to you is plain enough to obey before you understand it: confess the sin, call the man you wronged, open your Bible tomorrow before work. Pick one thing His word has already told you to do and do it this week, without waiting to see how it turns out. The power was never in the pool. It is in the One who sends.

practices.title: OWN THE MAN YOU WERE
practices.body: The neighbors argued over whether he was the same man. He settled it: I am he. Grace did not erase his years as a beggar. It opened the beggar’s eyes. Tell one man this week, plainly, what you were before Christ found you and what He has done since. Leave out the polish and the excuses. Name the darkness you lived in, and then name the Man who opened your eyes. You are the same man, and you can see.

practices.title: GIVE THE RIGHT MAN THE CREDIT
practices.body: When the man told how he was healed, he began with A man called Jesus. He did not know much yet, and he said so. Listen to your own talk this week when something goes well. Catch the sentences that make you the hero of the story. Say one of them again out loud with Christ as the subject: He found me, He opened my eyes, He keeps me. Do it again the next day, until it comes without thinking.

title: Mud on the Eyes
subtitle: from dust to eyes that see
keyVerse: Jesus answered, “This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents; but, that the works of God might be revealed in him.

passage.text: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth.
His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”
Jesus answered, “This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents; but, that the works of God might be revealed in him.
I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. The night is coming, when no one can work.
While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”
When he had said this, he spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, anointed the blind man’s eyes with the mud,
and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So he went away, washed, and came back seeing.
The neighbors therefore, and those who saw that he was blind before, said, “Isn’t this he who sat and begged?”
Others were saying, “It is he.” Still others were saying, “He looks like him.” He said, “I am he.”
They therefore were asking him, “How were your eyes opened?”
He answered, “A man called Jesus made mud, anointed my eyes, and said to me, ‘Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.’ So I went away and washed, and I received sight.”
Then they asked him, “Where is he?” He said, “I don’t know.”

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE OPENED EYES
stationsIntro: Take these verses one at a time, slowly, with the mud and the pool in front of you. Answer each question plainly, and let each Greek word press its weight into the verse you have just read.
lifeIntro: Jesus saw the man first, worked the dust Himself, and spoke the word that sent him to the water. Everything below is an answer to what He has already done. Take these the way a blind man takes a road: one step, on His word.
lifePulls: Christ saw the beggar before the beggar could see Him. He put His hands in the dust, put the dust on the man’s face, and sent him to a pool called Sent. The man went, and he came back seeing.
prayer: Father, You saw me before I could see You. I was born in the dark, and I could not find the light on my own. Thank You for sending Your Son to the place where I sat. Thank You that His hands were not too clean for my dust. Forgive me for hunting for someone to blame when trouble comes. Show me what You mean to reveal of Yourself in the hard places this week. Give me faith to go where Your word sends me, before I understand it. Wash me, and open my eyes to see Jesus, the light of the world. When I am sent, let me go on Your word, and give Him the credit when I come back seeing. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You saw me before I could see You.
I was born in the dark, and I could not find the light on my own.
Thank You for sending Your Son to the place where I sat.
Thank You that His hands were not too clean for my dust.

Wash me, and open my eyes to see Jesus, the light of the world.
When I am sent, let me go on Your word, and give Him the credit when I come
