bottomLine: The disciples saw a blind man and asked who sinned. Jesus saw the same man and said the works of God would be revealed in him. Then He spat on the ground, made mud, put it on the man’s eyes, and sent him to a pool called Sent. The man went and came back seeing. Stop hunting for a culprit. Christ sees you, works the dust you are made of, and His word still sends.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, toward the One who saw you first. He saw you before you knew His name. He saw you sitting with your hands out and your eyes shut, and He did not walk past. He saw the darkness you were born into, the things you blame yourself for and the things you blame your father for, and He did not stop to work out whose fault it was. He stopped for you, and He has not moved on.

The dust has told you that your trouble is a bill with your name on it, and that what you started with is all you will ever have. But the Light of the world stood beside the beggar and refused that question. That the works of God might be revealed in him: that is what He said over a beggar no one else would touch. He has not told you the reason for every hard thing. He has told you who will be at work in it. The disciples wanted a culprit. Christ gave a beggar his eyes.

Look at His hands. They went down into the dirt. The hands through which all things were made took up a little dust from the ground, worked it wet, and pressed it onto a blind man’s face. Those same hands were nailed to a cross near the city for men who sat in the dark. On the evening of the day the grave broke open, He showed them to frightened men behind locked doors, still marked, and the men were glad. There is no part of you too low for those hands, and no darkness you were born into that they cannot reach back past. You are dust, and dust is what He works with.

So go where His word sends you this week. Go with the mud still on your face, if that is how it is. Go before you understand, on His word alone. The man went to Siloam with nothing but a sentence from Jesus and came back seeing. The same Christ who sent him has made you a promise: He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life. He is still the light of the world, and He still finds blind men where they sit. Take that promise into the dark morning, and walk on it.
closingVerse: Jesus answered, “This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents; but, that the works of God might be revealed in him.
carry: Jesus answered the disciples’ question about who sinned with that the works of God might be revealed in him; in the hardest thing you carry this week, what would it mean to look for God’s work instead of a culprit?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust tells you to keep your head down. Believe what you like, it says, but keep it to yourself. Do not bring Christ up on the crew, at deer camp, or at your brother’s table. You will only make things strange. Somebody will ask you a question you cannot answer, and you will look like a fool. Somebody else will roll his eyes, and you will lose a place you spent years earning. So you keep the peace, and the peace keeps you quiet.

Under that lie sits another. It says you do not know enough to speak. You have not read the right books. You cannot field every hard question a sharp man might throw at you. Leave the talking to preachers and men with letters after their names. Your part is to sit still, nod at the right times, and hope nobody notices you have changed. Nobody wants to hear it from a man like you anyway, the dust says.

Then one day somebody does notice, and asks. Your mouth goes dry. You shrug and change the subject, and on the drive home you feel the old pull of the ground. You know that pull, and you know the prayer that answers it: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The dust would rather you stay quiet and safe than speak and be shown the door.

John 9:13–41 puts a man on the stand who knows almost nothing about theology and will not be shut up. He is questioned, mocked, and finally thrown out. Then Jesus goes and finds him. A man does not need every answer to bear witness. He needs one thing he knows, and the Christ who will not leave him outside the door. The beggar had one thing, and John wrote it down so that you would have it too.

sections.heading: Three Hearings and a Finding
pulls: The man on the stand could not answer every question. He knew one thing, and he would not unsay it: I was blind, and now I see. That was enough to get him thrown out, and enough to get him found.
paras: Last week ended with a beggar who could see and neighbors who could not agree on who he was. This week they bring him to the Pharisees, and John drops the detail that starts the fight: It was a Sabbath when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. What follows is a hearing in three rounds: the man, then his parents, then the man again. Every round tightens. The Sabbath is their question. The question John presses on you is who this Man is.

Watch two things as you read. The man’s view of Jesus keeps growing: A man called Jesus, then a prophet, then a man from God, and at last Lord, I believe. Meanwhile the men who keep saying we know see less with every round. Read all of John 9 through again at one sitting. The light that opened one man’s eyes is the same light that showed what was in the room.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: A DIVIDED BENCH
paras: They brought him who had been blind to the Pharisees. The neighbors do not know what to make of what happened, so they take it to the men who are supposed to know. And John tells you where the trouble lies: the day. It was a Sabbath when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. A man blind from birth has been given his sight, and the first thing the officials want to talk about is the calendar.
They make him tell it again, and he tells it shorter this time: He put mud on my eyes, I washed, and I see. He adds nothing and dresses nothing up. He knows what happened to him, and he says it.

Then the bench splits. Some say, This man is not from God, because he doesn’t keep the Sabbath. Others push back: How can a man who is a sinner do such signs? John says it plainly: There was division among them. Jesus does that wherever He goes in this Gospel. He will not sit quietly in anybody’s box. Sooner or later a man has to decide what to do with Him.

So they turn to the beggar. What do you say about him, because he opened your eyes? He has never seen Jesus’ face. He has heard His voice once and felt His hands once. But he has eyes that work, and he reasons from there: He is a prophet. That is not yet the whole truth, but it is more than he said an hour ago. Christ does not hand a man every answer at once. He opens his eyes, and the man begins to walk toward the light he has been given. Each true word the man speaks about Jesus opens the way to the next.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: AFRAID OF THE DOOR
paras: The leaders try another road. Maybe he was never blind at all. The Jews therefore didn’t believe concerning him, that he had been blind, and had received his sight, until they called the parents. If the sign can be explained away, the problem goes with it.

The parents answer exactly as much as they must. We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind. That much they will swear to. The rest they hand back: how he now sees, we don’t know; or who opened his eyes, we don’t know. He is of age. Ask him. Their son can see their faces for the first time, and they will not say the name of the Man who did it.

John tells you why. They feared the Jews; for the Jews had already agreed that if any man would confess him as Christ, he would be put out of the synagogue. The synagogue was where they prayed, where they belonged, where their names were known. To be put out was to lose your people. They weighed that against one word about Jesus, and they kept their seat.

Do not sneer at them. You know that fear. You have stood in a room where the name of Christ would have cost you something, and you have said your own version of we don’t know. John does not set them up to be mocked. He shows you a door, and the fear of that door, so that you will see what it means when Christ goes out through it after a man on the other side. Later in this Gospel even some of the rulers believed and kept quiet for the same reason. The fear is old, and it runs through every heart in the room.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ONE THING I DO KNOW
pulls: He could not win their argument, and he did not try. He knew one thing and would not unsay it. A man who has been given sight does not need a degree to bear witness. He needs only to refuse to deny it.
paras: They call him back a second time and try to put words in his mouth. Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner. They want him to sign their verdict. And the beggar gives them the line this week is named for: I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.

He does not pretend to know what he does not. He cannot win their argument about the Sabbath, and he does not try. But he will not deny what has been done to him. That is witness. A man who has been given sight does not need a degree to say so. He needs only to refuse to unsay it.

They press again, How did he open your eyes? and he presses back: You don’t also want to become his disciples, do you? So they insulted him and set Moses against Jesus: as for this man, we don’t know where he comes from. Now the beggar is the one teaching. You don’t know where he comes from, yet he opened my eyes. He argues from what they all believed. Since the world began it has never been heard of that anyone opened the eyes of someone born blind. Then the plain conclusion: If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.

They have no answer, so they reach for the old ledger. You were altogether born in sins, and do you teach us? It is the disciples’ question from the road, turned into a weapon. Then they threw him out. The man who sat in the dark for years has been given his eyes, and for opening his mouth he has lost his place.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: FOUND OUTSIDE THE DOOR
paras: Now comes the verse this chapter has been walking toward. Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and finding him. The man did not go looking for Jesus. He did not know where He was. Jesus heard, Jesus went, and Jesus found. The door shut behind the beggar, and the Lord was already on the outside of it.

He asks one question: Do you believe in the Son of God? The man answers like a man ready to bow: Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him? Jesus says, You have both seen him, and it is he who speaks with you. The eyes Christ gave him that morning now look into Christ’s face. And John records where the long road ends: Lord, I believe, and he worshiped him. The eyes were the sign. This is the gift. The man thrown out of the synagogue worships the Son of God and has life in His name.

Then Jesus speaks to everyone standing near: I came into this world for judgment, that those who don’t see may see; and that those who see may become blind. Some Pharisees hear it and bristle: Are we also blind? His answer is the hardest line in the chapter: If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, ‘We see.’ Therefore your sin remains.

That line runs through the room and through you. The man who knows he is blind goes home seeing. The man who insists he sees needs nothing from Christ, and so receives nothing. Christ does not save men who think they are fine. He finds men outside the door with nothing to show but the eyes He opened, and He tells them who He is.

stations.verse: Again therefore the Pharisees also asked him how he received his sight. He said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, I washed, and I see.
stations.question: Questioned by the Pharisees, the man told it in one plain sentence: He put mud on my eyes, I washed, and I see; if a doubting man asked me tomorrow, what would my plain sentence about Christ be?
stations.gloss: to look up; to recover sight
body: Anablepō carries two senses. It can mean to look up, as when Jesus looks up to heaven before He breaks the loaves. It can also mean to recover sight, and that is how John uses it in this chapter (9:11, 15, 18). It turns up in twenty-three New Testament verses, and many of them are Jesus giving sight.

When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask about Jesus, this word headed the answer: the blind receive their sight. Saul received his sight in Damascus under the same word (Acts 9:18). Each time it marks something only God does, and does as a gift. Eyes that were shut are opened.

The dust says your story is too small to tell. Anablepō says your story can be one sentence long, as long as Christ is in it: I washed, and I see. Tell that. You do not have to win the argument. The sight He gave you is the argument.
stations.live: Write your own version of 9:15 in one line: what He did, what you did when He spoke, what is different now. Say it to one man this week when he asks, and do not dress it up.

stations.verse: His parents said these things because they feared the Jews; for the Jews had already agreed that if any man would confess him as Christ, he would be put out of the synagogue.
stations.question: The parents knew who had opened their son’s eyes but would not say, because confessing Jesus as Christ meant being put out of the synagogue; whose good opinion am I protecting when I go quiet about Him?
stations.gloss: put out of the synagogue; expelled from the congregation
body: Aposynagōgos means expelled from the congregation, put out of the synagogue. Only John uses it, in three verses (9:22; 12:42; 16:2). It is a word for losing your people: your place in worship and your name among the men you grew up with.

In chapter 12 John says that many of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they didn’t confess it. In chapter 16 Jesus warns His men, They will put you out of the synagogues. He told them ahead of time, so that when it came they would remember He had said it.

The dust wants you to keep your seat at any price. Aposynagōgos shows you the price, and then shows you Christ outside the door. The beggar lost his place in the synagogue and gained the face of the Son of God. He lost a room and gained a Lord. The door that shut him out could not shut Christ out.
stations.live: Name the room where you go quiet about Christ. Go into it this week and say one true sentence about Him, and let the cost be what it is: ‘He opened my eyes.’

stations.verse: They insulted him and said, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.
stations.question: The Pharisees meant You are his disciple as an insult, but it was the truest thing said about the man that day; what changes in how I take a jab about my faith when I hear it as being named with Christ?
body: Loidoreō means to abuse or revile, to throw hard words at a man. The English here has They insulted him. It appears in four New Testament verses: here, Acts 23:4, 1 Corinthians 4:12, and 1 Peter 2:23.

Peter uses it of Christ Himself: When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. Paul uses it of the apostles: When people curse us, we bless. The Pharisees reviled the beggar for being Jesus’ disciple, and that put him in the same company as his Lord and the men He sent.

The dust tells you to answer insult with insult, or else to go quiet and ashamed. Loidoreō points you to the One who took every word thrown at Him and committed himself to him who judges righteously. You can bear the abuse because He bore it first, for you, and the Judge has never lost a case. He will rule on every word thrown at you.
stations.live: The next time someone throws a hard word at you about your faith, do not throw one back. Hold your tongue, answer plainly if you can, and pray for him by name that same day.

stations.verse: We know that God doesn’t listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God, and does his will, he listens to him.
stations.question: The beggar reasoned that God listens to him who worships Him and does His will, so the Man who opened blind eyes must be from God; on whose standing do I expect God to listen to me this week?
body: Theosebēs means God-fearing, godly. The English here has a worshiper of God. This is its only verse in the New Testament. In the Greek Old Testament it stands for the Hebrew phrase about fearing God, as when Moses is told to choose able men which fear God (Exodus 18:21).

The man reasons from what everyone in that room believed: God listens to the one who fears Him and does his will. Only one Man has ever done that without a crack in it. Jesus said, I always do the things that are pleasing to him, and at Lazarus’ tomb He said, I know that you always listen to me.

The dust says God will hear you once you have become godly enough. Theosebēs points past you to the only fully God-fearing Man. The Father always hears His Son, and the Son lives forever to make intercession for you. You are heard in Him, every time, because He is heard every time.
stations.live: When you pray this week and feel you have no right to be heard, stop and pray in His name on purpose: ‘Father, You always hear Your Son. Hear me for His sake.’

stations.verse: Jesus said, “I came into this world for judgment, that those who don’t see may see; and that those who see may become blind.
stations.question: Jesus said He came that those who don’t see may see; and that those who see may become blind; in what part of my life am I still telling Christ I see, when I most need Him to open my eyes?
stations.gloss: judgment; the decision that comes down
body: Krima is the issue of a judicial process: the judgment, the decision that comes down. It appears in twenty-seven New Testament verses, often of the judgment of God. John uses it only here, where Jesus says why He came: I came into this world for judgment.

That sounds hard beside John 3:17, where God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world. Both are true. Christ came to save, and His coming divides men. The light that gives sight to those who know they are blind also exposes the men who insist they see. The verdict turns on how a man answers the Light.

The dust wants you to defend yourself in that court. Don’t. Plead blind. Paul says the free gift came of many trespasses to justification. The man who pleads blind is given sight, and the verdict over him is grace. Christ took the judgment, so the blind could go home seeing.
stations.live: Say the plain thing to God this week, out loud: ‘I am blind without You. I do not see myself as clearly as I think. Give me sight.’ Then ask Him to show you one place you have been wrong.

practices.title: WRITE YOUR ONE THING
practices.body: The beggar could not answer every question, but he knew one thing: though I was blind, now I see. Sit down this week with a pen and write your own one thing in two or three plain sentences. What were you before Christ? What has He done? What is different now? Keep it short enough to say in a minute. Carry it in your wallet until you know it by heart, and then give it away when someone asks.

practices.title: SAY IT IN THE QUIET ROOM
practices.body: His parents knew the truth and would not say the name. Name the place where you keep quiet about Christ: the crew, the lunch table at work, the family table, the feed store counter. Go there this week and say one true sentence about Him when the chance comes. Do not preach and do not argue. Just refuse to say we don’t know when you do know. Let the cost be whatever it is. Christ is outside every door they can shut.

practices.title: TAKE THE INSULT WITHOUT RETURNING IT
practices.body: They insulted the beggar, and he kept talking sense. Christ was cursed and did not curse back. When a man mocks your faith this week, let the word land. Do not trade cuts with him. Answer plainly if you can, keep your temper if you cannot, and pray for him by name before you go to bed. The One who judges righteously has your case. Leave the last word with Him, and sleep.

practices.title: PRAY IN THE NAME GOD ALWAYS HEARS
practices.body: The man said God listens to the one who worships Him and does His will. Only Christ has done that perfectly, and the Father always hears Him. Each morning this week, before you ask for anything, say why you expect to be heard: for the sake of Jesus, who lives to pray for you. Then ask plainly, the way a son asks his father for what he needs. He will not turn away the Son’s name.

practices.title: ADMIT THE BLIND SPOT
practices.body: The Pharisees said We see, and their sin remained. Ask your wife, or a man who knows you well, one question this week: where do I not see myself clearly? Listen without defending yourself. Take what you hear to Christ that same day and confess it to Him plainly. The men who admit they are blind are the men He gives sight, and He has not stopped giving it. Thank Him for the sight before you leave the room.

title: One Thing I Know
subtitle: from dust to a witness who will not be silenced
keyVerse: He therefore answered, “I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.

passage.text: They brought him who had been blind to the Pharisees.
It was a Sabbath when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes.
Again therefore the Pharisees also asked him how he received his sight. He said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, I washed, and I see.”
Some therefore of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, because he doesn’t keep the Sabbath.” Others said, “How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?” There was division among them.
Therefore they asked the blind man again, “What do you say about him, because he opened your eyes?” He said, “He is a prophet.”
The Jews therefore didn’t believe concerning him, that he had been blind, and had received his sight, until they called the parents of him who had received his sight,
and asked them, “Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?”
His parents answered them, “We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind;
but how he now sees, we don’t know; or who opened his eyes, we don’t know. He is of age. Ask him. He will speak for himself.”
His parents said these things because they feared the Jews; for the Jews had already agreed that if any man would confess him as Christ, he would be put out of the synagogue.
Therefore his parents said, “He is of age. Ask him.”
So they called the man who was blind a second time, and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.”
He therefore answered, “I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.”
They said to him again, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”
He answered them, “I told you already, and you didn’t listen. Why do you want to hear it again? You don’t also want to become his disciples, do you?”
They insulted him and said, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.
We know that God has spoken to Moses. But as for this man, we don’t know where he comes from.”
The man answered them, “How amazing! You don’t know where he comes from, yet he opened my eyes.
We know that God doesn’t listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God, and does his will, he listens to him.
Since the world began it has never been heard of that anyone opened the eyes of someone born blind.
If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”
They answered him, “You were altogether born in sins, and do you teach us?” Then they threw him out.
Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and finding him, he said, “Do you believe in the Son of God?”
He answered, “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?”
Jesus said to him, “You have both seen him, and it is he who speaks with you.”
He said, “Lord, I believe!” and he worshiped him.
Jesus said, “I came into this world for judgment, that those who don’t see may see; and that those who see may become blind.”
Those of the Pharisees who were with him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?”
Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, ‘We see.’ Therefore your sin remains.

stationsIntro: Read each verse slowly and hear the questions the man faced in that room. Answer your own as plainly as he answered his, and let each Greek word bring its weight down on the verse in front of you.
lifeIntro: Christ opened the man’s eyes, gave him one true thing to say, and went looking for him when he was thrown out. You have the same Lord, and He has done the same for you. These practices are the witness of a man who has been found.
lifePulls: The door they shut behind the beggar could not keep Christ out. Jesus heard, went looking, and found him. The man who lost his seat for one true sentence gained the face of the Son of God.
prayer: Father, I was blind, and now I see, and Your Son did it. He opened my eyes before I knew His name. Forgive me for the rooms where I said nothing because I wanted to keep my seat. When I am mocked for Him, hold my tongue, and remind me that He was cursed and did not curse back. I have no standing of my own to be heard. Hear me for Jesus’ sake, because You always hear Him. Show me where I still say, ‘I see,’ when I am blind. When I am shut outside a door for His name, let Him find me there. Give me one plain sentence to say about Him this week, and the nerve to say it. Lord, I believe, and I worship. In Jesus’ name, amen.

He opened my eyes before I knew His name.
Forgive me for the rooms where I said nothing because I wanted to keep my seat.

and did not curse back.

In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: A beggar who could see was put on trial for it. His parents went quiet to keep their seat. He would not. He could not answer every question, but he knew one thing: he was blind, and now he sees. It got him insulted and thrown out. Then Jesus heard, went, and found him, and he worshiped the Son of God. Say your one thing plainly. Christ finds the men the door shuts out.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, for the One who found you is standing in front of you. Look at Him when they question you and you do not have the answer. Look at Him when the room goes cold and the men you grew up with stop meeting your eye. Look at Him when the door shuts at your back and you are standing in the road with nothing but the sight He gave you. He is already there, and He came on purpose. He found the beggar. He has found you.

The dust told you to keep your head down and your mouth shut. It told you that you needed every answer before you could say one word, and that a seat among men was worth more than a sentence about Christ. But the beggar had one sentence, and it was enough: though I was blind, now I see. Nobody could take that from him. They could insult him. They could throw him out. They could not make him blind again. The sight was not theirs to give, so it was not theirs to take. Your one thing is the same. Christ gave it, and no room of men can take it back.

Now listen to what Christ did next. Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and finding him. He did not wait for the man to find his way back in. He went out to the place where the door had left him and stood in front of the eyes He had opened. That is your Lord. He was cursed and did not curse back. He suffered outside of the gate so that men thrown out for His name would never be outside of Him. And He walked out of His own grave, and He lives forever to pray for you.

So say your one thing this week, and let it cost what it costs. You may lose a seat. You will not lose Him. He has given His word: He who comes to me I will in no way throw out. Men threw this beggar out. Christ never will, and He will not throw you out either. The Father gave you to Him, and the Son does not lose what the Father gives. Stand where the door left you, look up into His face, and say what the man said: Lord, I believe.
closingVerse: He therefore answered, “I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.
carry: The beggar could not win the Pharisees’ argument, but he said, One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see; what one thing do you know Christ has done for you that you will not unsay this week, whoever asks?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man has been handled by someone who was paid to care. The foreman who knew your name until the bid went bad. The pastor who took a bigger church the year your marriage cracked. The boss who said you were family and then sent the notice by email. You learned something from each of them, and the dust has been teaching it back to you ever since: when the wolf shows up, the man in charge looks after himself.

That lesson does not stay down at the level of men. It climbs. The dust says God is the same — a hired hand on a larger scale, kind while the season is easy and gone when the bill comes due. So you keep a back gate open. You keep your own counsel, your own cash, your own way out. You listen to every voice that promises grass, and you trust none of them, His included.

A man who believes that lives like a stray. He is fed by no one and follows whoever whistled last. The psalmist knew that flat-on-the-ground place and did not dress it up: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) He did not ask for a better mood. He asked for a word.

John 10 is that word. Jesus does not argue with your history. He sets Himself beside it and says, I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. The hired hand runs. This Shepherd dies for the flock, and then He takes His life up again.

sections.heading: Spoken to Men Who Threw a Beggar Out
pulls: A hired hand counts the cost and runs when the wolf comes. The good Shepherd counted the cost and laid His life down anyway — and the sheep He died for are the sheep He keeps.
paras: There is no break between chapter 9 and chapter 10. The Pharisees have just thrown out the man born blind, and Jesus has gone and found him. They have asked, Are we also blind? and Jesus has told them their sin remains. Then, without a pause, He starts talking about sheep, thieves, and a door. The parable is aimed at the men who just put a sheep out of the fold. The man who was found is the picture of what a true shepherd does.

The image was not new to them. Their own Scriptures sang, Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. Through Ezekiel, God had pronounced woe on the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves and promised, I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep. When Jesus says I am the good shepherd, He steps into that promise, in front of men doing what Ezekiel’s shepherds did. Read John 10:1–21 straight through before you go further, and keep track of who is speaking and who is being spoken to.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE DOOR AND THE VOICE
paras: Jesus opens with a fold and two ways into it. One who doesn’t enter by the door into the sheep fold, but climbs up some other way, is a thief and a robber. The man who goes over the wall has no right to the sheep. He wants what they can give him — wool, meat, a living. The true shepherd has no wall to climb. The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, because the sheep are his.

Then comes a line to read slowly. He calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out. Not by number. By name. The Shepherd does not know you as a headcount or a line in the giving record. He knows the name your mother used and the one the crew uses, and He calls the one that is yours. Nor does He drive His sheep from behind with a stick. He goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice. He walks the ground first.

The sheep know His voice the way you know your father’s cough from the next room. And they know the other voices too. They will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him. That is not the cleverness of sheep. It is what the Shepherd’s voice does to them over time. A man who hears Christ in the Scripture morning after morning grows an ear. The stranger who sells pasture by the bottle, the screen, or the next deal starts to sound wrong.
Then John adds a hard note: they didn’t understand what he was telling them. Men who had just watched a blind man see still could not hear. Hearing the Shepherd is a gift before it is a habit.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: ONE DOOR, OPEN WIDE
paras: So Jesus says it again, plainer. I am the sheep’s door. Then He says it once more. I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved, and will go in and go out, and will find pasture. Mark both sides of that. There is one door. And the one door is open to anyone. The beggar thrown out in chapter 9 may come in. So may the Pharisee who threw him out, if he will come by the door and not over the wall.

The dust hates both the narrowness and the width. It tells the proud man there must be other ways in — his decency, his years in the pew, his family name. It tells the broken man that the one door is shut to him. Jesus answers both with the same four words: I am the door. You do not climb your way in by being good. You are not barred out by having been bad. You come in through Him, and He does not check your hands at the threshold.

Look at what is on the other side. Saved. Going in and going out — the easy coming and going of a sheep that belongs somewhere and is not afraid. Pasture. Then the contrast: The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly. Every voice that promised you grass behind Christ’s back has taken more than it gave. The second drink took your evening. The screen took your sleep. The money took your peace with your wife. The Shepherd came to give — life now, life in full measure, life that does not run thin by Thursday.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE SHEPHERD WHO STAYS
pulls: Jesus does not merely risk His life for the sheep. He lays it down by His own authority and takes it up again — and a Shepherd who has power over His own death is safe to follow past yours.
paras: Now the center of the chapter. I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. Jesus does not say He will risk His life. He says He lays it down. A shepherd in the hills might die fighting off a wolf, and the flock would scatter for it. This Shepherd dies on purpose, and His dying is the very thing that saves the flock. The cross is not where the wolf won. It is where the Shepherd paid.

Set Him beside the other man in the field. He who is a hired hand, and not a shepherd, who doesn’t own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. The hired hand is no villain. He simply has nothing at stake but his wage. When the cost of staying climbs past the pay, he goes. Jesus says why: he is a hired hand, and doesn’t care for the sheep.

You have known hired hands. You may have been one — at home, in the marriage, in the church where you sat in the back row and slipped out before the last song. Christ is not that. The sheep are His own, given to Him by the Father, and He will not walk off the hill when the wolf comes. I know my own, and I’m known by my own. Then He gives the measure of that knowing: even as the Father knows me, and I know the Father.

Sit with that. The way the Father and the Son know each other — fully, with no shadow between them — is the pattern of how Christ knows you. Then He says it a second time, so you cannot miss it: I lay down my life for the sheep.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: ONE FLOCK AND AN EMPTY GRAVE
paras: I have other sheep, which are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice. The fold Jesus stood in was Israel. The other sheep are men from outside it, scattered across the nations and down the centuries, and that is where you come in. Notice the must. Christ is not hoping to find a few. The Father has given Him sheep, and He will bring every one. They will become one flock with one shepherd.

Then He tells of the Father’s love toward His dying. Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again. The death is not the end of the sentence. He lays His life down, and He takes it back up — the tomb opened from the inside by the One who went into it. No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. The soldiers, the priests, the governor will each have a part, and none of them will take His life from Him. He will give it.

I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. That is what makes Him safe to follow. A shepherd who can be killed protects you as long as he lives. A Shepherd who holds authority over His own death protects you past yours.

The crowd splits again. Some say He has a demon. Others answer with the man from chapter 9: It isn’t possible for a demon to open the eyes of the blind, is it? The opened eyes are still standing in the street. You stand in that split too. The Shepherd is calling your name. Believe Him, and live.

stations.verse: Most certainly, I tell you, one who doesn’t enter by the door into the sheep fold, but climbs up some other way, is a thief and a robber.
stations.question: Jesus aimed His word about the thief who climbs up some other way at leaders who had just thrown a healed beggar out; whose voice have I let into my life that takes from me rather than giving me Christ?
stations.gloss: a thief; one who steals in secret, by fraud
body: Kleptēs is the plain word for a thief. Jesus sets it beside a second word, robber. The robber takes in the open, by force. The kleptēs takes in secret, by fraud and cunning. The word stands in sixteen verses of the New Testament, and outside this chapter John uses it only of Judas, who kept the money box and stole from it.

That is the thief Jesus warns you about. He does not kick in the door. He climbs in at night. The habit that started small. The second screen after the house goes dark. The way the money talks to you. None of them announced that they came to steal, kill, and destroy. They came offering grass.

The dust says nothing is being taken — you are only unwinding. Christ names the thief so you will stop calling him a friend, and then He stands in the gate Himself. The fold has a Shepherd. You are not left alone with the thief.
stations.live: Name one thing that has been taking from you in secret — sleep, money, your evenings, your wife’s trust. Write it down plainly. Then say over it: ‘You came to steal. Christ came that I may have life.’

stations.verse: The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out.
stations.question: The shepherd who comes in by the open gate calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out; what difference would it make on my worst morning this week to believe Christ calls me by name and not by my record?
stations.gloss: a doorkeeper; the one who guards the door
body: Thyrōros joins the word for a door to a word for a guardian: the doorkeeper, the porter. Mark uses it for the man left at the door to keep watch. John uses it again in chapter 18, at the high priest’s courtyard.

Hold John’s two scenes side by side. In chapter 10 the doorkeeper opens the gate for the true shepherd, because the shepherd has every right to the sheep. In chapter 18 the one who keeps the door asks Peter whether he is one of this man’s disciples, and Peter answers, I am not. One gate opened for Christ. Another gate where His own man denied Him.

The dust says you must guard your own way in and argue your case at the threshold. But the gate swung open for the Shepherd, and you come in behind Him. Peter came back in too. The risen Jesus restored him and told him, Tend my sheep.
stations.live: This week, start each prayer by naming whose right you stand on. Not your record and not your apology list. Say it plainly: ‘I am here because the gate opened for Christ, and I came in behind Him.’

stations.verse: I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved, and will go in and go out, and will find pasture.
stations.question: Jesus promised that the man who enters by Him will go in and go out, and will find pasture; where have I been looking for pasture outside the door He opened?
stations.gloss: pasture; a place of grazing and feeding
body: Nomē comes from a verb meaning to pasture. It names the pasture itself, and it names the act of grazing and feeding. It occurs in only two verses of the New Testament. Here it is the grass the sheep find when they come in and go out by the door.

The other use is a warning. Paul says that empty talk will consume like gangrene, and the word behind that spreading is nomē — a sore grazing outward through the flesh. One pasture feeds the sheep. The other feeds on the man. Every field you wander into either gives you life or eats it, and not one of them is neutral.

The dust says the grass is greener anywhere but by the door. Christ says the pasture is found through Him, and He is not stingy with it. The man who enters by Him will go in and go out, and will find pasture. The pasture is His gift, not your wage.
stations.live: Pick one hour this week you usually spend grazing — the late scroll, the noise on the drive home. Give it to one chapter of John read aloud. Tell yourself: ‘This is the pasture. I came in by the door.’

stations.verse: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
stations.question: Jesus showed what makes a shepherd good by a death, not a speech: He lays down his life for the sheep; which fear about my standing with God have I not yet set beside His cross?
stations.gloss: a shepherd; one who tends and feeds a flock
body: Poimēn is a shepherd, the man who tends a flock. It occurs in seventeen verses of the New Testament. Some are working men in a field — the shepherds near Bethlehem who heard the angel’s news. Several of the rest point to Christ. Paul uses it once of the pastors Christ gives His church.

Jesus does not call Himself a good manager of sheep. He calls Himself the good shepherd, and then He defines good: He lays down his life for the sheep. Hebrews calls Him the great shepherd of the sheep, brought again from the dead. Peter writes to men who were going astray like sheep and tells them they have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.

The dust says you are one head in a herd too big to notice. The Shepherd says He knows His own. He died for the sheep, rose for them, and still tends them — the one standing in your boots this morning included.
stations.live: Read Psalm 23 aloud once a day this week, slowly. When you reach the first line, add the name John gives Him: ‘Jesus is my shepherd. He laid down His life for me.’

stations.verse: He who is a hired hand, and not a shepherd, who doesn’t own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. The wolf snatches the sheep, and scatters them.
stations.question: The hired hand sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees because the sheep are not his; where at home have I stayed only while it paid, when Christ stayed for me at the cost of His life?
stations.gloss: hired; a hired servant who works for wages
body: Misthōtos comes from the verb to hire. It means a man working for wages, a hired servant. It appears in three New Testament verses. Two are here. The third is in Mark, where James and John leave their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and follow Jesus.

There is no shame in a wage. Most men reading this earn one. The trouble Jesus names is a wage with no love behind it. The hired hand doesn’t own the sheep, so when the wolf comes the math is simple, and he leaves. A man can treat his marriage that way, and his kids, and his God — staying while the pay is good.

The dust says Christ is one more hired hand, and you had better keep your exits open. But Christ owns the sheep. The Father gave them to Him, and He paid for them with His own life. He does not run. The One who stays is the One who paid.
stations.live: Name the place you have been working for wages only — putting in the hours and holding back your heart. Do one thing there this week that costs you and pays nothing back. Not to earn anything. Because He stayed.

practices.title: LEARN THE VOICE
practices.body: The sheep follow because they know the Shepherd’s voice, and they come to know it by hearing it. Read John 10:1–18 aloud every morning this week, before the phone and before the news. Do not study it to death. Listen to it the way you listen for a familiar truck in the drive. By Friday you will start to notice when another voice is talking, and how different it sounds from His.

practices.title: NAME THE THIEF
practices.body: The thief does not announce himself. He climbs in at night and takes a little at a time. Sit down one evening and write what has been leaving your house in secret — the hours, the money, the attention your kids used to get. Do not shame yourself over the list. Bring it to the Shepherd who came to give life, and ask Him plainly to put the thief out.

practices.title: COME IN BY THE DOOR
practices.body: Stop opening your prayers with a résumé or a list of apologies. Neither one is the door. Jesus said, I am the door. Begin every prayer this week by naming Him as your only way in: you come to the Father because Christ came for you. Notice what that does to the fear that usually sits on your chest when you pray. The door does not open wider on your good days or narrower on your bad ones.

practices.title: STAY WHEN IT COSTS
practices.body: The hired hand leaves when the price of staying climbs past the pay. Christ stayed, all the way to the cross. Find the conversation at home you have been walking away from — the money, the silence, the old hurt — and stay at the table for it this week. You are not earning His love by staying. You stay because He stayed for you, and because the wolf at your house is smaller than the One who already faced the real one.

practices.title: CALL ONE STRAY BY NAME
practices.body: The Shepherd calls his own sheep by name, and He says He has other sheep He must bring. Think of one man who has drifted out of the fold — a brother, an old friend, the guy who quit coming. Call him this week. Use his name. Do not preach. Tell him you noticed he was gone, that you have been thinking about him, and that the door is still open. Then leave the bringing in to the Shepherd.

title: The Good Shepherd
subtitle: from dust to the Shepherd who lays down His life
keyVerse: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

passage.text: “Most certainly, I tell you, one who doesn’t enter by the door into the sheep fold, but climbs up some other way, is a thief and a robber.
But one who enters in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.
The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out.
Whenever he brings out his own sheep, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice.
They will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him; for they don’t know the voice of strangers.”
Jesus spoke this parable to them, but they didn’t understand what he was telling them.
Jesus therefore said to them again, “Most certainly, I tell you, I am the sheep’s door.
All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep didn’t listen to them.
I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved, and will go in and go out, and will find pasture.
The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.
I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
He who is a hired hand, and not a shepherd, who doesn’t own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees. The wolf snatches the sheep, and scatters them.
The hired hand flees because he is a hired hand, and doesn’t care for the sheep.
I am the good shepherd. I know my own, and I’m known by my own;
even as the Father knows me, and I know the Father. I lay down my life for the sheep.
I have other sheep, which are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice. They will become one flock with one shepherd.
Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again.
No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.”
Therefore a division arose again among the Jews because of these words.
Many of them said, “He has a demon, and is insane! Why do you listen to him?”
Others said, “These are not the sayings of one possessed by a demon. It isn’t possible for a demon to open the eyes of the blind, is it?”

stationsIntro: Read each verse aloud, slowly, the way a man reads the terms on a deed to land he did not pay for. Then answer the question plainly, and let the Greek word turn you back to the Shepherd who stands behind the verse.
lifeIntro: Christ has done the work. He came in by the door, called His own by name, laid His life down for them, and took it up again. What follows is a man’s answer to that, worked out in five ordinary places this week. None of it buys a place in the fold. All of it is what a sheep does once he knows whose he is.
lifePulls: The thief takes in secret. The hired hand runs in the open. The good Shepherd walks toward the wolf. Everything you need for this week starts with knowing which voice is calling your name.
prayer: Father, You gave Your sheep to Your Son, and He laid down His life for them. Thank You that Jesus did not climb the wall to take from me; He came through the door to give me life. Thank You that He knows my name and goes ahead of me into this week. Teach my ear His voice in Your Word, and make the stranger’s voice sound wrong to me. Forgive me for the places I have worked like a hired hand, at home and before You. Show me what the thief has been taking in secret, and put him out of my house. Bring in the other sheep You have given Your Son, and make us one flock under one Shepherd. Keep me near the One who laid His life down and took it up again. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You gave Your sheep to Your Son, and He laid down His life for them.
Thank You that Jesus did not climb the wall to take from me; He came through
the door to give me life.
Thank You that He knows my name and goes ahead of me into this week.
Teach my ear His voice in Your Word, and make the stranger’s voice sound
wrong to me.
Forgive me for the places I have worked like a hired hand, at home and before
You.
Show me what the thief has been taking in secret, and put him out of my house.
Bring in the other sheep You have given Your Son, and make us one flock under
one Shepherd.
Keep me near the One who laid His life down and took it up again.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Jesus is the door and the good Shepherd. The thief climbs the wall to take. The hired hand runs when the wolf comes. Christ came in by the gate, calls His own sheep by name, goes ahead of them, and lays down His life for them by His own authority — then takes it up again. You are not a stray, and He is not hired help. Learn His voice. Come in by Him. Stay where He has put you.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the One who came in by the door. Lift them to the One who calls you by the name that is yours and not by your record. Lift them to the One who walks ahead of you up the hill, into the week you are dreading, and reaches every bend before you do. Lift them to the One who did not climb in to take, but came to give life, and to give it in full.

The dust has told you that every shepherd is a hired hand in the end. You have scars to back that up. Men who were paid to look after you looked after themselves when the cost came. The thief came in secret, the hired hand left in the open, and between them they taught you to keep your own gate and trust no one inside it. But hear Him say why He is different. The sheep are His own. The Father gave them to Him, and He does not weigh what it will cost to keep what His Father gave.

So look at the wolf, and then look at the Shepherd. He did not run from the cost. He walked into it. No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. On a hill near the city, He laid His life down for the sheep, by His own authority and under His Father’s command. And then, because He had power to take it again, He took it up. The grave could not hold the Shepherd, and so the grave will not keep His sheep.

That is what you carry into Tuesday. Not a feeling about Him, but a fact about Him. He knows your name. He knows the field you are standing in, and He has already walked it. He laid His life down for you, He has it again, and He is spending it now to lead you. When the wolf comes this week — the accusation, the fear, the old appetite — you are not alone in the field. The good Shepherd stands between you and it, and He has already shown you what He was willing to pay to keep you.
closingVerse: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
carry: If the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, and Jesus has done exactly that for you, which voice that has never laid anything down for you will you stop following this week?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men picture their hold on God like a man hanging from a rope over a drop. Faith is the grip. As long as your hands stay closed, you are safe. Every lost temper, every month away from the Word, every night you went back to the thing you swore off feels like a finger slipping. You lie awake doing the math on how many fingers you have left.

The dust loves that picture, because it puts everything on your hands, and your hands are dust. They shake. They tire. They let go of things they meant to keep. So the dust tells you that your standing with God is only as strong as your grip, and that your grip gets weaker every year. It points to the men who fell away and says their fingers gave out first, and yours are next.

Some mornings that is not a theory. It is how the floor feels under your feet when you get up. On those mornings the old psalm is not poetry. It is a report from the floor: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)

The word God sends to a man in that place does not tell him to grip harder. It tells him whose hand he is in. Jesus says it plainly, in winter, with stones about to fly: no one will snatch them out of my hand. The promise comes from the One who has just said He will lay down His life for the sheep, and who means to take it up again.

sections.heading: Winter at the Feast of Dedication
pulls: The dust says your safety with God is only as strong as your grip. Jesus says His sheep are held in two hands — His and His Father’s — and no one is able to pry either one open.
paras: John marks the time and place with care. It was the Feast of the Dedication at Jerusalem. Then, in the next breath, It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s porch. The feast kept the memory of a temple dedicated to God. Walking its porch is the One whose body is the true temple, and the men who keep the feast come around Him and press Him for an answer.

Since chapter 7 Jesus has been in Jerusalem, teaching in the temple and answered with arguments and stones. The men who press Him here are not worse than you. Every man has stood in that porch at some point, demanding that God prove Himself on his terms. In a few verses the stones come up once more, He slips out of their hand, and He goes back across the Jordan to the place where John the Baptist first pointed to Him. Read John 10:22–42 through in one sitting. Count the hands: the hands that pick up stones, the hands that reach to seize Him, and the two hands that hold His sheep.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: TELL US PLAINLY
paras: The men around Him want a straight word. How long will you hold us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly. It sounds like an honest request. Jesus does not treat it as one. I told you, and you don’t believe. He has told them in words, and He has told them in works — a lame man carrying his mat, five loaves feeding thousands, a beggar washing mud from his eyes and coming back seeing. The works that I do in my Father’s name, these testify about me. The trouble was never a lack of evidence. A man who will not come does not lack proof. He lacks a new heart, and only God gives that.

Then the hardest line in the passage: But you don’t believe, because you are not of my sheep. Read the order with care. Jesus does not say they are not His sheep because they do not believe. He says they do not believe because they are not His sheep. Belonging comes first. Believing is how belonging shows itself. A man is not made a sheep by mustering enough faith. He believes because the Father has given him to the Son, the same truth chapter 6 told: All those whom the Father gives me will come to me.

That line is not a door slammed in the face of any man who wants in. A few verses earlier Jesus said, If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved. The invitation stands wide open. What this line gives is a floor under the man who has already come. If you believe, it is because you were given, and what the Father gives the Son He does not take back.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: MY SHEEP HEAR
paras: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. Three short clauses, with Christ standing in the middle of them. They hear. He knows. They follow. His knowing does not wait on their following. He knew you before you took the first step, and He knows every step you got wrong since.

Then the gift. I give eternal life to them. Not a loan, and not a trial period. Eternal life is the life Jesus has been promising since the well and the pool, a life a man holds now and not only later: he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. A life that could end was never eternal to begin with.

They will never perish. Never is a long word. It covers the bad year and the relapse. It covers the funeral, and the morning you wake up and cannot feel a thing toward God. It covers the day you die. Jesus does not say they will rarely perish, or will not perish if they hold on. He says never, and the promise is His to keep.

Then: no one will snatch them out of my hand. Snatch is the word Jesus used of the wolf a few verses back — The wolf snatches the sheep, and scatters them. The wolf is real, and he still comes. But his jaws cannot open the Shepherd’s hand. Not Satan, not the accuser in your own head, not the man you used to be, not the man you are afraid of becoming. You may lose your grip on a hundred things this year. You will not slip out of His.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: TWO HANDS, ONE GOD
pulls: Your hand is dust, and dust shakes. His hands were pierced and raised again, and the Father’s hand closes around His. No one in heaven or on earth is able to open either one.
paras: Then Jesus closes a second hand around the first. My Father who has given them to me is greater than all. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand. The sheep were the Father’s gift to the Son. The Father who gave them is greater than all — greater than the wolf, greater than death, greater than your worst week. And mark the word able. Jesus does not say no one is permitted. He says no one is able.

Look at where your safety sits. It is not in your grip on Him. It is in His grip on you, and His Father’s grip around His. Your hand is dust, and dust shakes. His hands were pierced and raised again, and they do not shake. The Father’s hand is the hand Isaiah says calculated the dust of the earth in a measuring basket. He knows exactly how much dust you are, and He has not lost one grain He gave His Son. None of this is leave to stop caring how you live. A held sheep follows, as verse 27 said. You do not follow to stay in His hand. You follow because you are already there.

Then comes the sentence that brings out the stones. I and the Father are one. The two hands make one grip, because the Father and the Son are one God. Jesus is not a lesser keeper backing up the Father’s work. He is the Word who was with God, and who was God. That is why His hand is enough. A man’s hand can be pried open by a stronger man. No one is stronger than God.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: STONES AND THE FAR BANK
paras: Therefore Jews took up stones again to stone him. They understood Him well enough. We don’t stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy: because you, being a man, make yourself God. They had half of it right. He is a man. But He did not make Himself God. He is God, and He made Himself a man — The Word became flesh, and lived among us.

Jesus answers from their own Scriptures. Isn’t it written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods?’ If God’s word could call men by that name, how is it blasphemy for the One whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world to say I am the Son of God? And He lays down a line for every man who wonders whether the Bible will hold his weight: the Scripture can’t be broken. Even with stones in their hands, He offers them a way in: believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in the Father.

They sought again to seize him, and he went out of their hand. Their hands could not hold Him. His hand will not lose you. Then He crosses the Jordan to the place where John was baptizing at first. Out there men say the Baptist did no sign, but everything that John said about this man is true. The chapter ends quietly: Many believed in him there. The plain word the leaders demanded was spoken, and it was believed by men across the river who simply listened. That is still how it goes. Men who will not hear keep arguing. Men who are given ears believe.

stations.verse: It was the Feast of the Dedication at Jerusalem.
stations.question: At the feast that remembered the temple’s dedication, Jesus walked its porch as the One whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world; where am I still trying to make myself fit for God’s house instead of coming in through Him?
stations.gloss: dedication; the feast of the temple’s dedication
body: Enkainia means dedication. In the Greek Old Testament it names the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah’s day. In the New Testament it stands in this verse alone, naming the feast that kept the memory of the temple cleansed after it had been defiled.

So Jesus walks in the temple at the feast of its dedication. In chapter 2 He had told the leaders, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up, and John explained that he spoke of the temple of his body. The One walking its porch is the true dwelling of God with men, and He is about to be torn down and raised again.

The dust says you must scrub yourself and dedicate yourself before God will let you in. But Christ is the One whom the Father sanctified and sent, set apart so that dirty men could be made clean in Him. You do not dedicate your way into God’s house. He brings you in.
stations.live: Name the thing you think you must clean up before you can come near God again. Bring it to Him as it is this week, and say: ‘Christ is the clean house of God, and I come in through Him.’

stations.verse: It was the Feast of the Dedication at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s porch.
stations.question: In winter, men circled Jesus in Solomon’s porch and demanded a plain answer He had already given in word and work; what plain word of His am I still asking Him to repeat before I will rest on it?
stations.gloss: winter; a winter storm, a tempest
body: Cheimōn means winter, the cold season. It can also mean a winter storm, a tempest. In Acts it names the weather that battered Paul’s ship when no small storm pressed on us. It occurs in six New Testament verses, and in one of them Paul asks Timothy to come before winter.

John does not waste words, and still he tells you it was winter. The cold is part of the story. Men stood under a covered porch in the chill season and argued with the Son of God. And He was there, walking among them, in the months when nothing grows in the field.

The dust says the cold months prove God has stepped away. But John puts the Shepherd in the winter, in the porch, and has Him speak the clearest promise in the chapter there: They will never perish. Winter did not keep Him away from His sheep. It will not keep Him away from you.
stations.live: Name your winter — the slow season at work, the cold house, the grief that will not lift. Each morning this week say it out loud: ‘It is winter, and Jesus is walking here. No one will snatch me out of His hand.’

stations.verse: I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.
stations.question: Jesus says of His sheep, They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand; what changes on the night my faith feels thin when I measure my safety by His grip instead of mine?
stations.gloss: the hand; by extension, a person’s power
body: Cheir is the hand, and it occurs in 168 verses of the New Testament. Often it is simply a hand reached out to heal, to lift, to touch. But the word also stands for a person’s power, what he can do and hold. Used of God, it names His own power at work.

John uses it on both sides of this passage. In verse 28 the sheep are in the Son’s hand. In verse 29 they are in the Father’s. In verse 39 the men who came to seize Jesus find that he went out of their hand. Their hands could not keep Him. His will not lose you. John told you why: The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.

The dust says your safety rests on your grip. Cheir moves the weight off you. You are held by the power of the Son and the power of the Father, and the Son’s hands carry the marks Thomas was told to touch.
stations.live: When you wake in the night this week doing the math on your own faithfulness, open your hand on the blanket and say: ‘I am not holding Him up. He is holding me, and so is His Father.’

stations.verse: Therefore Jews took up stones again to stone him.
stations.question: The men in the porch picked up stones the moment Jesus said I and the Father are one; which of His claims on me do I push back on hardest when it comes close to my own life?
stations.gloss: to stone; to pelt with stones
body: Lithazō means to stone, to throw stones at someone, to pelt him. It appears in eight New Testament verses. Four of them are in John, and every one is aimed at Jesus. The others include Paul, who could write, Once I was stoned, and the faithful of old who were stoned for their faith.

Stones are what men pick up when they have run out of answers. Jesus asks, For which of those works do you stone me? He had healed, fed, and opened blind eyes. They had nothing to charge Him with except who He said He was. A man can do the same with his temper, reaching for a stone when the truth comes too close.

The dust says the stones always win. They did not win here. He walked out of their hand, and when His hour came He went to a death no mob could force on Him, laid down by His own authority. The stones settled nothing. His cross settled everything.
stations.live: Find the stone you keep ready — the cutting word for your wife, your son, or the man on the next crew. Set it down before you speak this week. Say: ‘Christ answered stones with good works. I can answer with one too.’

stations.verse: The Jews answered him, “We don’t stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy: because you, being a man, make yourself God.
stations.question: The stones came up because Jesus, being a man, claimed to be God; where have I quietly treated Him as only a good teacher, so that His claim on my life feels lighter?
body: Blasphēmia is railing speech, slander. It can be aimed at men, and Paul tells the church to put slander away along with bitterness and anger. Its sharper use is speech against God Himself.

Again and again in the Gospels the charge lands on Jesus because He does what only God may do. When He forgave a paralyzed man, the scribes asked, Who can forgive sins, but God alone? At His trial the council heard the charge and condemned him to be worthy of death. Here the stones come up for the same reason: you, being a man, make yourself God.

Their logic was sound and their verdict wrong. If He were only a man, it would be blasphemy. He is God the Son made flesh. The dust would rather have a Jesus who is only a good man, because a good man cannot forgive you or hold you. The One they called a blasphemer does both.
stations.live: Read John 10:30 and 10:33 together each morning this week. Then say plainly what the stone-throwers would not: ‘Jesus is God, and He became a man for me. His hand is God’s hand.’

practices.title: LET HIS VOICE SPEAK FIRST
practices.body: His sheep hear His voice before they do anything else. Each morning this week read John 10:27–30 aloud before you check the weather, the news, or your own account of yesterday. Let Him speak first about who you are. Your own voice will have plenty to say later. It does not get the opening word, and it never gets the last one. When your mind runs to the day’s list, bring it back to verse 28 and read it again, slowly.

practices.title: FALL INTO HIS HAND
practices.body: When you fail this week — and you will — do not answer the failure by clenching harder in a panic. Tell God what you did, plainly, without dressing it up. Then say John 10:28 out loud, word for word. Then get up and go back to work, at the bench, in the cab, wherever the failure found you. A held man confesses quickly because he is not afraid of being dropped. Shame tells you to hide until you feel worthy again. The Shepherd never held you because you were worthy.

practices.title: KEEP WALKING IN THE WINTER
practices.body: Jesus walked the porch in winter. If you are in a cold stretch, do not wait for warm weather to keep the ordinary things. Sit with God’s people on the Lord’s Day. Read the passage at the table. Pray the short prayer at the end of the day. Show up cold if you must. Those plain means are where the Shepherd has promised to be found, cold month or not. Winter is not proof that He has left the porch.

practices.title: PUT DOWN THE STONE
practices.body: The men in the porch reached for stones when they could not answer Him. Find the place where you reach for one — the sharp word, the slammed door, the silence that punishes. This week, go back to one person you have stoned with your tongue and own it in plain words. Do not explain or defend yourself. Name what you did and stop. Christ did not throw stones at you. He took the cross for you.

practices.title: COUNT THE WORKS
practices.body: Jesus told His accusers, believe the works. Write down the works John has shown you in these chapters: the loaves, the mercy to the woman, the light, the opened eyes, the Shepherd laying down His life. Add one work He has done in your own house. Keep the list in your wallet or lunch pail. When doubt comes, read it before you argue with it. The works testify, and they testify about Him.

title: No One Will Snatch Them
subtitle: from dust to hands that never let go
keyVerse: I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.

passage.text: It was the Feast of the Dedication at Jerusalem.
It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s porch.
The Jews therefore came around him and said to him, “How long will you hold us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.”
Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you don’t believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name, these testify about me.
But you don’t believe, because you are not of my sheep, as I told you.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.
I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.
My Father who has given them to me is greater than all. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand.
I and the Father are one.”
Therefore Jews took up stones again to stone him.
Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of those works do you stone me?”
The Jews answered him, “We don’t stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy: because you, being a man, make yourself God.”
Jesus answered them, “Isn’t it written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods?’
If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came (and the Scripture can’t be broken),
do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God?’
If I don’t do the works of my Father, don’t believe me.
But if I do them, though you don’t believe me, believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in the Father.”
They sought again to seize him, and he went out of their hand.
He went away again beyond the Jordan into the place where John was baptizing at first, and he stayed there.
Many came to him. They said, “John indeed did no sign, but everything that John said about this man is true.”
Many believed in him there.

stationsIntro: These five words carry you from a winter feast to a pile of stones and into the hands that hold the sheep. Read each verse, answer the question without dressing it up, and let the Greek word press home what the verse has already said.
lifeIntro: The Father gave you to the Son. The Son gives you eternal life and holds you in His hand, and the Father’s hand closes around His. These five practices are a held man learning to live like one. None of them keeps you in His hand. He does that. They are what a man does with his hands once he knows they are not the ones holding on.
lifePulls: You were never asked to hold yourself in the fold. The Son holds you, the Father holds the Son’s sheep, and the two are one. Your grip will shake this week. Theirs will not.
prayer: Father, You gave me to Your Son, and You are greater than all. Thank You that Jesus gives eternal life and says I will never perish. Thank You that my safety does not rest on my grip but on His hand and Yours. When my faith feels thin this winter, let me hear His voice again. Forgive me for the stones I keep ready, and for every way I have made Jesus smaller than He is. Keep us from the wolf, and keep us in Your hand when we cannot keep ourselves. Thank You that the Father’s hand closes over the Son’s, and that no one is able to open it. Make me a man who hears, follows, and rests in being held. In Jesus’ name, amen.

bottomLine: In winter, at the Feast of Dedication, men demanded a plain answer, and Jesus gave one. His sheep hear His voice, He knows them, they follow Him, and He gives them eternal life. They will never perish. No one will snatch them out of His hand or His Father’s, and He and the Father are one. Your safety does not rest on your grip. It rests on two hands that do not shake.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and look at the hands. Look at the hands that took five loaves on a hillside and fed thousands. Look at the hands that stooped and wrote on the ground while the stones waited. Look at the hands that spat in the dirt, made mud, and pressed it on a blind man’s eyes. Look at the hands that were pierced for the sheep and shown to Thomas, still marked, after the grave was empty. Those are the hands that hold you.

Through these five chapters John has set Him before you again and again. The bread from heaven that does not run out. The One with the words of eternal life when everyone else was walking away. Rivers of living water. Neither do I condemn you, spoken to a woman while the stones were still in the crowd’s hands. The light of the world. The Son who makes you free indeed. The clay, the pool, and a beggar saying though I was blind, now I see. The Shepherd who lays down His life. It is one Christ, and every one of those gifts is in His hand.

Now it is winter, and the stones are coming up again. The men in Solomon’s porch wanted Him to speak plainly, and He did. What He said plainly was for His sheep: I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. Then He closed a second hand around the first: No one is able to snatch them out of my Father’s hand. The stone-throwers could not hold Him, and their stones did not reach Him. No hand in heaven or on earth is strong enough to pry open the grip of the Father and the Son, who are one.

So carry that into Tuesday, when your grip is weak and the cold has settled in. You did not put yourself into His hand, and you are not the one keeping yourself there. The Father gave you. The Son holds you. The Father’s hand closes over the Son’s. Next John will take you to Bethany, to a tomb four days shut and a Man who says, I am the resurrection and the life. Before you go, rest here: you will never perish, because no one is able to snatch you out of the Father’s hand.
closingVerse: I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.
carry: Jesus told men with stones in reach, I give eternal life to them. They will never perish; when your grip on God feels weakest this week, what will it mean to rest your weight on His hand instead of your own?
